chapters.title: The Blank on the Dial
chapters.html:
The radio on the cigar counter in the Selkirk lobby said General Eisenhower had carried thirty-nine states and Governor Stevenson had conceded in the night. The man behind the counter was sorting pipe cleaners by length and gave the news the attention you give a stranger’s cough. A landslide, the announcer said, and then said it again, as if the word might not hold the first time.

The elevator wore a card tied to its gate with string. I took the stairs, fifty-two of them counting the half-landings, and I do count the half-landings. On the third floor somebody had tacked a pink paper to the frosted glass of 309, square across the gilt of my name, so that the door now read PRIVATE INQUIRIES and, above that, PAY OR QUIT. The Selkirk’s bad news used to come on white. I decided the pink was a courtesy.

Eighty-four dollars, it said, two months at forty-two. I had eleven dollars and forty cents, which I knew to the penny, having counted it on the kitchen table at six and again on the Number 14 streetcar in case it had changed.

There was a man on the bench across the hall, and he had been there long enough to leave a small lake under it. He was small himself, and stooped, past fifty, with white eyebrows that stood off his forehead like the wings of a moth. Under an open raincoat he wore the maroon jacket of a hotel, a brass nameplate on the breast: T. WOZNIAK. He held his hat by the brim in both hands and turned it a quarter inch at a time, and every time it drifted off true he turned it back. I look at hands first, and shoes. His hands were small and tidy, the nails cut square. His shoes were black, thick in the sole, made for standing, and wet to the laces.

“Miss Szymanski?” He rose. I looked down at the parting in his hair, which had been combed with water and then rained on.

“That’s the name under the pink,” I said.

“Forgive me. I was told that you open at eight.”

“I open when I get here.” I peeled the notice off the glass with my thumbnail, folded it in four and put it in my coat pocket. “Come in out of the wet, Mr. Wozniak.”

Room 309 holds a desk, two chairs, a filing cabinet with a typewriter case on top of it, and a window onto Cutter Street with rain running down the glass and a dark stain on the sill where some of it got in. The radiator knocked three times and stopped. I hung up my hat, lit the first of the six Luckies I allow myself in a day, which was early for it, and sat. He would not sit until I had. Then he perched on the front of the client’s chair with the hat on his knees.

“If I may,” he said, “I will tell it in order. It is the only way I am sure of it. But I must say the worst first, or you will think I am coming to it slowly on purpose.”

“Say the worst.”

“Last night, Miss Szymanski, I found a dead man on the ninth floor of the Harbor Hotel.”

“Say again.”

“On the ninth floor.”

“The Harbor’s got eight. I’ve walked under it all my life.”

“Yes.” A gold tooth showed, top left, in an apology. “That is what Mr. Quill says also.”

I took the pink notice out of my pocket and turned it over. It was the only paper in the office I owed money on, and the back of it was clean. “Smaller pieces,” I said. “Who are you, and who is Mr. Quill?”

“I am the night clerk. Eleven to seven, thirteen years at the desk and twenty-one in the building. I began as a bellhop. Mr. Quill is the resident auditor. He keeps a room on the eighth floor and speaks for the Estate that owns us. A gentleman.” The hat went another quarter turn. “Last night was the Councilman’s party for the election, in the Pacific Room. A great many men who were very happy. At ten minutes to one, the guest car stopped answering the buttons.”

“Stopped.”

“People pressed, and the lamps lit, and nothing came. I telephoned the basement and spoke to Lambert, the porter. He said the car was sulking and would come down when she was ready.”

“She.”

“Lambert has run her twenty-two years. He says she has moods. The few guests still about took the service lift, which is slow and smells of linen. Most were not in a condition to mind.” He drew a breath through his nose. “At ten minutes past two I looked across the lobby at the dial above the lift doors. One can see it from the desk.” He held up two fingers an inch apart. “A half circle of brass, and a needle, and the numerals one to eight. Beyond the eight there is a stop with no numeral. The needle was sitting on it.”

“Past the eight.”

“On the blank.”

“What did the lobby clock say?”

“The lobby clock runs three minutes slow. I allow for it. Ten past two.” He saw me look at him. “Everyone in the building allows for it. It is the one clock we trust, because it is wrong by a known amount.”

I wrote that on the back of the notice, with the times. “And at ten past four?”

“The same. Two hours exactly. I am a man who counts the keys at night, Miss Szymanski. I am not a man who dreams.” He did not smile at himself. “At ten past four I turned my key at the lobby panel and the car came down, and I rode up.”

“How many buttons in the car?”

“Eight. L, and two through eight.”

“Then how did you get to nine?”

His hand went toward his waistcoat and stopped. Something small and made of tin rattled in the pocket, a dry sound, seeds in a pod, and the hand came away empty. “There is a key.”

“Whose?”

“Forgive me.”

“What does it turn?”

“Forgive me,” he said again, gently, as if I had asked to borrow something he had already promised away.

In the wire room I learned that a caller who won’t give you the address will give you everything round it if you leave the line open. I left it open. “Go on. The doors open.”

“On a corridor, very low. Then a long room at the end of it, with a ceiling a tall man could touch with the flat of his hand. I carried the flashlight from the desk drawer. There was a man on a cot against the wall, on his back, in his stocking feet. I looked for his shoes. I do not know why. His left sock had a hole in the heel, and the heel was very white.” The hat made a half turn. “A man’s heel is a private thing. I looked at it longer than I looked at his face.”

“Dead.”

“I am not a doctor. I touched his wrist. Beside the cot was a card table, and on the table two glasses. Tumblers. Empty.”

“Two.”

“Two.”

I wrote 2, and went over it until the pen nearly went through the paper. “Then what?”

“I went down and telephoned Mr. Quill, as one does for a death in the house. He said to wait at the desk, and I waited. A little before six the police came, and they did not go to nine. They went to 807, where a guest named Delaney, of Portland, dried fruit, had been registered since Friday, and he was there on the bed with his shoes on and the spread across his legs. A doctor’s man said it was the heart.”

“The same man.”

“I checked him in myself. I would know him anywhere.” He studied the brim of the hat. “Afterwards Mr. Quill took me into the office behind the desk and gave me tea. Very kindly, and I believe he meant it kindly, he said the party had run until two, that there had been a good deal of noise and a good deal of rye, and that a man who has been on his feet for thirty hours sees things.” The gold tooth again, and again not a smile. “I have been on my feet longer without once seeing a dead man.”

The radiator knocked. I let my cigarette burn down an inch. “There are a dozen men on Cutter Street who’d take a job like this one, Mr. Wozniak. Most of them own better hats than mine. Why did you climb my stairs?”

From inside the raincoat he took a folded square of green blotting paper, opened it on my desk and squared it to the edge. His hands did that without consulting him. “This was the top sheet of the blotter at the desk. Mr. Delaney wrote on it on Monday night, while I was making up the keys. In pencil.”

I turned it round. A night blotter keeps a week of other people’s signatures, backwards and doubled, but the pencil stood clear of them in a clerk’s neat hand with the sevens crossed. Ruth Szymanski. Selkirk Bldg., Cutter & Second. Rm. 309.

“He said that you used to be on the police wire,” Wozniak said. “He said that you were honest.”

I looked at the typewriter case on the filing cabinet, which is what I do when anyone uses that word. “I never heard of a Delaney.”

“He was a very quiet guest.”

“Dried fruit,” I said.

“So he said.”

My fee is fifteen dollars a day and expenses, and I told him so. He took a flat leather purse from his jacket, counted out a ten and two fives and squared them to the blotter. It was more than half of what a night clerk makes in a week, and I took it, which tells you what was in my pocket.

“Go home and sleep,” I said. “I’ll come to the Harbor.”

“I cannot sleep. I will go back to the hotel. I have to stay near the cab.”

“It’s a box on a rope.”

“Yes,” he said. “But I would like to be near it, if I may.” He put on the hat. On the stairs he took the steps one at a time, like a man who has been warned about a loose one, and the tin in his pocket rattled all the way down.

The telephone in 309 is on a party line with a dentist and a woman who sells corsets by appointment, and both of them listen. I walked along Cutter to the drugstore and shut myself in the booth, which had a folding door that would not fold and a seat that would if you sat on it. I gave the operator Central Station, Detective Bureau, and heard the clicks go through, a sound I had spent nine years at the other end of.

“Dolan.”

“It’s Ruth.”

“I know who it is. You breathe like a woman counting.” A wooden matchstick moved from one side of his mouth to the other. I could hear it against his teeth.

“Somebody died at the Harbor Hotel last night.”

“Natural,” Dolan said. “Heart. Room 807, where else would a man die in a hotel, Ruth?” He said it like a man repeating something he had already said once that morning.

“Who was he?”

“A guest. Out of town. I got the call at twenty past five and haven’t sat down since, and Ostrander’s man looked at him and signed. Heart, and a skinful. What’s your interest?”

“Habit.”

“Then break it. Go and find somebody’s husband, Ruthie. They’ve all been up to something since the election.”

The line went to a dial tone. I stood holding the receiver. Frank Dolan had been the voice in my headset for eight years before I ever saw his face. He had signed my application for a licence in 1949, and we had not talked about why. I had thirty-one dollars and forty cents in my pocket, a night clerk’s twenty of it, and I had not told him about the needle, or the stocking feet, or the two glasses. It was a small thing to hold back. It came so easily that I noticed it.

From Cutter to Front the street runs downhill, and the rain came down it with me. A Number 14 swayed past toward the Flats with its windows steamed white. The air smelled of tar, diesel and the fish market, which on a wet day you can taste before you reach it.

The Harbor Hotel stands at the corner of Front and Ferry Slip Row, brick below and buff terracotta above, the colour of a boiled crab. I crossed to the water side, where the kerb is low and a bollard gives a woman something to stand beside, and I counted the way I used to count calls on the board, with a finger, under my breath. The lobby’s tall windows, one. Two. Three. Rain went down my collar. Four, five, six, seven. Eight. Eight rows, curtains drawn on most, and above the eighth the cornice that the hotel’s postcards call the Frieze: waves in terracotta with fish swimming between them, and over the waves a band of vents, louvred, slatted, painted black, like the gills of something very large. By eye I put it at fourteen feet. A storey is ten, and this was a storey and a bit. I had walked under it three thousand times. Nobody looks at the part of a building that is only there to finish it.

“Eight,” I said aloud. Mr. Quill said so, and the city directory, and everyone in Port Calder who had ever looked up at the Harbor in the rain.

I started over, with my finger at the lobby windows, and this time when I reached the top row I did not stop. I went up through the waves and the fish and the black slats, and the number I got was nine.

Out on Calder Point the Heifer gave its first moan of the day, two notes, the second lower than the first. Somebody out there had decided the rain was thick enough to count as fog. I stood on the kerb with the water running off my hat brim and counted forty to see whether it would come again. It did.

chapters.title: Paint on the Brass
chapters.html:
A man in a grey porter’s coat was vacuuming confetti off the lobby floor of the Harbor Hotel, and he was losing. The confetti came in red, white and blue discs the size of dimes, and for every one that went up the hose another showed itself in the grout between the black marble squares and the white. Over his head a banner hung across the doors of the Pacific Room. PLUM FOR THE PEOPLE, it said, in red felt, except that the last E had lost its pin and swung by one corner, which left the people to PEOPL. Beneath it an arch of balloons had gone soft at the shoulders and shrunk to prunes, which I took for editorial comment.

The lobby clock said twenty-seven minutes past ten. My father’s Waltham, which I wear with the face on the inside of my wrist, said half past, and I believed the Waltham. The clock has run three minutes slow since before the war, and the staff, as far as I could tell, kept time by it and arrived at everything three minutes late with perfect confidence.

The place smelled of floor wax and wet wool and a night’s worth of cigars, and under that, from the direction of the lift, of something sharp and sweet that I put down to the hotel putting its face on after the party. The lift stood across from the desk with its doors shut. Beside the call button was a brass plate the size of a silver dollar, bored through for a keyhole, and over the hole one word, SERVICE, in gilt worn down to a rumour. I looked at it longer than a plate deserves. A man had told me that morning that he turned a key at the lobby panel, and here was the panel.

“Mind the hose, miss.” The porter had switched off his machine to let me by. “They threw it by the bucket. Eisenhower’s welcome to the country, but I’ve got the lobby.”

Behind the brass rail the day clerk worked a wad of spearmint with the whole lower half of her face. She was twenty or so, in a maroon jacket cut for a bigger girl, with nails painted fire-engine red and bitten to the quick underneath. The nameplate said D. NASH. I laid a card on the desk and she read it upside down, and then the right way up.

“I’m a friend of Mr. Wozniak’s,” I said. “I’d like a word with him, or with whoever he answers to.”

“Mr. Wozniak’s off. He goes off at seven.” The gum went round once. “He’s a lovely man for a shift.”

“Was he himself when you came on?”

“He’s a lovely man for a shift.”

“Say again,” I said.

“A lovely man for a shift.” Behind me the vacuum started up and swallowed my next two questions whole, and she answered them anyway, in the same words, a note higher. I admired it. I spent nine years at the end of a telephone listening to callers try tears, rage, the wrong address and a dead mother, and nobody had ever refused me as thoroughly as a girl with spearmint.

“Mr. Quill says anybody who asks about last night goes to Mr. Quill,” she said at last, all in a rush, and lifted the house telephone. “It isn’t about you. It’s anybody.”

“Who’s Mr. Quill?”

“The auditor. He lives here.” She said it the way you’d mention that the building had a roof. Into the receiver she said that there was a lady about last night. She listened and hung up. “He says come through, and mind the step.”

The office behind the desk had been a cloakroom once and still had the hooks, which now held a brown umbrella and a calendar from a marine insurer. There was a roll-top desk, a green-shaded lamp, a gas fire, and a wall of ledgers in black cloth with their years painted down the spines in white. Over the fire hung an architect’s elevation of the hotel in pen and wash: eight rows of windows under a deep cornice, and a pennant on the roof that nobody had flown since. A tea tray stood on the blotter. The cups were thin enough to read a newspaper through.

The man behind the desk rose when I came in, which men don’t, and I noticed that before I noticed him. He was tall and narrow, with silver hair parted so exactly down the middle that the two halves of his head might have been issued separately. Charcoal suit, a collar high enough to disagree with the decade, pale blue eyes, and long hands the yellow-white of old piano keys. With the right one he drew an ebony stick off the edge of the desk, a silver collar at its head, and hooked it over his left forearm the way a waiter carries a napkin.

“Miss Szymanski. Ambrose Quill. Please.” He cleared his throat, twice, a dry little double click like a man knocking at his own door. I wrote it down in the place where I keep such things. “You will take tea. It is the one thing in the building at this hour that I can vouch for.”

It tasted of tarred rope, and I liked it, which I wrote down as well.

“I take it Mr. Wozniak sent you,” Quill said, pouring. The tea made no sound at all. “No, don’t trouble to deny it. He is not a man who can leave a building without telling somebody where he is going, and he left this one at a quarter to eight with a wet hat and the face of a man carrying a full cup.”

“He asked me to listen to something he saw.”

“Yes.” Click, click. “I should like to say a word about Teddy before we come to what he saw. He has been in this house twenty-one years. I would trust him with my watch, my cheque book and my sister, had I a sister. I want that said first, because the rest will sound unkind, and is not.”

“Say the rest.”

“He has been on his feet thirty hours, my dear. A Councilman’s victory is a labour in itself, and a man at the end of one sees things. At thirty hours I once saw my mother standing in the Pacific Room, and she has lain in a Dorset churchyard since 1923.” He turned a cup toward me by its saucer. “Teddy believes he rode up to a ninth floor. There isn’t one. The Harbor has eight, as the plans, the licence and the Board of Underwriters will tell you. I would offer you the plans, but they are dull. The elevation is over the fire, and you are welcome to count.”

I counted. It’s what I do. Eight rows of windows, and above them the cornice, drawn deep in terracotta wash with fish swimming in it; the architect had been proud of his fish. The cornice took up a fifth of the paper. I said nothing about that.

“He didn’t tell me he thought he saw a floor,” I said. “He said he rode up and found a man on a cot.”

“Did he.” Click, click. “Then he has told you in more detail than he told me. At ten past four he telephoned my room in some confusion, and I told him, quite firmly, I think, to wait for me at the desk. A little after five Lambert took the early papers up and found the unfortunate gentleman in 807, and sent for me, and I for the police. There was nothing in it that would trouble a coroner, and nothing did.”

“Who was he?”

“A Mr. Delaney, of Portland. Dried fruit. He took the room on Friday.” Quill spread his long hands. “I should be lying if I said I knew him. A guest is a hat and a coat to me, my dear. Teddy sees faces. I see the column the cheque goes in.”

“And Tuesday night? Where were you?”

“Looking in on the Councilman’s party for an hour, and retiring a little before midnight. Victory is a young man’s exercise.”

“Retiring where?”

“Eight, at the quiet end. I have kept a room in this house since 1938, which makes me its longest-serving guest and its smallest expense.”

“I’d like to see the car,” I said. “And the room.”

“My dear Miss Szymanski, you may see whatever you like. Nothing in this building is locked to anyone who asks. It is the whole art of hospitality.” He took a buff card from a drawer, and from a squat glass well of ink so dark it looked like a hole in the blotter he filled a steel pen and wrote. The line went on green-black. By the time he had blotted it the strokes were browning at the edges, and as I watched they went brown all through, the brown of old blood on a bandage. VISITOR, the card said. Miss R. Szymanski. Wed. 5 Nov. And under that, A. Quill, in a hand that ran uphill.

“Your ink changes its mind,” I said.

“It has never been decisive.” He blew across the card and gave it to me by its edge. “Lambert will take you up. He is the one man alive whom the car trusts.”

Dorrie Nash’s head came round the door to say that Lambert was at the lift. Quill’s stick came off his arm and tapped the carpet twice, briskly, like a man putting on a hat for a photograph; when her head went away, the stick was back across his forearm as if it had never left. I had seen what I had seen. The tip in the second it touched the floor was as clean as a new pencil eraser. I noticed it the way you notice a stranger’s good shoes, and put it in the drawer where I keep things that have no use yet.

Lambert waited at the lift with his cap against his chest, a short man, bowed at the shoulders, in porter’s grey. I looked at his hands. They were scarred white across the knuckles by old cab rope, with grease worked into the creases where soap had given up years ago. His shoes were big and black and cracked at the toe, and blacked over the cracks. A black shoelace went round the back of his neck and down inside his collar. Some men wear a saint there. I didn’t ask.

“Eight, Miss,” he said, not as a question, and pressed the call button. The doors slid back.

The cab was oak veneer and brass, polished by someone who did it every morning at the same hour. The eight buttons ran in a row across a cream-painted panel beside the door, L, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, each stamped in its brass ring. Over the door a brass arc repeated the numerals along a curve, with a needle hung beneath it on a pivot. Past the 8 the arc ran on another inch and a half to a tick with no number at all. Nothing on the panel led to that tick. The sharp sweet smell was stronger in here, and I filed that too.

Lambert pressed the 8. The doors closed and he began to hum through his nose, slowly, “Abide with Me,” with the patience of a man keeping a machine company. The floor pressed up through my shoes. One, I counted. Two.

“Mr. Quill says you found the gentleman in 807.”

“Yes, Miss. A little after five.”

The humming had stopped. I have taken a good many calls from people who saw the same thing. When two of them give you the same sentence, down to the “little after,” it isn’t corroboration. It’s rehearsal. Lambert’s eyes stayed on the dial and his hands hung in front of him, one holding the other, the way hands do in church.

A framed card hung on the back wall of the cab at eye level, its glass dulled by the thumbs of people reading it. CERTIFICATE OF INSPECTION, it said, STATE DIVISION OF ELEVATORS, No. 4471. Passenger, traction, Otis. Capacity 2,500 lbs. I read it as I used to read a log, top to bottom and then the part someone has typed in. Landings served: 9. And under it, on a line of its own, in the same black ribbon: Floors open to public: 8. A signature at the foot, H. Pomeroy, Inspector, and a date in March. Twenty-two, I counted. Twenty-three.

“Landings served, nine,” I said. “Floors open to public, eight.”

“The fellow in 807 read that, Monday.” Lambert said it to the dial. “Stood where you’re standing. Read it a good minute, like a letter from home. Then he laughed, and said it was the only honest thing in the building.”

“Did you ask him what he meant?”

“No, Miss. A porter’s not asked what a guest means. He’s asked for the floor.”

At thirty-eight the needle crept round the arc and settled on the 8 a hair short of the mark, as if it had considered going on. The doors opened.

The corridor was oxblood carpet and brass numbers, with a window at the far end gone small with distance. Lambert said that he would hold her, that 807 was on the left, and that Miss Hightower was in there.

“Is that good or bad?”

“It’s Miss Hightower, Miss,” Lambert said, which was an answer.

A linen cart stood outside 807 with a green chenille spread folded on top of it. The room was what four-fifty a night buys: a double bed, a walnut dresser, one window on Ferry Slip Row, a radiator ticking as it cooled. The police had taken the man and his things, and what remained was a mattress in striped ticking and two women taking the rest of the bed apart. The smaller was a girl with her hair in a net, who tucked a pillow under her chin with the stillness of someone listening to a thing she has been told she didn’t hear. The other was tall and upright, in a grey frock with a white collar, gold spectacles on a chain, and on her hip a ring of keys, forty or so, gripped in her left hand against her thigh so they couldn’t speak. I started to count them and she shifted her grip. Not one chimed. Her shoes were black, laced, and resoled by someone careful.

“This room is not available,” she said, without turning round.

“I’m not renting it. Mr. Quill gave me a card.”

She took it by one corner, read the front, turned it over and read the blank back, and returned it the same way, as though the ink might still be wet. “That is Mr. Quill’s hand. I am Hightower. Housekeeping.”

“I’m told a man died in here.”

“A guest was taken ill in this room. I have it to turn by two.”

“Were you here when they found him?”

“I was sent for at a quarter past six, to see that the room was fit for the police. I am sent for.” She shook out a sheet.

“What did you see?”

“A bed.” She folded the sheet, corner to corner. “Twenty-six years I have made the beds in this hotel, Miss Szymanski, since the week it opened, and I tell every girl who comes to me the same thing. A person who dies on a bed leaves a dent in it. The dead are heavier than the living; they do not hold themselves up. There was no dent in that spread. It was drawn smooth, and he lay on it like a folded sheet.” She set the sheet on the cart and squared its edge. “He had been laid there.”

“Laid there by whom?”

“I do not guess, Miss Szymanski. I make beds.” She did not raise her voice. She shut the subject like a drawer, and I heard the runners go. “Kasia, the other pillow.”

“I’d like to see the corridor,” I said.

“It is a corridor.”

“I have a card.”

Pearl Hightower looked at the card in my hand, and at me, and turned back to the bed. I took it for leave.

Past 807 the corridor ran on for two more doors and ended at the small window onto the light well. To the right of the window a cream door was lettered LINEN. Someone had fitted it with a padlock, a brass one the size of a hen’s egg, in a hasp whose screws were bright, and below the hasp a few pale curls of wood lay on the skirting where nobody had yet swept. Hotels lock their linen, since towels walk. Hotels don’t often do it with a padlock still shining from the shop. I didn’t touch it. In the glass of the window I could see 807’s doorway behind me, and Pearl Hightower standing in it, not working, her fist closed hard on the keys.

When I came back to the lift Lambert had gone from it. The car stood open at eight with its lamp lit and nobody in it. I stepped inside, and the doors, having no orders, stayed where they were.

Teddy Wozniak had said there was a key. I had spent a morning among people telling me what they wouldn’t say, and a key was the one thing so far that had told me something, because a key is a fact with a hole in it. I had found one hole already, downstairs, in a plate marked SERVICE. A key that could call this car down to the lobby could send it somewhere else, and that would want a hole in here too.

I read the panel the way you read a face you’re not supposed to be reading. Eight brass buttons in a row, the cream enamel round them, no keyhole anywhere. I put my nose close. The sharp sweet smell was strongest at the right-hand end, under the 8, where a round of metal the size of a half dollar sat flush in the panel. It had been painted the same cream as everything else, and you would have taken it for the head of a rivet if the paint had gone clear to the rim. At one edge a hairline of brass showed. I laid my thumb on it.

The plug didn’t move. The paint did. It gave under my thumb like the skin on cold custard, and when I took the thumb away a perfect round of cream had come off on it and the brass showed through, dull and old, a good twenty-six years older than the paint. The Waltham, turned in on my wrist, said one minute past eleven. Wet paint at eleven in the morning, on a button that the plans, the licence and the Board of Underwriters said was never there to paint.

I worked my thumbnail into the hairline at the rim, for a better look.

“Don’t, Miss,” Lambert said, quietly, from the doorway.

chapters.title: Property of the Deceased
chapters.html:
Orville Pugh peeled a pickled egg over a canvas body bag, and the bag, being the one party in the room that wouldn’t mind, took the shell. He was a long, stooped man in his sixties, in a rubber apron over a brown cardigan, with a scalp the colour of a candle and a tin sandwich box open on the trolley beside the dead. The room was white tile to the ceiling, with a drain in the middle of the floor and three rows of steel doors along the east wall, twelve to a row, each with a brass frame for a card. It smelled of carbolic and cold brine. The egg smelled of vinegar and was the more cheerful of the two.

“Wipe your feet,” he said to me, who had. “Don’t touch the drawers,” he said to Dolan, who hadn’t. He pointed the egg at each of us in turn. “I’ll tell you what I tell everybody. I only talk to people who don’t interrupt.”

“I never interrupt,” Dolan said.

“He interrupts,” Pugh told me.

Frank Dolan took the matchstick out of his mouth, looked at it, and put it back on the other side. He had driven me up Lamplighter Hill in the Plymouth without a word, the heater blowing on his side of the car and not on mine, the way a man drives a witness he hasn’t made up his mind about. All he’d said, when I climbed in on Cutter Street, was: “You called twice yesterday, Ruthie. A woman who calls twice is working. I’d rather know who for.” I said a friend. He said a friend was what a lawyer called a client, and I wasn’t a lawyer, and he would show me one thing and then I could go back to finding husbands.

Now he stood by the drain with his freckled forearms folded, and the plain gold ring he wears on a chain round his neck had swung out of his collar. He tucked it back with one finger. He does that whenever he leans over something dead.

“Ostrander’s report,” he said, and held out a sheet of paper.

I read it under the lamp over the trolley. Cause of death, cardiac failure. Contributing, acute alcoholism. Manner, natural. It ran a page and a half, and the half was the signature. Dr. Lyman Ostrander is seventy, and the county pays him by the certificate, which makes him the fastest pen in Port Calder.

“Did he open him?”

“Why would he open him? Heart and a skinful. You could smell the skinful from the door.”

“Doc opened him a little,” Pugh said. He had taken a bite and spoke round it, to me. “A little is what the county pays for. He takes the stomach contents and puts them in a jar on the shelf, same as any man who comes in smelling of a bottle. A week on the shelf, in case anybody wants to know what the fellow had for his supper.” He swallowed. “Nobody has asked for a jar since the war.”

“Orville,” Dolan said.

Pugh stopped. He wrapped what was left of the egg in its paper, laid it in the sandwich box, closed the lid, and turned his face to the ceiling like a man who hears a telephone ringing in another house.

“He’s interrupted me,” he said to the ceiling.

“I’ll make it up to you,” I said. “Which drawer?”

It took him a second to decide I was sincere. Then he crossed to the east wall and laid his palm flat on a door in the middle row. The card in the brass frame said CARDINALS.

“I don’t care for numbers,” he said. “A number’s a cold thing to be. Top row is the National League, middle row the American, and the bottom row is the Coast League, which is where I put anybody that’s come out of the bay. The good clubs go to men who come in with a decent suit.” He rapped the steel once with a knuckle, politely, the way you’d knock on a neighbour’s door. “Mr. Delaney had a decent suit. Mr. Delaney is a Cardinal.”

The drawer ran out on its rollers with a noise like a streetcar braking a long way off, and Pugh folded the sheet to the dead man’s breastbone.

I looked at the hands first. They lay at his sides, small and clean, the nails trimmed to the quick, and the fingers curled a little, as though they had been about to straighten something. On the second finger of the right hand there was a callus on the side from a pen held hard, with a stain of blue in it that a lifetime of soap had not got out. The face above them was forty-seven by the card and looked it, in the way of men who have spent their years in rooms with the lights on. Dolan looked at the drain. I noticed that he looked at the drain.

“Pull the sheet off his feet,” I said.

“Why?” said Dolan.

“Habit.”

Pugh lifted the sheet from the bottom like a man turning down a bed. The left heel was very white. Teddy Wozniak had said that a man’s heel is a private thing and that he had looked at this one longer than at the face. I gave it a count of five.

“You and your shoes,” Dolan said.

“Nobody’s got any on.”

“They’re in the envelope.” He took a manila envelope from Pugh, who held it out by one corner as if it might leak, and tipped it onto the steel table by the sink. “Which is the one thing I brought you up here to see, so look at it, and then say thank you.”

The wallet came first, brown pigskin, worn pale at the fold. Two hundred and twelve dollars: ten twenties, a ten, two ones. “Nobody robbed him,” Dolan said. A comb. A handkerchief with a laundry mark. A grey felt hat in a paper bag, which Pugh would not let me take out, because he did not allow hats on the table; hats, he said, were bad luck, and he wasn’t a superstitious man. A pawn ticket from a loan office on Front Street, for one pair of field glasses, seven by fifty, fourteen dollars, dated the twenty-eighth of October and not redeemed. A card in a stiff cardboard sleeve, gate pass, Pier 6, Calder Pier & Terminal Company, good through the thirty-first of December this year.

“Pier 6,” I said.

The matchstick stopped moving. It lasted about as long as it takes to say so. Then it went on, from one side of Dolan’s mouth to the other. “Passes go round like handbills,” he said. “Plum’s company gives them to anybody who’ll wave at a ship.”

“This one’s current.”

“Ruth.”

I let that sit, and picked up the last thing in the pile, a folding leather case with a brass snap. Inside was a card with a photograph on it, a man with a pale, worried face under a Customs cap, and typed across the bottom, UNITED STATES CUSTOMS SERVICE, PORT OF CALDER. DECLAN F. MAHER, TALLY CLERK. Over the typing someone had stamped a purple SEPARATED 9-50.

“Your Delaney,” Dolan said, “isn’t.”

“Maher.”

“Declan Maher, forty-seven, a tally clerk, let go in September of ‘fifty for irregularities, which is the word they use when they can’t prove it and can’t stand the smell. I found him in the Customs file at seven last night. I’ve got a call in with a man there who is having a very long lunch.” He watched me. “Mean anything?”

“No,” I said, which was true as far as it went. The name knocked at something in the back of my head, the way a delivery boy knocks, and I didn’t answer the door. It would come back to me, as such things do, when I was doing something else and wasn’t ready.

The last of the envelope was a pair of black cap-toed shoes, size nine, resoled once. Pugh had stuffed a pair of grey wool socks into one of them at intake, and I shook them out. The left sock had a hole in the heel you could have posted a letter through. Under the hole the skin of the heel had been very white; I’d just seen it. I turned both socks over to the soles, and the soles were grey. Not dirty. Grey and felted, as if they’d been walked through a place nobody had swept in twenty years.

“Mattress dust,” Dolan said, over my shoulder.

“Pearl Hightower makes the beds in that hotel,” I said. “There’s no dust in them.”

“Who?”

“A woman I met.” I set the socks down. “His shoes are on, Frank.”

“They’re in a bag, Ruth.”

“They were on him when they found him. Tied. And the spread over his legs, smoothed. You’d have to be tucked in to look like that.”

“Men wear shoes.” The matchstick went across. “Half the men who die in hotels die in them. They come in tight and lie down on the bed and the shoes go with them.”

“Tight men don’t tie their shoes.”

“Then somebody was sober enough to do it. A bellhop. A maid. Hotels are full of people who go round tying things.” He gathered the pawn ticket and the pass and the card back into the envelope, one at a time, in no particular hurry. “You want to see a fool, hold a man’s shoes up and ask the wrong question about them. He died in his bed, Ruth. The heart goes when it goes.”

I looked at the shoes again, because he’d told me not to. Leather laces keep every knot they have ever held. These had two pairs of old creases, a bow’s, tidy on either side, the marks of a man who tied his shoes the same way every morning for forty years, and across them lay a granny knot, square and crooked and tight, like a stranger’s signature on somebody else’s cheque.

I didn’t mention Teddy Wozniak. I didn’t mention the stocking feet on a cot, or the two glasses, or a floor that the Board of Underwriters said wasn’t there. It was the second day in a row I’d kept my mouth shut for a client, and I kept it shut while Pugh slid the Cardinal home, and while Dolan drove me down the hill with the heater on his side, and while he let me out at Cutter and Second with the words, “Go and find somebody’s husband.”

At ten to three I climbed the Selkirk’s fifty-two steps and found my office door standing open and the glass swept clean where the pink notice had been.

A man sat in my chair. He sat in it the way an owner sits in a rented one, with his hat on his knee and his ankles crossed, and he rose, a little, when I came in, like a man getting up for a lady in a streetcar and not meaning it. Forty or so, plump through the cheeks and narrow through the eyes. His hair had been oiled until it shone like a patent shoe. The room smelled of bay rum. A pair of small gold anchors held his cuffs shut, and I looked at his shoes, which were tan and polished and had never once been to the Flats.

“Miss Szymanski. Gilbert Swain. I hope you will forgive the liberty.” He had a soft voice with an upward turn at the end of every sentence, as if each one were a question he didn’t need answered. “Your superintendent let me in. He has a weakness for lawyers. Would a man in my profession wait on a stair in this building? Would the stair survive it?”

“Get out of my chair.”

“Of course.” He rose all the way and moved round the desk to the client’s chair and sat there instead, and it was a good deal lower than mine. I took mine back. “I act for Councilman Plum,” he said, “and, in certain matters, for the owners of the Harbor Hotel. The Councilman is distressed. A man dies at the Harbor on the very night of his victory. Do you know what the Beacon does with a coincidence, Miss Szymanski? It marries it.”

“The owners. The Estate.”

“Estates are shy. Shall we say the owners?” He smiled. “I understand that Mr. Wozniak, a valued employee, has spoken to you. Mr. Quill mentioned that a lady had called. Is it so remarkable that a hotel talks to itself?”

“What do the owners want?”

“What does anyone want? A little peace.” He took an envelope from his breast pocket, a thick one of cream-coloured paper, and set it on the blotter between us without letting go of the corner. “Mr. Wozniak is a good man and has had a very long night. The owners would be grateful for a short, independent report from a licensed investigator, setting down that he was honestly mistaken. Tired, in good faith, nothing sinister. A few pages for the file, and a letter to be shown to the Board of Underwriters if it should come to that. Five hundred dollars. Would that be unreasonable?”

“It’s more than I make in a month,” I said. “Which is a funny thing to pay for a report you’ve already written.”

“The conclusion is not for sale, Miss Szymanski. It comes free with the looking. Does anyone ever look into this and come away astonished?” He let go of the corner. “You are, of course, at liberty to say that Mr. Wozniak is right. I would be astonished. I would also be paying you.”

I turned the envelope over. The flap was blank, no name, no crest. Inside were ten fifties, crisp but not new, the kind you can spend at a grocer’s without a question. I counted them, because I count, and put them back. My landlord wanted eighty-four dollars. My mother’s gas meter wanted a quarter every four days and had begun to sulk about it. I told myself that a woman could serve two clients, up to the moment one of them asked her for a lie, and that I would know that moment when it arrived.

“I’ll write what I find,” I said.

“That is all anyone has ever asked of you.”

“And if I find the night clerk is right?”

“Then you will write it, and I shall be very much surprised.” He picked up his hat, and then, as an afterthought he had plainly carried up the stairs with him, put it down again. “One small thing. The Councilman gives a luncheon tomorrow for the Friends of the Waterfront, at the Elks on Lamplighter Hill, half past one. Two hundred of his friends and a great deal of chicken. He would like to meet you. Wear your best hat; he likes to be photographed beside a hat.”

“Why would he want to meet me?”

“Why do men give luncheons, Miss Szymanski? Because they have nowhere better to put the chicken.” He took up the hat again. At the door he stopped, with his back half turned. “Would I pay you five hundred dollars to look, Miss Szymanski, if there were anything to find?”

He went down the stairs one flight at a time, and I listened to his shoes all the way to the street.

I held the envelope up to the window to see whether anything else was in the corners. There was something in the paper itself, three pale letters woven into the weave like the ghost of a thumbprint on a glass: C.E.T. A stationer’s mark, I thought. I put it in the desk drawer with the pink notice and did not think about it again that afternoon.

When the street lamps came on, I lifted the typewriter out of its case, set it on the blotter, and pressed my thumb into the corner of the felt. The board beneath it lifted. I have opened that case perhaps a dozen times in four years, and each time I had the sense of lifting the lid on something I had nailed shut myself.

Three sheets of onionskin, folded in four, soft as cloth from the folding, and the colour of a bruise: the blue-violet carbon of a wire-room log. Station copy sheet six of nine. At the head, in my own capitals, SUNDAY 14 MARCH 1948. Two lines above the one I wanted there was an entry I did not read, because I did not need to; I had taken it down word for word on a night when a good many cars had been told to be somewhere else. I put my finger below it.

2314 Caller D. Maher, Customs tally, asks if cars will clear Pier 6 gate.

My typing, four years old, with the capital R that always sat a hair too high. A sad, soft, frightened voice came back with it, a voice that had held a telephone in both hands and asked for a friend. I had advised him there was no information. He had said thank you. He had been very polite.

Outside the rain started again, and in the pipe under the window the water took up a small, steady tapping, like someone at the door who was in no hurry at all.

chapters.title: Over the Bakery
chapters.html:
At eight o’clock Mrs. Sobczak’s ovens came up to heat, and the wall of the stairwell at 1131 Hake Street turned warm under my hand, like a flatiron left standing on a shelf. The whole stair smelled of rye and caraway and the sour of the starter. Downstairs, through the glass of the shop door, I could see her in a white apron to her ankles, shaping tomorrow’s loaves on a floured board with a hand on each end, as if she were wringing necks. Eighteen steps to the landing, one of them a board that sounded a note. A card was tacked to the door: T. WOZNIAK, in a small square clerk’s hand that I would have known anywhere by now.

He opened before I knocked. He had heard me on the stair, he said, and he had known the step, and I wondered when I’d begun to be a step.

His two rooms were one room and a closet. The front room held a table with an oilcloth cover, two straight chairs, a hot plate on a shelf with an enamel kettle on it, and a crucifix over the door whose Christ had been dusted that morning. A shelf of Polish books ran along one wall, the spines cracked white, a missal at one end and a paperbound Pan Tadeusz at the other with its back broken. Through the closet door I could see a narrow iron bed made so tight you could have bounced a coin off it. He wore a clean collar and his waistcoat, and the jacket with the brass nameplate hung on the back of a chair, ready for eleven o’clock the way a man’s good shoes are ready on the mat.

“Please. Sit.” He gave me the chair that faced the window and took the other himself. “I have coffee, but it is a Polish coffee. It will be an ordeal.”

“I’ll be careful.”

He made it anyway, in a glass, with the grounds still floating on it, and set it in front of me on a saucer, and I drank it, and it was an ordeal. Above the shelf hung a photograph in a frame of black wood: a heavy man in a sexton’s long black coat, with a face like a locked door and hands as large as shovels, and beside him, coming to the height of his shoulder, a small woman in rimless spectacles, holding a handbag in front of her with both hands. Neither one was smiling. They looked as if they had been told not to.

“Who’s that?”

“My sister’s husband.” He didn’t turn his head. “Dead.”

“And the lady?”

“My sister.”

I let that lie, the way you leave a lamp on in a room you may need to come back to. I took out my notebook, which was the pink notice, and laid it flat on the oilcloth.

“The man you found wasn’t named Delaney,” I said. “His name was Declan Maher. He worked for Customs as a tally clerk until the autumn of 1950, when they let him go.”

Teddy Wozniak’s hand had reached for the pencil that lay on the oilcloth beside a blotter, a green one, folded in the corner where he must have written his letters. The pencil was lying square to the blotter’s edge already. His fingers moved it a quarter inch to the left, and then back.

“Maher,” he said.

“Say it as if you’d heard it.”

“I have heard it now, from you.” His eyes were on the pencil. “I checked in a Mr. Delaney of Portland, and he signed the book as Delaney, and paid three nights in advance, in cash, which is why I recall it. I believed what was in the book. A night clerk who doubted the book would have no work.”

“Had you seen him before Friday?”

“No.”

“Never?”

“Never, Miss Szymanski. I have a memory for faces. It is the only property I own.”

“Then tell me why a man you’d never seen wrote my name on your blotter.”

He had an answer for that, and I saw it come up from somewhere low, the way a bucket does, with some effort and a little spilling. “On Monday night, while I made up the keys, Mr. Delaney asked in a general way whether I knew a private detective. He said, an honest one. I said I did not. I have no use for such persons. He said,” and the gold tooth showed, apologetic, “then I know one. And he wrote your name. A woman who had been on the police wire. I did not ask how he knew of you. It is not a clerk’s business to ask a guest how he knows things.”

“And you came to me because a stranger told you to.”

“I came to you because a stranger who was dead had told me you were honest. There is a certain kind of recommendation that cannot be improved upon.” He moved the pencil a quarter inch to the right.

I sipped the coffee, which fought back. “I’ll ask you again how you got to nine.”

“I will tell you when I know I can.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“No.” His hand went to his waistcoat. The tin rattled, a dry little fall of seeds, and he took the hand away again as if it had been caught at something. “It is a promise. I do not make many. May I ask one thing in return, Miss Szymanski? Please do not go near the cab. Mr. Quill will take it as an insult, and he is a man who is hurt by distrust. He has been a friend to me.”

Mr. Quill had also been very kind to me, and I’d noticed the cane. I thought of the round of cream paint on my thumb, and of the shoes in their bag, and of five hundred dollars in a drawer on Cutter Street that I hadn’t mentioned either. We sat at an oilcloth table, the two of us, each with a hand held back under it. It had the look of an honest transaction.

“I’ll stay out of the cab,” I said, which was not a lie in the tense I meant it in.

He bowed his head. Below us, in the shop, Mrs. Sobczak slammed a tray, and the floor hummed under our feet, and settled.

My mother’s kitchen is four doors down from the bakery, at 1127, up one flight, over a Lithuanian cobbler who sings. She had kept supper for me since six, and told me so on the landing before she opened the door. A short, wide woman in a head scarf with arms like rolled dough and her reading glasses on a string round her neck, Helena Szymanska can say more with a lid than most people do with a sermon, and the one she had on the pot was a reproach.

“Rutka. Sit. Eat. A detective who faints is only a woman lying down.”

“I haven’t fainted since 1931.”

“You are thin since 1931.” She put three cabbage rolls in front of me in a sea of tomato, a heap of potatoes with dill, and a plate of cucumbers in sour cream, and stood over them like a customs officer. “Eat first. Talk second. The Americans do it the other way and look what it gives them.”

I ate. Cabbage rolls are not a food you talk through. The kitchen was warm from the stove and the one lamp, and the window over the sink had gone silver with steam. The Philco on the shelf was off, which meant she had been saving something up. She waited until I had put away two of the rolls.

“So. A general.”

“Mama.”

“Thirty-nine states, the radio says. A general is a man who asks other men to die, and then writes a book about it. I would have voted for the other one, the professor, the one with the hole in his shoe. A man who admits to a hole in his shoe is a man who can be fed.”

“You did vote for him.”

“I voted for him twice. In my heart.” She sat down across from me and picked up her darning, a brown sock stretched on a wooden egg, and I thought of a sock with a hole in it, lying on a steel table, and put down my fork for a second. “You were at Sobczak’s,” she said.

“I was visiting a client.”

“Four doors away you could not come up for a glass of tea first?” The needle went in and out. “A client with eyebrows.”

“You saw him.”

“I see everything on Hake Street, Rutka, I have a window. A little man in a hotel jacket. He buys a rye on Saturdays and sits in the last pew at the six o’clock and goes out before the blessing. I have never heard him say a word to a living person.” She bit off the wool. “Wozniak. Yes? Tadeusz Wozniak.”

I had not said the name. I looked at her, and she looked at the sock.

“Bronia Kowal’s brother,” she said. “Everyone knows. You don’t know?”

“I don’t know a Bronia Kowal.”

“You know nothing. You were a policewoman, and you know nothing about the street where you sleep.” She said it kindly, which was worse. “Bronia Kowal, at the church. Small, black, glasses without a rim, a rosary on her wrist, and always the handbag, with both hands, as if it would run off. Seventeen months a widow. Her husband was Stefan Kowal, the sexton. He kept the St. Raphael box, God rest him.”

“What’s a St. Raphael box?”

“What do they teach you? Raphael is the saint of travellers. By the door of the church there is a box for the travellers, for Masses, for the poor sailors off the ships. Stefan Kowal emptied it every Friday and never said where it went.” She crossed herself, with the needle still in her hand, so that she drew a small silver cross in the air. “A saint, that man. With a temper. He once chased the bishop’s driver down Eleventh Avenue with a candle snuffer, because the man parked on the church steps. It was a Christmas. The snuffer was brass.”

“Did he catch him?”

“He caught the car. He broke a lamp.” She smiled, briefly, a thing that goes across my mother’s face like the shadow of a bird across a window. “Who is dead, Rutka? Is somebody dead?”

“A man in a hotel. A guest. The police say natural.”

“And what do you say?”

“I say I’m not yet paid enough to say.”

“Hm.” She went back to the sock. After a while she said, in a different voice, to the wool, “The Kowals were people who kept their doors open. That’s all. Eat your potatoes.”

I ate my potatoes. It struck me over the dill that she hadn’t asked me one question I would have asked in her place, and that my mother is a woman who asks every question there is.

At twenty past eleven I stood alone at the sink, with the dishes done and the lamp turned down, looking out of the window the way I do when something won’t sit still in my head. Helena had gone to bed at ten with a candle and a prayer for my future, the future part rather long. The window over the sink looks north, across the back yards of the Flats, the tarred roofs, the chimneys, the clotheslines hung like loose telegraph wire, and the rain had thinned to a mist the colour of dishwater. Past the roofs the ferry slip showed its red lamp. And beyond that, ten blocks off, set down on the edge of the water with nothing near it as tall, stood the Harbor Hotel.

I knew it by the shape. In the dark it had no windows to speak of, only a cliff of brick with a few lit squares, the night people, the late guests, a lamp that stayed on in an office on the second floor. Eight rows, I thought, and then did not think, because I was already counting from the bottom with a finger on the glass, and I came to the eighth, and above the eighth there was the black band of the cornice where no floor should be.

A light moved in it.

It was small and yellow, no brighter than a lantern held low, and it came out at the Ferry Slip end of the black band and slid along it from left to right, a little behind the slats, so that I saw it only in pieces, through the louvres, bar by bar, like a hand running along the keys of a piano. I counted. Eleven seconds. At the far end, toward Front Street, it stopped, and for a moment the whole row of slats stood out in faint dull lines, as if the cornice had been drawn on the dark in red pencil.

Then it went out.

The night clerk of the Harbor Hotel was at his desk by now, with his key in his watch pocket and his pillbox in his waistcoat. At ten I had seen him from the front window, going down Hake Street in his raincoat with a lunch tin under one arm, and he had turned the corner for the Number 14 without once looking back. Whoever had a lantern on that floor was not Teddy Wozniak. And whoever it was had gone, with the patience of a man doing something he did every night of his life, along a row of black slats from one end of the building to the other, as if inspecting them.

I stood at the window until the water in the sink had stopped draining. Out on Calder Point the Heifer sounded, two notes, the second lower, and the tin of the roofs took up the sound and gave it back to me as a kind of shudder in the glass. It came again at forty. The band above the eighth floor stayed black the whole time.

chapters.title: The Empty Folder
chapters.html:
“Number, please,” said Lucille Fong, and brought down a rubber stamp on a form without looking up.

I had no number. I stood at the brass grill of the counter in the Harbor Commission’s records room, on the ground floor of the Customs Annex at Front and Cutter, with the rain still on my hat, and watched the top of her head. A pencil stuck out of the dark hair above her left ear, sharpened that morning to a needle. Behind her, rows of green steel shelves ran back into the gloom under a sign that said NO FOOD NO SMOKING NO EXCEPTIONS, and in front of her stood a wire basket of forms, which she was working through with the blank, metronome pleasure of a woman playing a hand she knows she’ll win.

“Please hold,” she said, and stamped another.

“I’m holding.”

“Not yet you’re not. I can’t hear you holding.” She lifted her face at last. Small, round tortoiseshell glasses, a chipped front tooth, and eyes that had lain in wait behind the lenses for me since I came in the door. “Well. If it isn’t the woman who left the wire room and took the good chair with her.”

“It was a terrible chair.”

“It was a terrible chair that I got for nothing from the Water Department, and you walked off with it in June of ‘forty-eight in a taxi.” She came to the counter and looked me up and down. “You look like you’ve been sleeping in that hat.”

“It’s my best hat.”

“That’s what worries me, Ruth.”

We had shared a headset for seven years, her left ear and my right, in a room with no windows on the third floor of Central Station, and it left us with a way of talking in which neither of us has ever once been polite. Lucille Fong is thirty-four. She is the Senior Clerk of Vessel Records, and she will be the Chief Clerk of the Harbor Commission the day the Commission stops promoting men called Pruitt over her. She has never said a word against Mr. Pruitt. She says “Mr. Pruitt” the way other women say “the weather.”

Behind her a pale young man in a green eyeshade, with a frightened pimple on his chin, was shelving folders so slowly that every one of them was a conversation. “Mr. Tibbets,” Lucille said, not turning. “There’s a drawer in the back that needs looking at. Go and look at it from a long way off.”

“Which drawer, Miss Fong?”

“Any drawer.” He went. She leaned on the counter. “Now. Whatever you want, it’ll cost you lunch.”

“I want a man named Declan Maher. Customs tally clerk, let go September of 1950. I want to know what the word irregularities was covering.”

“I looked him up before you came,” Lucille said. “I’m a woman of foresight. He telephoned the Commission twice in October, and both times asked for Vessel Records, and both times the call went to Mr. Tibbets, who told him I was at lunch. I’ll want to talk to Mr. Tibbets about his judgement.” She took the pencil out of her hair, wrote on a slip, and put it back. “Tally Clerk, Grade Three. He counted what came off the ships and checked it against the paper. Dismissed for irregularities. That’s what they say when they can’t prove a thing and can’t stand the smell of it. Is he your trouble?”

“He’s dead.”

“I’m sorry. Was he nice?”

“I don’t know yet.”

“That’s the trouble with the dead.” She slid the slip over. “What else?”

“A date. Sunday night, the fourteenth of March, 1948. Pier 6. What came in.”

She didn’t move, and the way she didn’t was a sort of answer. The rain ticked on the high windows. “March of ‘forty-eight,” she said, in a lower voice. “That’s your month.”

“It’s a date.”

“You left in June. I thought about that for a long time, you know. I thought about it on the streetcar.” She waited for me to say something, and when I didn’t, she drew a breath through her nose, and the clerk came back into her face like a shutter coming down. “Sunday the fourteenth. I don’t need the berth book for that, which means I’ll look in it anyway. Hold the line.”

She went back among the shelves. I heard a drawer, a long pause, and a drawer again. She returned with a green folder under one arm and her glasses pushed up her forehead, which is how she wears them when she is angry.

“There was one ship at Slip 3 that night. Liberty ship, American flag, the Esther Vane, in from Antwerp by way of Halifax, docked at nine ten p.m., sailed on the tide the Tuesday. Master, a Captain Oakes.” She laid the folder on the counter and opened it. Five tabs, printed in the Commission’s blue: ARRIVAL. CREW. MANIFEST. TALLY. CLEARANCE. “Look at that and tell me what’s wrong.”

I looked. Behind the first tab lay a single sheet. Behind the other four tabs lay nothing at all. The cardboard dividers stood in their folder like empty chairs in a hall.

“There’s no manifest.”

“There’s a tab called MANIFEST with nothing behind it. The master’s copy goes to Customs, but we’re supposed to hold the Commission’s copy. It should be here. It isn’t. Somebody took it, or nobody ever put it in.” She tapped the one sheet. “And that. That’s the arrival sheet. Read it.”

The sheet was typed. At the top was the ship’s name and the time of docking, and beneath that the crew: seventy-one men, tallied by rating, deck and engine and steward. At the bottom, in the margin, someone had written a note and a figure in pencil, and the note said that thirty-one of them were “discharged ashore by mutual consent.”

“Thirty-one,” I said.

“A Liberty carries forty. Forty-one if the cook has a nephew. Nobody loses thirty-one men in a night. That’s a mutiny or a lie, and a mutiny would have been written up.” Lucille took her glasses down and put them on. “And look at the paper.”

I’d been looking at it without seeing it, which is how paper works. The Commission’s own sheets were on buff stock, thin and pulpy, the kind that smells of glue. This one was white bond, heavier, with a watermark that showed when I tilted it to the high window. It had been typed on a different machine, too. I know typefaces the way other people know hymns. This was an Underwood pica, and the capital E sat a hair low on the line, the way an old friend’s coat hangs lower on one side.

“Typed somewhere else,” I said. “Then slipped in.”

“Typed somewhere else, then slipped in. At night, I’d say, by somebody who has a key and a very good opinion of himself.” Lucille closed the folder with the flat of her hand. “I can’t take it out of the room, Ruth. I can’t even let you take notes in the room with Tibbets breathing. But I’ll let you put your thumb on the number so you remember it.”

I put my thumb on the pencilled 31. It felt like nothing, like paper.

“While I’ve got you,” I said. “The Harbor Hotel. Is there a 1926 building permit in this place?”

“The Commission holds permits for anything inside the pier-head line, for the fireboat easement. The Harbor’s inside it by about four feet, God help it.” She narrowed her eyes. “Why do you want a hotel?”

“To count the floors.”

“You always did count.” She wrote that on another slip. “I’ll find the permit. I can’t show it to you here either. Give me a day, and I’ll bring a copy, in an envelope, in my handbag, like a smuggler, and you’ll owe me a slice of pie at Tommy’s.”

“I owe you the chair.”

“You owe me the chair.” She took her coat off a hook. “Lunch. I said it’d cost you.”

Anchor Alley is off Front Street north of Cutter, a lane three people wide where the rain came straight down between the roofs and nowhere else. It was the old Chinese quarter, and what was left of it was a few blocks of tailors, herbalists and a steam laundry whose vents breathed out a warm, soapy cloud. Number 14 had a window with a half-curtain, three bolts of serge in it, and a hand-lettered sign in gilt on black: FONG & SON, TAILORS TO THE SEA.

“There’s no son,” I said.

“The Son is aspirational.” Lucille opened the door. “Dad has me.”

“You’re a clerk.”

“I’m a clerk who can hem.”

A bell rang over the door, and the shop took me in like a warm sleeve. It smelled of hot wool and camphor and a steam iron. Along one wall ran a shelf of bolts, serge and gabardine and a dark blue melton for pea coats, and beyond them a long cutting table scored with chalk, and two dress forms in half-made jackets, standing at attention. At the table, with a tape measure hung round his neck like a stole, a man in a waistcoat was marking a length of grey cloth with a sliver of tailor’s chalk. He was sixty-six, thin and upright, with cropped white hair and a pair of half-glasses low on his nose, and he did not look up until he had finished the line.

Then he looked at me, and it was an odd thing to be looked at. He did not meet my eyes. His gaze went to my shoulders, down my arms to my wrists, across my chest, down my back as I turned a little, which I hadn’t meant to do, then to my feet, and it came back to my face with the air of a man who has read a long letter and approves of the handwriting.

“Thirty-seven inch chest,” he said. “Thirty-six sleeve. You stoop a little, and the left shoulder is lower, because you carry something on that side.”

“A handbag.”

“A bag with a book in it, I would say, or a notebook.” He nodded at the belted navy raincoat. “Who cut this?”

“Sears.”

“Sears has never met you.” He said it to the chalk. Then there was a pause as long as a stitch, and the corner of his mouth moved. “I apologise. That was rude to Sears.”

Lucille groaned. “Dad. This is Ruth. Ruth Szymanski. The telephone Ruth.”

“The one with the chair.” He put down the chalk and inclined his head to me, a small, precise bow, and said, in a clear, slightly formal English that had not a rough edge anywhere in it, that he was Walter Fong and that I was welcome in his shop. He did not shake hands. His hands, I saw, were spotless to the wrist and scored across the first two fingers of the left with a hundred tiny white lines, the scars of a lifetime of needle.

We ate standing up at the cutting table, on newspaper, from a paper sack Lucille had fetched round the corner: pork buns, hot enough to hurt, and a pot of tea on a gas ring. For a while nobody said anything useful. Walter Fong talked about the weather, which he held to be the fault of the Navy, and about Eisenhower, whom he considered a tolerable cutter and no sort of tailor.

“Dad,” Lucille said. “Ruth is looking for a man named Maher. He’s dead. He worked on the piers.”

“I did not know him.”

“And she wants to know about a ship in 1948.”

“The Esther Vane,” I said. “A Liberty ship. Thirty-one of her crew were discharged ashore on the night of the fourteenth of March. Seventy-one men on the Commission’s sheet, and thirty-one of them let go at the gangway.”

Walter Fong set down his tea.

“Thirty-one,” he said.

“You know the number?”

“I know it because I made them.” He turned to the shelf, to where the pea coats hung, dark and square, and he laid one palm on a sleeve. “I was called to the shop on a Sunday evening, in March. A man came to the door, a man with a clerk’s voice, a very smooth voice, a voice that says sign here and means do not read it. He wished thirty-one pea coats and thirty-one watch caps, fitted, that night, at a pier. He paid in cash. I took the coats down on a handcart, with the boy from the laundry to push, and my tape and my chalk, and I fitted thirty-one persons in a shed by a lantern.”

“Persons,” I said.

“Men.” He looked at the sleeve. “Most of them were men.”

“Most?”

“In my trade, Miss Szymanski, you do not look at the man who pays cash for thirty-one coats. That is the first rule of the trade, and it is a good one. I did not look at him. I looked at shoulders.” A little dryness came into his voice a beat late, like the second note of a bell. “I was told not to ask what they were for. I did not. But I will tell you that not one of them spoke to me, and several of them held out their arms for the measure afterward as if they had been taught to do it by someone much worse.”

I did not trust myself with the pork bun. “Do you remember what he looked like? The man who paid?”

“I did not look at him.” He lifted his eyes, now, to mine, and kept them there. “I kept the order book. I keep all of them. Every coat I have made since 1912 is in a book in the back, with its measurements and its price and the name of the man who wore it, or the man who paid. If you should need those books, they will not be going anywhere. I have never thrown away a measurement.”

“That’s the best thing anyone’s said to me this week.”

“It is not a high standard.” He picked up the tea.

On the wall behind the cutting table, where the steam from the iron had been dulling it for years, hung a framed certificate. It was an old thing, gilt on black, with a border of lines and a row of tall characters across the top, and under them an English translation typed on a card: THIS IS TO CERTIFY THAT LAU WAI-LOK HAS SERVED HIS APPRENTICESHIP IN THE GUILD OF MERCHANT TAILORS AT CANTON AND IS FOUND SKILLED. A date, 1903. The name on the sign over the door outside said FONG. The name on the wall said Lau. I looked at it for about the time it takes to turn a page.

“Ruth,” Lucille said, from slightly too close. “Have another bun. You’re about to say something and you’ll be sorry. Have a bun.”

“I wasn’t going to say anything.”

“Good. Then eat.”

Her father looked at her. He did not say anything either, and in the pause the iron ticked, and the rain went on drumming in the lane. I took the bun. I have spent my life learning how much to leave out of a conversation, and it seemed a poor day to forget.

The rain had slackened to a drizzle by the time I went out. Lucille stayed behind to be scolded in two languages, and I stood in the lane under the shop’s awning to turn up my collar. The steam laundry across the way breathed its soapy cloud over the cobbles. A boy went by with a barrow of wet sacking. And in the arch of the laundry’s loading door, perfectly still, stood a man in a long dark coat and a snapped-brim hat, with the brim pulled down in front so that his eyes were a rumour.

He was peeling an orange.

He did it with a pocketknife, a thick one, held in a thick right hand, and he did it without once looking at it. The peel came away in a single spiral, a long coil of bright skin growing longer and longer and turning slowly on its own weight, and all the time his face, under the brim, stayed pointed across the alley at me. The lane was three people wide. I could have thrown a bun at him. He didn’t hurry, and he didn’t hide. He had the air of a man who has all the afternoon, and has chosen you to spend it on.

I held his look for a count of ten. Then the coil reached the end of the fruit, and he let it go.

It dropped from his hand to the wet cobbles whole, and lay there in a coil, as neat as a new telephone cord.

chapters.title: Victory at the Elks
chapters.html:
The cake was four feet long and had been iced in the shape of City Hall, with the clock tower in white sugar and a dome of green, and in the dome somebody had planted a sparkler, which was throwing a small, crackling, indignant light over the whole banquet room of the Elks Lodge on Lamplighter Hill. The steps had come out a little crooked. The Mayor’s window was a raisin. Two hundred people sat at long tables under paper cloths, working through creamed chicken on toast, and every one of them had one eye on the dome, waiting for it to catch the frosting alight.

“You’re late,” Gilbert Swain said at my elbow, “and in your best hat. Would it have hurt to choose a better one?”

“It’s the only one that’s dry.”

“Then the Councilman will be proud of it.” He had been waiting for me at the door of the banquet room, scented and glossy and agitated about the sleeves. He took my arm above the elbow, lightly, as a man takes a parcel he is not sure is his. “Come. He has asked for you by name. Do you know how many people the Councilman has asked for by name today? You and the caterer.”

The room had oak panelling to the shoulder and, above that, the heads of elks, glass-eyed, looking down at the chicken. A pennant hung from every ceiling beam: the Friends of the Waterfront, in gold fringe. A raised platform at the far end held a long table, a lectern, a microphone on a stand and two loudspeakers shaped like bread bins. At the centre of the table, with his napkin tucked into his collar like a bib, sat a man I had seen on a hundred telephone poles and had never met.

Everett Plum was round, and pink, and gleaming. He had ginger hair that did not occur in nature, and a diamond stickpin the size of a pea, and a damp upper lip, which he dabbed at intervals with a folded handkerchief he kept in his cuff. He saw me coming. His whole face lit up like a window.

“Friends!” he cried, and the microphone, which had been waiting, shrieked.

The whole room winced. A waiter dropped a spoon. Plum held up both hands, in the manner of a bishop calming a congregation, and when the howl had died he leaned into the microphone again, at an angle, as if it might bite.

“Friends. I want you to meet someone special. Someone who’s come up the hill today on a day of rain. A daughter of the working classes, friends, and an alumna of our fine police family! Miss Ruth Szymanski!” The microphone shrieked. “A woman of the waterfront!”

Two hundred forks stopped. A man at the next table, under a name card that said FRIEND OF THE LODGE, began to clap, and the room, unwilling to be left out, caught on. I nodded. I’m not built for standing in rooms while strangers clap at my family. I put my hand on the back of the nearest chair and kept it there.

“Don’t smile,” Swain murmured. “It makes him nervous.”

There was a punch bowl on a side table by the cloakroom door, a cut-glass thing the size of a bathtub, and a woman beside it who had plainly been guarding it for some time. She was tall and thin and faded, in a mink stole that had been brushed the wrong way, with a hat that carried one dusty wing, and she was ladling punch into a cup with the concentration of a surgeon. She looked up and smiled with her whole narrow face.

“You’re the girl from the police,” she said. “Have a cup. It’s the only honest thing in the room. It has rum in it, and it says so.”

I took a cup. “You’re Mrs. Plum.”

“Cordelia. Everett says I should be Mrs. Councilman Plum, but it sounds like a patent medicine.” She dipped her own cup again. “I’m told you’re looking into something at the Harbor. I didn’t hear it from anyone. I heard it from the chicken.” She leaned closer, and a wisp of the wing’s old dust floated off her hat. “I’m a Calder, you know. On my mother’s side, or the wrong side of one. My mother’s sister married a Calder. The Calders are all dead or in Santa Barbara, which is the same thing with better weather.”

“Do you see them?”

“I get a letter at Christmas from a lawyer saying that I’m still a Calder. It’s all I need to know.” She tipped her cup at the platform. “Do you want to know about Everett? Everett thinks the harbor is a pond he owns. I’ve told him it’s the Pacific Ocean. He says it’s on a lease.”

“Is it?”

“I’m the last person to ask. I once asked what a lease was, and he said, ‘Cordelia, it’s a thing you are not required to understand,’ and I have been very restful ever since.” She gazed at her husband with an expression that I found, to my surprise, was tender, and at the same time tired, like a woman looking at a clock she has long since stopped winding. “He’s a good man to be married to. He doesn’t hit. He doesn’t drink very much. He just loves the sound of himself, and what’s wrong with that? So does the church bell.”

On the platform Plum had risen for his address, and the sparkler on the cake died with a last hiss as he began. It was a long speech. He told the Friends of the Waterfront that the harbor was the artery of our hopes, the very aorta of prosperity, and that under the right hand on the tiller it would be a mighty stallion. He thanked the voters of the Seventh Ward. He thanked God, and the Lodge, and the chicken. And then, with a smoothness that I would have admired if I hadn’t been listening for it, he came round to the thing he had called me up the hill to hear.

“Friends, in the midst of our joy, on the very night of our triumph, this city lost a stranger. A guest at the Harbor Hotel passed away peacefully in his sleep. A tragic incident, on a night of joy. And I say to you, in the strongest possible terms, let us not be misconstrued. Let us not make a mountain out of a... a molehill of a mountain.”

“Oh, Everett,” Cordelia said, quietly, to her punch.

He found me by the cloakroom, afterward, because I had not been quick enough to be somewhere else. He came off the platform through a curtain with his handkerchief out, mopping, followed at three paces by Swain, who was walking like a man pushing a very large pram. Plum took my hand in both of his. They were damp, and warm, and soft, like a pair of poached eggs.

“Miss Szymanski. A woman of discretion. Gilbert says you are the soul of it. Such a business, you see, a terrible business, poor Maher, such a thing to happen at a time when...”

He stopped.

I’ve heard that stop on the wire a thousand times. It comes when a caller has said the one thing he meant to hold back and listens to it still ringing, and I let it ring. The handkerchief came up to his lip.

“Who?” I said.

“Delaney,” said Plum. “Poor Delaney. From Portland.”

“You said Maher.”

“Did I?” The pink had gone up to the roots of the ginger. “My cousin has a hardware store in Sacramento. Maher’s Hardware. I was thinking of a mishap in the... the paint department.” He dabbed. “A terrible week for hardware.”

“Everett,” said Swain, from behind him, quite gently. “The photographer is waiting by the cake. He says the sparkler is out and you wanted it lit for the picture.”

“The sparkler. Of course.” Plum let go of my hand as if he’d just remembered where it had been. “Miss Szymanski, a pleasure, a privilege, I hope you will lunch with us again. Friends of the Waterfront are friends for life!” And he went, blown across the floor by his own momentum, with the handkerchief going before him like a flag.

Swain stayed. His anchors winked. He looked at me as one looks at a clock that has begun to strike thirteen. “The Councilman is an emotional man,” he said. “He loves a good name. Would you hold it against him if he’d mislaid one?”

“The Beacon only printed Delaney,” I said.

“Did it? I haven’t looked.” He smiled, and bowed from the neck, and followed his employer across the room to the cake.

The Beacon had printed the name Delaney and only the name Delaney, on page three, below a notice about a dog show. I had read it on the streetcar. The card with Declan Maher on it was in a manila envelope at the county morgue, and in Frank Dolan’s head, and, I now understood, in a third place that I could not see.

I had meant to leave then. I’d got as far as the cloakroom for my coat, a long, dim room of hooks with a ticket girl asleep behind the counter, when I smelled orange.

You can smell an orange the way you smell a match. I turned. At the back of the banquet room, by the double doors and under the glass eyes of a particularly stern elk, a man sat with his chair tipped on its back legs against the panelling, and he wore his hat. The Elks have a rule that hats come off indoors. Nobody had told Aldo Ferrante, or everybody had.

I knew the hat first, the dark snapped brim. I knew the way he peeled the orange, the coil of skin hanging from the blade in a single ring and turning. I had left him standing in a laundry door in Anchor Alley two hours ago, and he’d beaten me up Lamplighter Hill, which a man with a car can do. He wore a dark overcoat, open. His forearms, where the sleeves were pushed up, were as thick as bedposts. The hand that held the orange was the left, and it lacked the top joint of the ring finger, cleanly, as if it had been cut off with a ruler.

Two men sat beside him with their hats on, too, and neither was eating.
