He let the chair down onto its four legs without hurry and rose, and took the hat off, which was the only courtesy he made to the Elks. His hair was black and thick, cut short. He had a broad, handsome, tired face with a nose that had met something, and he smiled at me with an air of such warm, personal welcome that I almost looked behind me.

“Anton’s girl,” he said. The voice was soft. There was a trace of Calabria in it, in the way he laid the words down one by one. “I have seen you from a distance all my life, and never had the honour. You are very like him. Around the eyes.”

“I’m Ruth.”

“Ruth.” He tried it. “Your father was a good man. I carried his coffin. There were six of us and I had the front left, and it was a heavy coffin for such a small man.” He held out a segment of the orange on the flat of the knife. “Please. From Florida. Everything good comes from somewhere else.”

“I don’t like being given things.”

“Everyone likes it, Ruth. It’s why they get so angry about it.” He ate the segment himself. “Remember that I carried it. It is a thing I like to be remembered for, and there is not very much else.”

“Mr. Ferrante,” I said. “Were you in Anchor Alley today?”

“Was I?” He considered this. “I am a man who likes a walk. The tailors there are the finest on the coast. I do not wear their coats, but I admire the principle.” The orange turned in his hand. “I will tell you something, Ruth, because your father had a right to hear it from somebody. Pier 6 is a bad place for a woman who sits in the dark.”

“I don’t sit much.”

“No? I heard you sat very still for nine years.” The knife moved round the fruit, taking a long thin curl, and he did not look at it. “It is a great gift, to be still. A rare one. I would not throw it away on a pier.”

A cheer went up at the front of the room as somebody relit the sparkler. The photographer’s flash went off, and for the width of a blink the whole banquet hall stood out white, two hundred faces, a hundred elk’s-eyes, a cake in the shape of a building. When my vision came back, Ferrante had put his hat on and gone through the double doors with his two silent men, leaving the peel on the arm of his chair in a loose bright spiral, like a spring that had come out of something.

I stayed in the Elks long enough to be photographed standing next to a cake. Then I walked down Lamplighter Hill in the rain, past City Hall, which was a good deal less sweet in stone, and at five o’clock I climbed the Selkirk’s stairs, found the superintendent in his basement beside a boiler that sounded like a dying cow, and paid him eighty-four dollars of Mr. Swain’s money. He wrote out a receipt on the back of a seed packet. I kept the packet. It had a picture of a very hopeful beet.

I ate a sandwich at Tommy’s. I walked along Front Street as far as the hotel and stood under the awning of the shop opposite, and the Harbor stood there in the wet with its curtains drawn, eight rows of windows under the fourteen feet of terracotta waves, and nothing on any of them to say what it was hiding. At nine I climbed the stairs again, because a thing isn’t known until it’s typed, and because the party line goes quiet after eight, and because I had a day’s worth of facts and no desk in the Flats to put them on.

My office door was unlocked.

I locked it every night. I lock it with a key on a loop of string that I keep inside my glove, and I had turned it at five. The glass with its gilt letters was dark. I pushed the door with two fingers and it swung inward on its hinges without a sound, and I stood on the threshold of room 309 and counted what I could see by the light from the hall.

The filing cabinet had four drawers and all four stood open. The folders from the bottom two lay on the floor in a long, even drift, as though a man had poured them out of a pail. The desk drawers had been pulled out and set on the desk in a row, each upside down. The chair was on its back. And from the filing cabinet, the typewriter case grinned at me with its lid thrown wide and its Royal portable still sitting in it, untouched, with the felt lining flat and the wire of the ribbon spool undisturbed.

I did not take the machine out. I lifted a corner of the felt with my thumbnail, in the dim, and slipped a finger under the board. The carbon lay where I had put it back, folded in four, soft as cloth. Whoever had been through my office had looked in the case for a typewriter and found one. They had not looked for anything underneath it. That told me they’d come for something that fit in a drawer.

The black address book with the rubber band was gone from the blotter. It had my mother’s number in it, and Lucille’s, and Dolan’s, and the night desk at the Harbor, all written in pencil, in my own hand. A thing like that you lose without knowing how much of yourself it held.

I picked up the chair. I turned toward the desk, to put it down, and saw what was lying on the middle of the blotter.

An orange peel. One long, unbroken spiral, a coil of bright skin, laid out on the green felt with the white side up, in a perfect round. The cut at the end was clean. It had not been dropped, or thrown. It had been placed, with the care of a man setting down a hat in a church, in the exact centre of the blotter, so that I couldn’t miss it, by somebody who had turned my office inside out and then taken the trouble to be tidy about the one thing he wanted me to see.

Somebody who wanted me to know he’d been polite.

chapters.title: The Frieze
chapters.html:
The building permit had been rolled for twenty-six years and resented being unrolled. It lay along Tommy’s lunch counter in a long blue curl, pinned at one end by the ketchup bottle and at the other by a sugar dispenser with a dent in its shoulder, and every time Tommy wiped his way down the Formica it tried to spring shut like a window blind.

“If that’s a menu,” Tommy said, “I want it known I never heard of half the dishes.”

“It’s a blueprint,” said Lucille Fong. “Keep the egg off it.”

She had come straight from the Commission, where Saturday hours end at noon in the spirit of a favour, and she had carried the roll up Front Street inside a folded Courier, walking like a woman with a salami up her sleeve. Now she sat on the stool beside mine with her tortoiseshell glasses pushed into her hair and her pencil stuck in behind them, and in front of her a slice of lemon meringue that I had paid for and she had described as a rumour.

Tommy ran the counter across Front Street from the Harbor Hotel. He was a big, slow, damp man with a dishrag on one shoulder and a paper cap that had stopped being white somewhere in the Truman administration. The shop had twelve stools, a coffee urn the size of a fire hydrant, and a window that steamed from the inside. At one o’clock I had wiped a porthole in the steam with my sleeve, and through it, across a street running with rain, the Harbor had been standing with its doors shut for an hour, doing nothing with such concentration that I’d begun to trust it less. I had spent the morning putting four drawers of paper back in the order I keep it, and screwing a Yale lock to the door of 309. The lock cost two dollars forty and was the first thing that week to do what it said.

“Eight storeys,” Lucille said, tapping the first sheet with the eraser end of her pencil. “Permit seven-three-one-two, Bureau of Buildings, January 1926. Lindqvist and Pratt, architects. Owner, the Calder Estate. Say it with me. Eight.”

“Eight.”

The elevation was drawn in white on blue, the way they print them: eight rows of windows ruled off with a straightedge, the lobby row taller than the rest, and over the eighth a deep band of waves with fish swimming in it, put in with the loving fussiness of a man paid by the line. A scale bar ran along the foot of the sheet. One-eighth of an inch to the foot.

“Lend me your rule.”

She kept a six-inch steel rule in her handbag, between the compact and the spare pencil. I laid it on the cornice. “One and three-quarter inches, lip to parapet. At an eighth to the foot, that’s fourteen.”

“Fourteen what?”

“Feet. Of fish.”

“That’s a lot of fish,” said Tommy, going by with the pot.

“Show me the cut,” I said, and Lucille turned the sheet.

The second drawing was a section, the hotel sliced down the middle so that you could see the floors stacked inside it, each one marked 10’-6” in a draughtsman’s capitals, and the elevator shaft running up through them in two heavy lines. Where the eighth floor stopped, under the cornice, sat a long box with a hatched lid. ATTIC, it said. TANKS & MACHINERY. 9’-0” CLEAR.

I put my thumb over it. Nine feet of clear air. Under it a floor, call it a foot and a half of beam and board; over it a roof and a parapet, call it three and a half. I did the sum twice and it came to fourteen both times, which is the only quality I ask of a sum.

“Nine feet clear,” I said. “A tank doesn’t need headroom. A tank needs a floor and a man with a wrench.”

“Maybe it’s a very large tank.”

“Look at the plan.”

The third sheet showed the attic from above: a rectangle the full width of the building, with two small squares drawn into one corner and labelled TANK. The rest was left as blank as a draughtsman leaves a space when he doesn’t expect to be asked about it.

“A storey in a fish hat,” said Lucille.

“Who passes a plan like that?”

“The Bureau of Buildings, on a Tuesday, in January 1926. The inspector’s initials are in the corner. Don’t look at me. I was seven.” She took the pencil out of her hair, considered it, and put it back. “Why do you want a hotel’s attic, Ruth?”

“I’ve a client who thinks his building has a floor too many.”

“Does it?”

“It has fourteen feet of terracotta on top that nobody’s accounted for.”

She didn’t answer. Her glasses came down out of her hair and onto her nose, which is where she keeps her worry, and she squared the three sheets with the edge of her hand.

“I signed this out as ‘fireboat easement, clearance check,’” she said, low. “The fireboat’s crane swings over the corner of that cornice, or says it does on days when somebody needs a reason. If anyone pulls the chit they’ll find a dull one. I’m very good at dull.”

“I know you are.”

“The hotel belongs to the Estate, Ruth. So does the ground under Pier 6, and I had to sign the deed index for that as well, which puts my name next to the Estate’s twice in one afternoon. I don’t like twice.” She slid the roll into the Courier. “I have a father and a desk, and a Chief Clerk who’d be glad of a reason. Don’t make me file for you again.”

Calder. Everything in Port Calder that stood still long enough had the name on it: the Sound, the Point, the Heights, a laundry on Third. I wrote Estate in my notebook beside it, without knowing yet how much of the town I had just underlined.

“Somebody turned my office over on Friday night,” I said. “They took my address book. You’re not in it any more.”

“I’ve always wanted to be unlisted.” But she looked at me over the glasses the way she used to look over a dropped call, and then she put her hand flat on my sleeve, once, and took it away. “Say it to the pie. Say you won’t make me.”

“I won’t make you.”

“You will.” She ate the rumour in four bites and left at three with the roll under her coat.

I kept my stool and the porthole. Tommy came down the counter and began to polish the urn, which is what a man does when he wants to be asked something.

“You were open Tuesday night,” I said. “For the returns.”

“Till two. I sold more coffee than the night the war ended. Lamplighter Hill came down in a body and sat right where you’re sitting, telling me who’d won what.” He put his cheek to the urn and examined himself in it. “Only odd thing was the gal out front.”

“Which gal?”

“White gloves. Stood across from the hotel doors, right under my awning, where you’d stand if you were working up to jump in the Sound. Ten minutes, in that rain, by the pie clock. I went to the door. I said, miss, you want coffee or you want to be rained on? She said neither, thank you, and she crossed over.”

“What time?”

“Midnight. A little after. The pie clock runs fast, so take it with salt.” He breathed on the urn. “I know the gloves. She sings at the Cormorant, up on Brine Street. Marchand. The wife made me take her for our anniversary, and I sat through a whole song about a sailor. It was in French, so I couldn’t tell you if it was dirty.”

“Marchand,” I said.

“Like I told you. French.”

I wrote it on the back of the pink notice, under Estate, and went off to find something to do with six hours.

By nine the rain was coming straight down in rods, with no wind behind it, which meant that a hat was no use and an umbrella was an advertisement. I wore the navy raincoat belted, the felt hat, and the flat shoes that can run.

The kitchen yard of the Harbor opens off Ferry Slip Row through a wooden gate that no one had thought worth locking, since the yard held only bins and the bins were spoken for. A line of galvanized cans stood along the wall under a lean-to of corrugated iron, with the kitchen door at one end throwing a yellow oblong onto the wet. Inside, a radio was playing a dance band, and a man was shouting about oysters. Over my head the rain on the iron made the noise of a thousand people clapping politely, which is the best cover God makes. A woman could take a piano apart under it.

Above the yard the back of the hotel went up around the light well, four brick walls pocked with small windows, and on the north wall a fire escape zigzagged into the dark, one flight to a storey. Its lowest stair was a counterweighted drop ladder, hooked up eight feet over the lean-to, out of reach of children and burglars. I am neither. I stood on the lid of a bin and then on the lean-to, where the iron bowed under me and boomed and nobody came out, and I took the bottom rung in both hands and hung my weight on it. The stair came down with the groan of a gate in a ghost story. The rain ate the groan.

Seven flights, thirteen steps to a flight, ninety-one in all. I count because counting is what my feet do instead of talking. On two there was steam at a window and a smell of onions. On four a radio gave the college football scores to nobody. On six a man snored so thoroughly that I heard him through glass and rain, and on seven I passed a curtained window with a woman’s shadow hanging a stocking on a nail, and kept my face to the brick like a bad child.

The eighth-floor landing was a grating three feet by five outside the little window at the end of the corridor. Through its chicken-wire glass I could see oxblood carpet, one bulb, and a cream door lettered LINEN with a padlock on it the size of a hen’s egg. The corridor was empty. The fire escape ended here. The building didn’t.

Bolted to the brick beside the window ran a ladder of plain iron rungs, painted black, that climbed past the lip of the cornice and ended in a staple. A painters’ ladder. Somebody has to reach the fish.

Eleven rungs. I counted them aloud under my breath, and the count was a rope. At the top the Frieze hung over me, and from underneath, with the rain running off its lip in cords, it looked less like ornament than like the hull of a boat turned over: terracotta waves curling above my hat, glazed green and gold, and in them the fish, each with its mouth open as though it had just been told the price. Level with my eyes, in the band above the waves, a row of louvres ran away along the wall, slats of the same clay set slantwise, shining wet, and behind every slat a black so solid that it didn’t look like a room at all, only like the bottom of something.

I put my eye to the third louvre and saw black. The fourth, black. At the fifth, in the lower corner of the lowest slat, someone had scraped the paint away from the inside, a patch no bigger than a postage stamp, and through it came a thread of yellow light as fine as a hair.

I laid my cheek on the wet clay and looked.

A lantern stood on a card table in a long low room, and it lit very little: a cloth of green baize gone grey, a ring of dust, a stack of folded tables against the far wall, and Joe Lambert’s back. He was in his porter’s grey, bent over the stack, running his palm along the underside of one table, lifting it down, starting on the next. He was humming. I couldn’t hear it through the clay, but I could see it in his shoulders, the slow lift and fall that goes with “Abide with Me.” Past the lantern’s reach the dark began, and in the dark there was somebody else. I couldn’t see him. I could see where the dark was thicker.

I could hear him. He cleared his throat twice, dry and short, and I want it noted that I did nothing with it. Half the men in Port Calder had a cough that week. The damp does it.

“It isn’t on him,” said the voice, level and unhurried, with the edges knocked off it by brick. “It isn’t in the room, and it isn’t up here. Paper doesn’t walk off, Joe. Somebody put it somewhere.”

“Yes, sir,” said Lambert.

Paper. I had a carbon in a typewriter case and an office that had been emptied onto its own floor for something that would fit in a drawer. Everyone in this business wanted paper, and I was the only one who knew what it cost to hold some.

The dry little click came twice again. “Mind the stair.”

Lambert straightened with a card table in his arms and turned toward the dark, and I leaned to follow him, and the foot I had on the wet rung went out from under me.

It is not a loud thing, a boot sole going down an iron rung. But a louvre is a kind of ear and a light well is a kind of horn, and all of it went in. The lantern went out.

I hung by both hands with my feet kicking at rain and eight storeys of nothing under them, and I did what I do, and counted. One. Behind the clay, nothing: a man standing in the dark with his hand over a flame. Six. Somewhere beneath me, deep in the building, a door shut with the heavy, well-fitted sound of a good door in an old house, and then there was no sound at all. Nineteen. I had sat at a desk for nine years, and my hands knew it.

At thirty-one I got a boot on the iron and came down the ladder like a bad idea. The drop stair took me to its last step and left me dangling over the lean-to, and the roof bowed, and I slid down the wet slope of it with my coat riding up and went off the eave into the nearest bin, six feet below, which was the one for potatoes.

I sat in it to the waist. There were peelings in my collar and an onion skin on my eyelash, and the kitchen radio played on with no idea. The Heifer moaned at Calder Point, two long notes with a hole between them, and I began to count to forty.

At twenty-six the rain slackened, and from eight storeys above me, from behind the black paint and the terracotta fish, a sound came down the light well the way sound comes down a chimney, small and clear and in no hurry. It was a key turning in a lock, once.

Somebody had stood in the dark until he was sure I was gone, and now he was locking up.

chapters.title: A Name Like Marchand
chapters.html:
Somebody in the trumpet section dropped a mute, and it went rolling across the stage of the Cormorant Room in a wobbling circle, a small aluminium cone ringing on the boards, and every head in the house turned to watch it except the singer’s. She stood at the microphone with her hands folded at her waist. A spotlight, hunted for in the wings by a boy who had been told to find it and found it late, came up on her blue and stayed, and the first thing it showed was her gloves. They were white cotton, wrist-length, spotless. They did not so much as twitch.

That was how I first saw Yvette Marchand, from the doorway, with half the contents of the Harbor’s kitchen bin drying on my coat.

It was twenty-five past eleven. I had walked up Brine Street from the hotel in the three minutes the map allows, and in the rain they had felt like nine. The Cormorant Room had been a ship chandler’s once and had kept the bones: brick walls, iron beams hung with brass lamps that had lit the holds of ships, fishing net swagged along the ceiling with cork floats caught in it, a ship’s wheel behind the bar. Over the bottles a stuffed cormorant spread its wings, one glass eye gone and a pearl-headed hatpin in its place. The house was full of sailors, dock clerks, a table of dentists in town for a convention, and couples who had come to be seen and stayed to hear.

The girl at the coat check, who had seen all kinds, took my raincoat by the tips of two fingers and turned her head away the way a woman does at the fish counter.

“Potatoes,” I said. “I fell in a bin.”

“We’ve had worse,” she said, with the generosity of the underpaid. “Not lately.”

The man at the piano was sixty or so, in a dinner jacket gone shiny at the elbows, with a pencil moustache and a toothpick in the corner of his mouth. He was marking a chart with a stub of pencil and did not look up when I came to the edge of the stage. The girl had called him Deacon. The sign over the door said CLARENCE TOLLIVER, PROP., in letters smaller than the cormorant’s.

“Mr. Tolliver. I’m told you can lend a woman a towel.”

“Mm-hm.”

“I fell in a bin at the Harbor. I’d like to hear Miss Marchand, and I’d like not to do it smelling like a root cellar.”

“Mm-hm.”

“I’d also like a word with her afterward.”

“Mm-hm.” The toothpick travelled from the left corner of his mouth to the right, which I took for punctuation.

“Is that a yes?”

“Mm-hm.”

“To which part?”

He lifted one long hand off the keys and took a folded towel from the lid of the piano, where it lay among the sheet music, and held it out without a word. It was white and clean and had the cormorant embroidered in one corner. I dried my face and the hair at my neck and was handing it back when he said, to the chart, “Mm-hm.” Since he was looking at the chart it could have meant anything. I kept the towel.

At half past eleven the house lights dropped and somebody found the blue again, properly this time, and Yvette Marchand sang.

She was very pale. She had a low coil of dark hair, a face made of angles and shadow, grey-green eyes that rested on the back wall of the room as if it owed her money, and on her chin a small crescent scar, white as a thumbnail, which the blue turned into a second, smaller smile. She sang in French, low, in a voice with nothing laid on it, no vibrato, no ache for effect, which is why it hurt. The song was about a sailor and a promise. That much French I had from the movies. And on the word for sky, the l went dark and thick in her mouth, the way it does in my mother’s, a sound like a coin dropped down a well.

The Cormorant didn’t notice. The Cormorant had paid for French.

The band took a long number without her, and I went through the door beside the stage marked ARTISTES, where the E had been added later in different paint. Nobody stopped me. The staff had taken my measure and decided I smelled too much to be a threat.

The dressing room had been a stockroom and still held the tar and hemp of its first trade in the boards. There was a table with a mirror ringed in bulbs, four of which worked, and round the mirror’s frame, tucked into the wood, a litter of cards and keepsakes: a postcard of Nice, a ticket stub, a dried daisy gone the colour of tea. Yvette sat before it in a grey wrapper over the slate gown, with a cup in her hand. She was still wearing the gloves. She looked at my shoes first, which is a thing I do myself, and I’d have liked her better if it hadn’t made me notice.

“Miss Marchand. My name is Szymanski. I’d like five minutes.”

“Everyone would like five minutes, mon cher. I have forty, and a set at one.” Her voice in the room was lower than on the stage and had a ragged edge that the microphone sanded off.

“A man died at the Harbor Hotel on Tuesday night. He was registered as Delaney. His name was Maher. Declan Maher, a Customs tally clerk.”

“I do not know such a man. I know sailors, and pianists, and these dentists.” She lifted the cup. “Are you the police? You do not smell like police. Police smell of cigars.”

“I don’t smell like much tonight.”

“No.” The corner of her mouth moved. “Potatoes.”

“You stood across from the Harbor on Tuesday night for ten minutes in the rain,” I said. “A man at the lunch counter timed you by his pie clock.”

“A man at a lunch counter has been timing women since the Flood.”

“Co słychać?” I said.

It is what my mother says to the grocer, to the priest, to a stray cat: how are you, what’s the news, what is there to hear. It is the smallest question in the language, and the cup stopped an inch below her lip. Only the cup. The rest of her went on as before, the pale face, the coil of hair, because she was a professional and the mirror was her friend. But I have watched hands all my life, and for the space of one breath that cup did not move at all.

She set it down in its saucer without a sound. “I do not speak this,” she said. “You have mistaken me for someone.”

“Is Marchand the name or the trade?”

“Marchand.” She said it to the glass. “Like people who sell things. Write it however you like, Miss Szymanski. The police do.” And my own name had come out of her mouth the way Americans never manage it, the sz soft and thick as butter, the y a short bright i. She heard it too. A muscle moved in the scarred chin.

I looked away from her, into the mirror, because it was the only place in the room where I could look at her face without being seen to. Pushed into the frame beside the postcard of Nice was a snapshot with a scalloped edge. Yvette, younger and thinner, in a man’s cardigan, with her hair not yet coiled or dyed, unsmiling, standing on a narrow landing. The ceiling behind her was so low that the plaster seemed to rest on the top of her head. Along the wall at her back ran a rail of coat hooks, and the hooks were set at about the height of my knee.

I studied the ceiling. A ceiling like that you can lay your palm flat against. I studied the hooks. Hooks that low are meant for someone who can’t reach higher.

“I have a set at one,” Yvette said. In the mirror her eyes had followed mine to the photograph and come back. “I would like you to leave my room.”

“Of course.”

“And the towel. It is Deacon’s. He will want it.”

“He gave it to me.”

“He gives everyone a towel,” she said. “It is how he finds out who gives it back.”

I took coffee at a table behind a pillar and listened to the one o’clock set, because there is nothing else to do in a nightclub when you aren’t drinking, and because I wanted to see if she would look for me. She didn’t. She looked at the back wall. By the door, at the end of the bar, a man in a dark overcoat sat with a beer he hadn’t touched. He had not taken off his hat. I noted the snapped brim and a pair of shoulders that did not belong to a man who listened to French, and I noted nothing more, because the singer was doing the thing with the l again.

At ten to two the house lights came up and the tables began the business of finding coats. Deacon Tolliver rose from the piano, buttoned his jacket over a stomach he carried with dignity, and crossed the room to my pillar.

“Miss Szymanski,” he said.

It was a sentence with a name in it, and I took it as a promotion.

“You brought the towel back folded in thirds. You left a dollar with the coat girl, who is saving for a hat. You sat through my whole second set without once looking at your watch, which is more than my wife can claim, and you did not try to buy my pianist a drink. I have been watching you for two and a half hours, which is how long I take to decide about a person who has fallen in a potato bin, and I would like to walk you out the back.”

“That’s more words than I’ve had from you all night.”

“I was making up my mind. It is slow work. Mm-hm.”

We went through the swing door at the side of the stage, past a crate of empty bottles and a rack of music stands, into a corridor that smelled of tar and hot lamps. He walked slowly, with his hands behind him.

“Yvette is a friend of mine,” he said, “in the sense that I pay her union scale and she does not drink on the job. She has been with me three years. I do not ask where she was before, and she does not tell me, and we both think it an excellent arrangement. But you said something to her in that room that made her put her tea down. She does not put her tea down.”

“Do you know a man named Maher?”

“I know a great many men named something. I own a share of this lease and I pay my band union scale. That is the whole of my interest in other people’s business.” He took the toothpick out and looked at it. “Tuesday was election night. The room was solid to the rafters. She did her three numbers in the eleven o’clock set, and when the band went into the long one she took her coat and went out by that door at the end. I thought, a walk, the room is hot. She came back at ten past one, as I was calling the last set. Her hair was wet through. She said not a word, and she sang that set like a woman paying off a mortgage.”

“Did you tell the police?”

“Nobody asked. When the police do not ask, Miss Szymanski, a man in my business takes it for a courtesy.” He put the toothpick back. “Everybody needs a walk. Some folks walk farther.”

Behind us the swing door opened. The man in the hat stood in it, with the light of the club at his back and his brim snapped down over his eyes, and he did not say anything at all. Deacon did not turn around. His eyes moved, once, to a door on his left with a round window in it and steam behind the glass.

“Mm-hm,” he said, and it was a different sentence this time.

I went through the kitchen door at a walk and then at something faster. The room was a long hot cave of ranges and steam, and a cook in a paper hat stood at a block breaking down a side of pork with a cleaver, with the calm of a man paid by the pound. He looked at me. He looked past me at the man who had come in behind, and he brought the cleaver down into the block so hard that the knives on the rack began to sing.

“My kitchen,” he said, “is not a street.”

We both heard it as addressed to us. I did not wait to see which of us he meant. I went down the aisle between a cauldron of chowder and a boy scraping plates, through a back door onto a wet flagged passage, and along it into Brine Street, where I could hear, behind me and fading, a man’s voice and a cook’s voice both saying something unkind about the other’s mother.

The Cormorant’s front awning was blue and white canvas, with the club’s name in script on its scalloped valance and the rain falling off the edge in a bead curtain. Under it, against the wall, with the collar of a grey coat turned up and a cigarette in an ungloved hand, stood Yvette.

The bare hand was small and white and bitten at the nails like a schoolgirl’s, and it went with nothing else about her.

“The police do not need to know I walk,” she said.

“I’m not the police.”

“You were something. It is in the way you stand, as though you were listening to a wire.” She drew on the cigarette. The red end showed the scar on her chin and the grey-green of her eyes and then let them go. “I have nothing to tell you about a dead man. I have a night’s work done, and I am going home.”

“Who else knows?”

She looked at me. I thought for a second that she was going to answer, because her mouth began to make the shape of a word. Then she dropped the cigarette on the pavement and put her heel on it, and turned up her collar a second time, and went out from under the awning into the rain and up Brine Street. I watched her until the dark took her, a slim straight shape with her heels going down hard on the wet, never once looking back, in the manner of a woman who has trained herself not to.

Hanging from the awning rope, where she must have hooked it to light the cigarette, was one white cotton glove. It still held the shape of her hand. It was dripping.

chapters.title: High Mass
chapters.html:
The bell was still going when my mother took me by the sleeve and towed me up the nave of St. Casimir’s like a tug with a barge, and the smell that came with us was wet wool, three hundred coats of it, steaming under the candles.

“Do not look at the people,” Helena said, in the voice she keeps for churches and customs officers, a whisper with a bayonet in it. “They have seen you. They are waiting to see if you will look.”

“Mama, I’m thirty-six.”

“Then you will know how.” She hauled me left into the fourth pew, the Szymanski pew since 1912, with a worn place at the aisle end where my father’s elbow used to go, and she genuflected on one knee with a creak like a barn door.

St. Casimir’s is brick outside and plaster Gothic within, with a ceiling of gold stars gone brown at the edges where the damp has found them, and over the side altar a Madonna with two scars on her cheek, who has been looking at the Flats for forty years with the patient contempt of a woman who has seen the bills. The choir sang the Kyrie from the loft in six parts, five of them sharp. The incense went up. My mother, beside me, put her lips to her missal and her eyes to the back of Mrs. Dobek’s hat.

Father Dziedzic climbed into the pulpit by eleven steps and spread his hands on the rail. He was a round, weary man with a pink face and grey under the eyes, the sort of priest you would pick out of a line for how little he wanted to be one that morning. He preached in Polish for the old and in English for the young, in that order, and in both he preached on the stranger within your gates. Thou shalt not oppress him, for you know the heart of a stranger, seeing you also were strangers in the land of Egypt. In Polish it rolled out whole, and my mother nodded at every comma. In English it came out smaller. He said a stranger might knock at any door at any hour, and that a Christian did not ask what it would cost before he opened.

His eyes travelled the church the way a priest’s do, row by row, and reached the fourth pew and stopped on me. I watched him find me and look at the red lamp over the altar instead.

Across the aisle, in the pew where I would have bet the Kowals had sat since the church had a roof, a small woman in black held a handbag on her lap with both hands. Rimless spectacles, a black felt hat with a pin, a mother-of-pearl rosary wound twice round one wrist like a bracelet. I had a photograph of her in my head from Teddy’s table, and she was smaller than the photograph. At the Gospel the congregation stood with a sound like surf, and she undid the steel clasp of the bag, which I heard from across the aisle as a click like a knitting needle, and took out a small black book with a brass clasp of its own. She held it shut against her chest through the whole of St. Matthew. She didn’t read from it. Holding it was the prayer. The clasp had been rubbed by thumbs until one side of the brass had gone the colour of a new penny.

I found Teddy by the rattle. In the hush after the Elevation, when the little bell is rung and nobody breathes, a pillbox shook in the last pew like a mouse in a biscuit tin, and I knew without turning round who sat there by the door with his hat on his knee, rattling in time with the Latin.

The basement of St. Casimir’s is a long low room under the church, with green wainscot, steam pipes, and eleven tables covered in oilcloth. By ten past eleven it held the entire parish and most of the Flats’ opinions. There was plum cake in slabs, and an urn the size of a boiler tended by a committee of four women, and at the table nearest the stairs three of them were arguing about Mrs. Eisenhower’s bangs: whether a woman who is going to be First Lady is entitled to bangs, and whether it was vanity or only Iowa.

My mother handed me a plate of cake as though she were arming me and went to the urn. Bronia Kowal stood at it with a cup in each hand, pouring for nobody. The two of them have been rivals at that urn for twenty years. It is the only war I know of in which both sides have always won.

“Pani Kowal,” said Helena.

“Pani Szymańska.”

“The coffee is thin.”

“It is the same coffee as last Sunday.”

“Then last Sunday was thin also.” My mother took a cup out of Bronia’s hand and drank from it, in the manner of an inspector, and found nothing to say, which she took as a victory.

Bronia turned to me. Close to, she was sixty-two and looked older in the face and younger in the hands, which were small and square and quite steady. She had the handbag hooked over her left forearm and held to her ribs with the elbow.

“You are the daughter who is a detective,” she said.

“Ruth. Mrs. Kowal, I’m sorry about your husband.”

“Seventeen months. It is kind.” She said it as though kindness were a coin she had been handed in the wrong currency. “Teddy is a good boy. He is fifty-four and a good boy. Leave him be.”

“He came to me, Mrs. Kowal.”

“He came to you because he is a good boy and did not know where else to go. Now he knows. Leave him be.”

I looked at the handbag. She saw me look, and moved it to the other arm, as you shift a child that has been stared at too long, and she said “Excuse me, Pani Szymańska, the milk,” and went away down the room between the tables, small and black and straight, and I watched her all the way to the kitchen door.

Father Dziedzic had come down the stairs in his cassock, still blotting his forehead, with a plate of cake in his hand that he did not mean to eat. I caught him by the sugar bowl.

“Father. The box in front of St. Raphael, the oak one with the iron bands. What is it collected for?”

“Travellers’ Masses,” he said at once; too at once, like a thing rehearsed in a confessional mirror. “A few dollars. For the sailors.”

“Which travellers?”

He put the cake down. “Stefan Kowal, God rest him, did many good works, Miss Szymanski. He emptied that box every Friday, and what he did with it is between him and his Maker, and I trust his Maker has settled the account. Excuse me. Mrs. Dobek has a grandson to baptise and a daughter-in-law to forgive.” He took his handkerchief and left the cake, and went off up the room at the speed of a round man in a cassock who has remembered an emergency.

My mother makes a pork roast on Sundays the way other people make a point. We ate in the kitchen at 1127, at the table with the good cloth, with the coal range ticking and the window over the sink turned grey with rain, and she talked about Mrs. Dobek’s cinnamon (too much), the tenor (he sings like a man looking for his hat), and the price of lard. Then, in the voice she uses to bring up a subject she has been carrying for hours, she said, “In forty-nine, Rutka, there was talk.”

“What talk?”

“In the parish. Women’s talk, over the urn. That there was a house for newcomers. For people who came off the ships with nothing. One woman said, I took a loaf, and another said, I took blankets, and the first one said, to where? And nobody said where.” She cut a potato in half to look at the inside of it. “Nobody said where and nobody asked. That was the sense of it. A quiet house. The kind where you carry a loaf to the door and not past it.”

I put it down beside the other things I’d been carrying about since Thursday: the light sliding along the black band over the hotel, and the snapshot in Yvette Marchand’s mirror, and a rail of coat hooks at the height of my knee. They lay down together very comfortably. They had been waiting for each other.

“Mama. Was there a house?”

My mother rose to see to the gravy. The gravy needed nothing. It sat in its boat in the middle of the table where it had been the whole meal, and she carried it to the range anyway and stood over it with the ladle and her back to me. Below us the Lithuanian cobbler had begun to sing, a long sad thing in a language of vowels.

“Mama.”

“The gravy is cold,” Helena said.

It was not cold. I could see the skin on it. I have watched my mother answer everything: the price of lard, the character of Roosevelt, the sins of the only young man I ever brought home. It was the first time in thirty-six years that I had watched her not answer. She stirred until the gravy was warm, and then she stirred some more.

My mother takes a walk round the block after Sunday dinner in all weathers, on the theory that pork not walked off turns to sin. We went under her umbrella, which she holds like a mast, down Hake Street to Eleventh and back past the church and the bakery, and she talked the whole way about coal and said nothing at all.

Someone was waiting in the doorway of 1127. He stood in the lee of the lintel with his hat in both hands and a furled black umbrella hung over his arm that he had never put up. The rain had got through his overcoat at the shoulders. How long he had been there I couldn’t tell, but his shoes had made two dark prints on the step, and the prints had begun to fill.

“Pan Wozniak,” said my mother. “You will come up and have pork.”

“Thank you, madam. No.” He did not look at her. “A word with your daughter, if I may.”

Helena looked at him, and then at me, and went past him and up the stairs with the umbrella, and her back said everything her mouth had decided to keep. I heard her door. I heard the third stair, which sings.

Teddy hung the umbrella on the iron rail of the stoop to free his hands. He squared his cuffs, one and then the other, though they were already square.

“Leave Bronia out,” he said.

“Out of what, Mr. Wozniak?”

He shook his head. The white eyebrows were beaded with rain. “She is sixty-two. She has lost a husband. If you go to her again I will... ” He did not finish it. “Please. I ask it as a man who asks very little.”

“Tell me what I’m leaving her out of.”

He looked at me then, the gold tooth showing a little as his mouth worked, and I thought for a second that he would tell me. But he said “Forgive me,” as he says it for everything, and went down the step and out into Hake Street.

He left the umbrella on the rail. I watched him walk, small and stooped and bareheaded, with the wet already dark across his back, and three paces on his right hand went into his coat pocket and stayed there. I could not hear it from the stoop. I heard it anyway: the small dry rattle of the tin.

chapters.title: The Shape-Up
chapters.html:
Three hundred men stood in a ring on the cobbles outside the Shape Hall at a quarter to six, in a fog so thick that the lamp over the door was only a stain, and their breath rose from the circle in one grey column, so that from the top of Capstan Row the whole assembly looked like a pot on a low flame.

I stood at the edge of it in my father’s overcoat. It hangs on a hook behind my mother’s door, brown wool with a patch on the left elbow that she set herself in 1938, and I had taken it down at five that morning while she was pretending to be asleep. She let me. It smelled of camphor and of a pipe that has been dead eleven years. With one of his caps pulled down over my hair I passed, from ten feet off, for a tall stevedore with a bad back, which is more or less what I am.

Nobody talked. They stood in peacoats and sheepskins with their cargo hooks hanging from their belts, the young ones shouldering toward the inside of the ring and the old ones drifting out to the edge, where I was, and every pair of eyes pointed at the same door. In it, under the dead lamp, with his hat on and a toothpick in the corner of his mouth, stood Aldo Ferrante.

I had heard about the shape-up and never watched one. A man raises a hook or touches his cap; the boss looks around the ring; the toothpick moves a quarter of an inch. A man who has been standing on one leg for twenty minutes puts his foot down and goes through the door with his hook already out. The toothpick moves again. A second man. A third. It took the best part of half an hour to hire the Slip 3 gang, and in that half hour I watched a hundred families’ week decided by a sliver of pine. The men who weren’t picked did not leave. They stood where they were, the way people stand at a streetcar stop after the last car.

“You’re in the wrong line, mister,” said the old man at my elbow.

He was seventy, with white stubble and a face like a boiled ham and one eye gone milky. He squinted at the cap and the coat, and down at the shoes, which were mine, and up again to the patch.

“Szymanski’s coat,” he said, very low. “That’s Helena’s mending. You’re Anton’s girl.”

“Everybody says so this week.”

“Then stand where he can’t see you, Anton’s girl.” The good eye went to the doorway and came back. “He’s seen you. He saw you from the corner.”

The toothpick moved. This time it wasn’t at a man in the ring. Two men inside the door came out across the cobbles, and the ring opened for them with the quiet of a thing arranged, three hundred men studying their boots and nobody looking at me at all, which is a kind of loud.

“Mr. Ferrante’s compliments, missus,” said the first, a large young man with the manners of a boy who has been told to open doors. “He says it’s no morning to stand in the wet.”

The back room of the Shape Hall was low and warm and smelled of coal smoke and oranges. It held a potbellied stove, a desk with the hiring ledger open on it, a radio on a shelf with its dial lit, a calendar from a macaroni importer showing a girl with a basket, and in the corner a plaster St. Joseph, patron of workers, with a votive lamp burning red before him and a dead cigar laid across his hands, as an offering or a joke. Ferrante sat behind the desk with his hat on, peeling an orange in one long spiral. The ledger was ruled in columns and filled with names in a clerk’s hand. I read three of them upside down. Skubic. Okonski. O’Hearn.

“Anton’s girl in Anton’s coat,” he said. “Sit, Ruth. The chair is clean.”

“I’ll stand.”

“Then stand. It is a good coat. I was with him when he bought it, at Gelb’s, in ‘thirty-eight. He wanted the one with deep pockets, for his lunch and his dignity. He thought a man could carry both.” The peel turned and lengthened. “A segment?”

“No.”

“That is the third time. A woman could starve on principle.”

“You sent two men across a ring for me. I’d say it was your morning, Mr. Ferrante.”

“Aldo. We are going to be a long time acquainted.” He cut the orange in half and ate neither half. “You are going to ask me if I killed a clerk. You came to ask, and you stood an hour in the wet working up to it. Ask.”

“Did you?”

“Declan Maher.” He laid the name down like a card he had been holding all night. “They tell you it is a sin to speak ill of the dead. I am Calabrian, and we consider it a sin not to. He bled me, Ruth. Two years. A hundred a month, and a hundred and fifty at Christmas, because Christmas is a time of giving. Last week he came into this office in a good suit with a worried face and asked for two thousand dollars in a lump, and I told him I would have to think.”

“What did he have on you?”

“He knew what I am. Not all of it. Enough.” The knife stopped. “A man in my position has things on a pier. A man like Maher counts them, as a boy counts stamps.”

“Where were you Tuesday night?”

“Here. With the returns. Forty men and a radio, eight o’clock to three in the morning, and not one of them left to make water, because in this hall a man does not leave during Ohio.” He nodded at the shelf. “Ask any of them. Ask the radio, if you like. It will tell you what time Ohio went, and forty men will tell you who cheered.”

It was a good alibi, and he knew it was a good alibi, and it was forty men deep, every one of whom drew his week from the end of that toothpick. I wrote it down in my head, with that last part underlined.

“Stay out of Pier 6,” Ferrante said. It came out gently. “Your father died on my pier. I paid for the funeral. Remember that I carried it.”

“You told me on Friday.”

“It bears repeating. It is the one good thing I have, and I do not like to see it spoiled.” He wiped the knife on a handkerchief and folded the blade. “The tide at Pier 6 is not for sitting in. You will hear a thing, and then you will hear another thing, and then you will find you have been sitting in it for years.”

The young man with the manners walked me out through the ring. Nobody looked at me this time either. The toothpick had moved again as we crossed the cobbles, and a man behind me put his foot down, and I did not turn to see whose week it was.

The Selkirk’s elevator was out again, so I heard Dolan before I saw him. He climbs a staircase the way other men sing: loudly, and so that you know where he is. Fifty-two steps, counting the half-landings, with a stop at the third floor to rest against the radiator and say something to it. By the time he reached 309 I had the new Yale open, the kettle on the gas ring and my face arranged.

“Ruthie.”

“Frank.”

“I brought doughnuts.” He held up a paper sack gone translucent in two places. He was breathing through his mouth. The matchstick was in its corner and the brown hat in his hand, and the collar of his shirt stood open on the chain with Moira’s ring, which he doesn’t tuck in on days when he has stairs.

“I can see them. What do you want?”

“Can’t a man bring doughnuts?”

“A man can. You never have.”

He sat in the client’s chair, which creaked, and laid the sack on the blotter where an orange peel had been on Friday. I thought he might look at the place. He looked at the door.

“New lock.”

“Old tenants.”

“I didn’t know you had tenants.”

“That’s the point of a lock, Frank.”

He chewed the matchstick. “Two hundred men saw a woman in Anton Szymanski’s coat walk into Ferrante’s office at six this morning. I had four phone calls before eight o’clock, and one of them was from a priest.”

“Which priest?”

“I’m not a man who tells you which priest.” He opened the sack and held it out, and the smell of hot sugar went through the office like an amnesty. “Eat. Listen. Rafferty retires on the fifteenth.”

“Saturday.”

“Saturday. He’s got a gold watch in a drawer and a dinner at the Harbor Hotel, God help us all, and a wife who’s picked out a bungalow at Santa Cruz. Forty years a policeman, and he’d like the last five days to be quiet. He doesn’t want a story about a dead clerk in a hotel the week he leaves.”

“A natural death isn’t a story.”

“That’s what I told him.”

“Did he believe you?”

“He believed me like he believes in the weather. He doesn’t think I made it.” The matchstick moved. “The lab went over 807. Nothing. A maid’s prints, the dead man’s, a Gideon Bible nobody opened. It’s a sad little business, Ruth, a man dies in a hotel bed.”

“Did anyone ask the lab to look at anything else?”

“Like what?”

“Like a jar on Dr. Ostrander’s shelf. Pugh says it’s what a man had in his stomach, and nobody’s asked for one since the war.”

The matchstick stopped.

Dolan said nothing. His big freckled hand, which had been lying on the arm of the chair, left it and travelled, as if without him, across the three feet of floor to the filing cabinet, and came to rest flat on the corner of the typewriter case, the way you lay a hand on a dog you aren’t sure of. We both looked at it. Neither of us said what was under the felt. Then he took the hand back, as a man takes his hand out of a pocket he has put it into by mistake, and held out the sack again.

“Doughnut,” he said.

“Thank you.”

“I’m a policeman, Ruth,” he said, to the wall above my head. “It’s a very small job. They give you a badge so you’ll stop asking for a bigger one.” He put on the hat. “Stay out of Capstan Row. And don’t take any more calls from priests.”

“You said you weren’t a man who told me which priest.”

“I’m not,” said Dolan, and went down the fifty-two steps the way he had come up them, loudly, so that I would know where he was.

Gundersen’s Drug on Cutter has a soda fountain with eight stools and a telephone booth whose folding door doesn’t fold. At ten to six I was on the fourth stool with a grilled cheese sandwich and the Beacon, which had found room for a map of tomorrow’s parade route on page one and a missing Pomeranian on page three, and for Declan Maher or Delaney or anyone at all at the Harbor Hotel nowhere.

“Szymanski!” Mr. Gundersen leaned over the counter in his bow tie with a fountain pen in every pocket. “Telephone, in the booth. The tall one, they said. I’ve only the one tall one.”

The receiver was warm from someone’s hand. I shut the door as far as it would go.

“Szymanski.”

“Miss Szymanski.” A man’s voice, slow and low, held close to the mouthpiece, like a man carrying a candle cupped in his hands. “This is Lambert. Joe Lambert, the porter at the Harbor. I took your card off Dorrie’s desk. Your office line has a lady on it who sells corsets, and she told me where you take your calls. She told me a good deal else.”

“Mr. Lambert.”

“I can’t stay on. They’d...” He stopped himself. I heard him breathe, and behind the breath a machine was ticking, something with gears. “I carried him. I’m the one carried him down. I can tell you from where and to where and who said do it. I won’t say it on a wire. Tomorrow night, after the parade, down by the boiler. Midnight. Come to the Ferry Slip door and ring the kitchen bell.”

“Why me?”

“The gentleman in 807 told me you were honest. I don’t know about honest. I know I haven’t slept since Wednesday, and I’m a deacon on Sundays.” There was a silence, and in it I heard what he had left out. The Miss was gone, and the sir, and every manner the job puts on a man. It was the voice of Joe Lambert with his collar open. “Midnight. Bring nobody.”

The line clicked and went to a tone.

I stood in the booth with the tone in my ear and the door half open on the fountain and the smell of grilled cheese. Out on the Point the Heifer began, low, and the fog took the sound up and carried it over Cutter Street and down the hill. I held the receiver until the tone gave up and became a buzz, and then I held it some more.

chapters.title: Armistice Night
chapters.html:
A drum corps came down Front Street in the rain, forty boys in borrowed tunics beating their drums as though the war had been personally rude to them, and on the kerb outside the Customs Annex a man in a garrison cap stood holding an umbrella over a boy with his one good hand. The boy was eight or so. The umbrella was a man’s, and large, and it covered the boy entirely and the man’s cap not at all, so that the rain ran off the visor and down his face and into his collar, and neither of them seemed to think this a matter for comment. His other sleeve was pinned across his chest beside a ribbon.

Lucille stood next to me under a lady’s umbrella the size of a dinner plate, which she held at the height of her own comfort, so that the spokes lay across my eyebrows and a steady drip came off the ferrule into my left ear. She had on her good navy coat and a hat with a cherry on it. It was Armistice Day, and the Harbor Commission had given its clerks the holiday, and she had spent the first part of it in the records room, “because Chief Clerks like to see who goes in anyway.”

Legionnaires in overseas caps went by in the step of men who had stopped counting at the second war. Girl Scouts in yellow oilskin capes. A Ford truck of Spanish War veterans under a banner, one of them asleep. A Sea Scout band came behind them playing “Anchors Aweigh” half a tone flat, with a tuba that was plainly the one in charge.

“Ruth,” said Lucille, “I have to tell you something and I need you not to say anything clever.”

“I’ll try.”

“The Esther Vane sheet is gone.”

“Gone.”

“The arrival sheet. The only paper in that folder. I locked the room at five on Monday with the folder in its drawer, and at eight this morning it was in the same drawer with its five tabs, all five of them empty.” The glasses came down onto her nose. “The lock wasn’t forced. There are three keys to that room: mine, Mr. Pruitt’s, and the night watchman’s, who is seventy-one and sleeps with his mouth open. And nobody breaks into a records room to take one sheet of paper. They take it because they know which drawer.”

“Who knew you’d pulled it?”

“You. Me. Tibbets, and Tibbets tells his barber.” She looked at the drum corps instead of at me. “I’ve filed for twelve years, and I’ll tell you what a stolen sheet sounds like. It sounds like nothing. A drawer with nothing in it where something was. It sounds like a switchboard with all the plugs out.”

“I saw it. Seventy-one crew. Thirty-one discharged ashore by mutual consent.”

“You saw it. I saw it. Which means that if anyone asks me whether the Commission ever held such a sheet, I am going to say what a Senior Clerk says, that I can’t confirm a document I can’t produce.” She turned the umbrella, and the drip moved from my left ear to my right. “Don’t say it. Don’t say how unlike me that is. I know exactly how unlike me it is.”

I didn’t say it. I took her arm instead, which she permitted for as long as it took the Sea Scouts to find the end of the song.

A black-and-white Ford came down the far side of Front Street behind the Legion float, slowly, with Karras at the wheel and Dolan in the passenger seat staring at the back of the float with the attention of a man reading a document written on the road. Karras saw me and lifted two fingers from the wheel. Dolan, I would have sworn, saw me in the wing mirror. He did not turn his head. The matchstick went from one side of his mouth to the other, and the car went on past the Annex, and the one-armed man lowered his umbrella an inch to let it by.

By half past eleven that night the rain had gone and the fog had come in behind it, up from the Sound, with the Heifer sounding every forty seconds from the Point, two long notes and a gap. Ferry Slip Row had vanished except for one bulb over the kitchen gate, with a halo round it the size of a hat. I went in past the bins and did not look at the potato one. The kitchen door had a brass bell-pull on a wire, put in for deliveries, and I pulled it and heard it clank somewhere deep in the building, and the Heifer came and went twice before the door was opened.

Teddy stood in it in his maroon jacket, with the brass nameplate and a pencil behind his ear and a face the colour of candle wax. “Miss Szymanski,” he said. “It is half past eleven.”

“Joe Lambert asked me to be here at midnight. He said to ring the kitchen bell.”

He did not move. The gold tooth caught the bulb. “Joe asked you.”

“He telephoned yesterday. He said he carried him.”

“Carried,” said Teddy. His hand went to his waistcoat, and the pillbox rattled once, and he took the hand away from it as a man takes his hand out of a fire he has found he is holding. “Please. Come in. Come in quickly.”

He led me through the dark kitchen, where a tap dripped and a row of copper pans hung on the wall like faces, down a passage and out into the lobby, which at that hour was a cave of black and white marble lit by one lamp on the desk. The clock said eleven thirty-two, which made it eleven thirty-five. Teddy took the brass bell off the counter and set it face down on the blotter, the only concession I think he had made to the dark in thirteen years. “A guest who finds a clerk missing waits,” he said. “A guest who finds the bell face down goes to bed.”

Over the lift doors the brass repeater hung with its needle stopped between the 3 and the 4, on neither, in the gap where a needle has no business to stay. Across the doors, held by a drawing pin to the oak, a leaf torn from the register said in pencil OUT OF ORDER.

“Since seven,” said Teddy. “Joe said the guide shoes. He said he would be in the pit by ten, and I was to send the guests to the service lift.” He looked at the needle. “I have never seen it do that. It goes to a floor. It does not go between.”

“Where is Miss Hightower?”

“Miss Hightower went off at ten. She said she had a headache.” He rubbed his eyebrow with one knuckle. “In thirteen years I have not heard her say that word.”

Down the passage behind the desk was the housekeeper’s room, where on other nights, I would have bet, a lamp stayed lit until the last linen cart came down. It was dark. A straight chair stood by the door with its seat pushed square to the wall, as though someone had tidied it for an inspection.

The basement stair went down beside the service lift. Teddy took it ahead of me, one hand on the wall, calling “Joe?” into the dark below in a voice that seemed to be asking permission.

The boiler room was a low brick vault as hot as a bread oven, with the boiler squatting in the middle of it and whitewashed pipes sweating overhead. Against the far wall stood an iron cot with a grey blanket folded at its foot, and beside it a crate with a thermos on it, the cup standing by, the coffee in the cup gone cold with a skin. A hurricane lantern hung lit on a nail. Under the nail on the flags lay a porter’s grey cap, crown down, as if it had fallen off a head that had not meant to leave it.

I had known Joe Lambert for an hour of one morning, and I would have bet my father’s watch that he was a man who capped his thermos.

“Joe,” said Teddy. “Joe, it is Teddy.”

The pipes took it and passed it along.

Behind the boiler, in the north wall, was an iron door at chest height, the kind you find on a locomotive’s firebox, standing a hand’s breadth open. A draught came out of it, cold, smelling of oil and iron and something under the oil.

“The pit,” Teddy said. “For the guide shoes. He goes in at night when the car is stopped. But he would not leave the lantern lit, and he would not...”

“Hold this.”

He took the lantern off the nail and held it. I pulled the door. It swung on its hinge with a long iron note, and the dark beyond went up, a throat of it, as far as the light would carry: ten feet of guide rail black with old oil, a ladder bolted to the wall and, far above, so far that it might have been a playing card dropped down a well, the pale underside of the car, stopped between floors. I looked down.

Seven feet below the sill a trouble-lamp hung from a hook on the pit wall at the end of its cord, swinging a little in the draught, and in the circle of it lay a pair of shoes. I counted them, because I count everything. Two. They were big and black and cracked across the toe, and blacked over the cracks, and they pointed at the roof of the world.

“Wait here,” I said.

“Miss Szymanski...”

“Wait.”

There were seven rungs, and I counted them aloud going down, in the voice of a man reading a list at a railway station.

The floor of the pit was concrete with a skin of oil on it and a squat iron buffer at the middle like a footstool for a giant. Joe Lambert lay on his back between the buffer and the wall with his arms out from his sides, as if he had been put down by someone who wished him to be comfortable. His head was turned further than a head turns. I did not look at it long. His grey hair, cropped short, looked like frost in the lamp. Beside his right hand stood a heavy brass oiler with a long spout, upright, as though he had set it down so as not to spill it. I did not touch it.

I knelt. I put two fingers under the angle of his jaw, because you do, and there was nothing to find, and the skin was cool at the edge and warm in the crease. A black shoelace ran round his neck and down inside the collar of his shirt. I had seen it on the Wednesday and hadn’t asked. I lifted the lace on one finger and drew up what hung at the end of it: a long brass key with a square head, stamped OTIS INSP. It was warm from him, which was the worst thing yet.

I lifted the lace over his head. I didn’t decide to. My hand did it, the way it used to reach for a pencil when a call came in, before the rest of me had heard the address. I put the key and the lace in the pocket of my raincoat and stood up with them.

Above me, in the square of the open door, Teddy stood with the lantern, a small stooped shape with the light behind him. He had said nothing since I went down. Now I heard him. “Joe,” he said. And then, quietly, again: “Joe.” It is a thing I had heard on the wire from people who found the one they had called about, the name said over and over in the voice of a man trying to wake someone in the next room.

I went up the ladder with the key against my hip. It was warm in my pocket. Above me, Teddy went on saying the name to the dark.

chapters.title: The Pit
chapters.html:
A policeman’s flashlight swung across the wall of the pit and found a rat.

The rat did not run. It sat on a bracket of the guide rail at about the height of my knee, with its forepaws together like a deacon at a graveside, and looked into the beam with the settled calm of a tenant who has been in residence longer than the landlord. The patrolman holding the light said a word Father Dziedzic would not have liked. For some seconds nobody in the boiler room of the Harbor Hotel did anything but consider the rat. Then Detective Karras, at the foot of the pit ladder, said “Excuse me” to it, quite politely, and set his tape measure down on the concrete.

It was twenty past twelve. Teddy had telephoned Central Station at five to, in the voice of a man reading a telegram to himself, and they had come: a patrol car, a second car, a photographer who turned the pit into a white room six times over and went away, and Dolan and Karras in the coats they had worn to the parade. I stood at the sill of the pit door with one hand on the iron. Dolan stood at my shoulder with his hat on the back of his head and his matchstick motionless. He had not said a word to me yet. He had looked at me and then at the pit, in that order, and I understood that the order was the message.

Karras measured. Seven feet from sill to floor; a ladder of seven rungs, slick where the oil off somebody’s boots had been trodden onto them; a squat iron buffer, its top edge bright where something had struck it. He wrote it all down in a notebook held shut by a rubber band, which he took off and put back on for each entry. He was twenty-nine, with clean fingernails and a Greek profile that had been wasted on the police, and he had brought Teddy the grey blanket off Lambert’s cot for his shoulders and called him “sir” three times, which was three more than anyone had called Teddy all night.

Dr. Lyman Ostrander came at half past twelve in a camel overcoat over striped pyjamas and carpet slippers, smelling of sleep and Sen-Sen, and went down the ladder one rung at a time like a man testing a bath. He was seventy and had signed forty years of death certificates, and he looked at Joe Lambert for about as long as it takes to unscrew a pen.

“A fall,” he said, to the pit at large. “The rungs are wet with oil, the man has a can in one hand, he misses the fourth. Left temple against the edge of the buffer plate. He would not have known it.” He straightened with a hand on his knee. “I’ll sign in the morning, Sergeant. Accidental.”

“Doctor,” I said from the sill. “His hands.”

They all turned. A flashlight beam came up the wall and across my face, which I thought unfair.

“What about his hands, Miss...?”

“Szymanski. Look at them.”

He looked, because he was an old man and polite. Lambert’s hands lay open on the concrete, palms up, white across the knuckles with old cab-rope scars. There was grease in the creases, years of it, where soap had given up. The fingers were clean. The palms were clean. Beside the right hand the brass oiler stood upright, and Karras, kneeling, tipped it toward the light and said, “Full, sir. Right to the spout.”

“He hadn’t started,” said Dolan.

“He’d come down to do the guide shoes. Those rungs are as slick as a fish, Doctor. A man who slips off a slick rung grabs at it. His palms would be black to the wrist.” I could hear my own voice, flat as a plate, the voice I had used on the wire for nine years when someone at the other end of it needed a fact and not a feeling. “I took calls from men who’d fallen off roofs and ladders and a church once. They all say the same thing. I grabbed.”

“Miss,” said Ostrander, with great kindness, “I have seen a great many dead men. They do not follow a pattern.”

“Doc says a fall,” said Dolan, and took me by the elbow.

He walked me back through the pipes as far as the boiler, where the heat came off its brick flank like a hand, and let go.

“You were here at midnight,” he said. “The night clerk phones it in at five to, and at ten past he tells Karras that Ruth Szymanski was standing at his elbow when he found it. Why were you standing at his elbow, Ruth?”

“Mr. Wozniak asked me to look at the cab. He’s had it in his head since Wednesday that somebody’s been at it.”

“At midnight.”

“He works nights. Midnight’s his noon.”

“And Lambert?”

“I wanted to ask him whether the guide shoes hum.”

Dolan looked at me. He took the matchstick out and looked at that instead. “A friend of Mr. Wozniak’s asks you to look at a lift in the dead of night, and you come, and you find the porter, and the first thing you do is get a good view of his hands.” He put the matchstick back. “You were never any good at it, Ruth. It’s the one thing I always liked about you, and the one thing I asked of you once.”

I said nothing. Behind him, at the foot of the stair, Karras had opened his notebook to a clean page. I watched him write a single word and underline it. I couldn’t read it upside down at that distance, but I would have bet the Waltham it wasn’t cab.

“Teddy,” said Dolan, over my shoulder. “Is that right? Did you ask her?”

Teddy sat on the cot in his blanket. His eyes came to me, once, and went away. “I did, Sergeant. The car has behaved strangely since the fifth. I thought that a woman of Miss Szymanski’s judgment...” He stopped there, for want of an end to it, and I owed him one.

That was when the stairs spoke. Someone was coming down them from the lobby, slowly, with the swish of quilted silk, and a cane with a rubber tip was set on each tread like a pencil being put down.

At the foot of the stair Ambrose Quill stopped. He wore a dark red quilted dressing gown tied with a cord, and soft leather slippers, and his silver hair was parted as exactly as if a professional had done it and set it. The cane lay over his left forearm like an umbrella. On his right cheek stood a single tear, which he did not wipe. I believed it. I’ve believed worse.

“Sergeant Dolan.” He cleared his throat twice. “They woke me only now. I came as soon as I could stand. Poor Joe. He has been with this house since 1930.”

“Mr. Quill. I’m sorry for your trouble.”

“It is the house’s trouble, Sergeant. Joe was the house.” He looked across the pipes at the open pit door, and I watched the tear travel to the corner of his jaw. Then the pale eyes found me. “Miss Szymanski. You are here before me again. I wonder whether you would do me the kindness of taking tea in the morning. Nine o’clock, in 806. There is something I ought to say, and I would rather say it in daylight than in a cellar.”

“Nine,” I said.

“I am obliged.” He bowed from the neck, to Dolan, to Teddy, and to the dead man he could not see, and went back up the stair, the quilted silk going before him.

Dolan watched until the silk was gone. “Ten years I’ve known that man,” he said, “and I’ve never once seen him in a dressing gown.”

“He’s allowed to wear one in his own hotel.”

“I know it.” The matchstick went round. “Go home, Ruth.”

I slept four hours in my clothes with my shoes on the floor beside me and Joe Lambert’s key under the pillow, a thing I’d have been ashamed of in a child. At nine I was in the Harbor lobby again, in daylight, with the fog burnt back to the water. Dorrie Nash stood behind the brass rail with no gum in her cheek and her eyes pink to the lids.

“He gave me a peppermint every Monday,” she said, to nobody, when she saw me. “He called me Miss Nash.” It was the only thing I ever heard her say in that building that wasn’t a rule.

The car was running again. I rode it up with a bellhop who studied the floor between us like a man at a graveside. The plug under the 8 was dry now, a cream coin that anyone could have pried up with a nail. Over the door the needle swung across its arc and settled on the eight a hair short of the mark, and past it the brass ran on another inch and a half to the tick with no number on it.

Quill opened the door of 806 himself. He was in the charcoal suit and the high collar, with the cane over his arm, looking like a man who had sat up all night and had it pressed afterward. The room was a sitting room like a captain’s cabin. A narrow bed made tight as a drum stood behind a lacquered screen. There was a round table at the window with the tea things laid out, two chairs, a shelf of black cloth ledgers like the ones in the office downstairs, and in the corner a squat green safe with a vase of bronze chrysanthemums on top, as if to apologise for it. The window gave on the ferry slip and the Sound beyond, grey on grey. Over the door hung a brass arc with a needle, a sister of the one in the cab, and below it, screwed to the plaster, a small brass toggle under a hinged glass cap, like the fire alarm in a school corridor. On a hook behind the door hung a dark red quilted dressing gown. It had been on him seven hours before. I looked at all of it left to right, the way I look at any room, and sat where he showed me.

“Tea,” said Quill, and poured. It was tarred rope again. “I owe you an apology and a correction, Miss Szymanski, and at my age I find they are very nearly the same animal. On Wednesday I told you that the Harbor has eight floors. It has nine.”

“You said the plans, the licence and the Board of Underwriters would tell me eight.”

“And so they will. They have been telling it since 1926.” He cleared his throat twice before he went on. I wrote it down. A hotel full of men with colds in a wet November, but I wrote it down anyway, on the back of the pink notice, under Estate and Marchand. “The Mezzanine was never put on the licence. It was the Calder Club once, in the dry years, a card room for old Mr. Calder’s friends. After Repeal it was shut. I have kept the key to it for twenty years.”

“Mezzanine.”

“Forgive me. The ninth floor, as I suppose I must call it now.” He had said it the way my mother says Hake Street, without noticing there was another way to say it. “A habit of the old days.”

“What happened on it on Tuesday night?”

“I do not know.” He set the pot down. “That is the plain truth, my dear, and I should be glad if you would believe the other plain truth with it. Teddy telephoned my room at ten past four. I came. A man helped me. We found Mr. Delaney on a cot in the Mezzanine, dead, and I knew that if it were known the hotel would be closed by Friday and sixty people turned out of their places: the maids, the kitchen, Miss Hightower, a porter who has been here since 1930. So I moved him. I put him in a bed he had paid for, and I told Teddy there was no ninth floor, which was cruel, and I told you the same, which was merely necessary. I did it for them. I would do it again.” Click, click. “It is a curious thing to find that one cannot go on telling a woman what she does not believe.”

“The man who helped you.”

“I will not name him. He is past being hurt by it, but I will not hang his name on a nail.”

“Joe Lambert.”

“I did not say so,” said Quill gently, and drank his tea.

I let a gull cross the window. “You told the police Mr. Delaney’s heart.”

“I told them what they would accept. Dr. Ostrander says heart; Dr. Ostrander says a great many things. But Joe has oiled those rails for twenty-two years, and I do not believe he came off a ladder in the twenty-third.” He turned his cup a quarter turn by the saucer. “A man has died in my house, and I think a second. I would like you to find the person who did it. I will pay you fifteen dollars a day and your expenses, and you may tell the Sergeant whatever you judge best.”

“I’m working for Mr. Wozniak.”

“Teddy cannot afford you for long. The Estate can.”

“The Estate’s lawyer paid me five hundred dollars last Thursday to say there was no ninth floor.”

Something went over his face, very fast, and was folded and put away. He sighed. “Gilbert,” he said. “Yes. I am only the Estate’s auditor, Miss Szymanski. Mr. Swain holds the pen, and sometimes he holds it too tightly. I count what I am shown.”

“And what are you shown?”

“A great deal less than you suppose. Think it over, my dear. Drink your tea.”

I drank it. It was good tea. He talked for ten minutes about the Dorset churchyard where his mother lay and a spaniel he had owned in 1904, and I listened, and liked him, and watched the glass cap on the toggle over his door take the light from the window and give it back.

In the corridor the oxblood nap had been brushed that morning, in long stripes, by one of Pearl Hightower’s girls. Across the stripes, from the door of 806 toward the lift, ran a line of small round dents, evenly spaced, each the size of a half dollar. I counted them. Eleven. I looked along the line for the odd one, as you look for the odd man in a queue, and there wasn’t one. They were as round as coins.

I stood there with Joe Lambert’s key in my pocket and a thin cup’s worth of tea going cold inside me. I put my hand in and found the brass cold. It had been warm all night, from him and then from me, and I couldn’t have told you when it stopped.

I liked Ambrose Quill. I stood in his corridor and noted that, as you note a draught, and could not have said why it worried me.

chapters.title: What Teddy Left Out
chapters.html:
Teddy Wozniak stood at the hot plate with his back to me, watching a pan of milk the way other men watch a horse they have money on. He had hung the maroon jacket on its chair, and in his shirtsleeves and waistcoat he looked narrower across the shoulders than he did behind a desk, like a boy sent to the tailor in his father’s clothes. He hadn’t asked what I would drink. He had put the pan on when he heard me on the stairs, all eighteen, the board that sang giving its note, and I had come in and sat at the oilcloth and let him.

“My sister’s remedy,” he said to the wall. “Hot milk. For grief, for fever, and for Russians.”

“I’ve had the shock, Mr. Wozniak. I had it last night, in a cellar. I’d like to get to the rest.”

“Yes.” The milk climbed the side of the pan. He lifted it off the ring half a second before it went over, and the half second cost him, because I heard the pan chatter against the rim of the glass as he poured. Below us in the shop Mrs. Sobczak dropped a tray, and the floor hummed and settled. “Please. Drink. It gives me something to look at while I decide.”

I drank. It had a skin on it. I took the skin out with the spoon, and he was kind enough not to see.

“Mr. Quill gave me tea this morning,” I said. “Room 806, nine o’clock. He told me the Harbor has a ninth floor.”

Teddy had been about to sit. He stopped with a hand on the chair back, and I watched the colour go out of his face from the forehead down, the way water leaves a basin: first the brow, then the cheeks, then the long upper lip, until the gold tooth was the only thing in it still carrying light. Then he sat.

“He told you.”

“He called it the Mezzanine. A card room in the dry years, he said. He’s kept the key to it for twenty years.”

“He said he would never.” It came out in a whisper, and he heard it, and tried again at speaking pitch. “Forgive me. In six years, if I may, Mr. Quill has not once said that word in my hearing. He said to me a single time, in the winter of 1947, that he had a great respect for the tank room above the Frieze, and did not wish to be told what he had no need to know. I took it as a promise. I believed it would hold to the end of his life.”

“He also told me he moved Mr. Maher. Himself, with another man, after you telephoned. To save the licence and sixty jobs.”
