“That is what I supposed.” His hands lay on the oilcloth and found no pencil, and settled for the corner of the blotter, which they squared. “When he told me that morning there was no ninth floor, I thought: he is closing the door on it. He is a gentleman, and he is protecting us, and he cannot say so. I have never been so grateful to a man. And now you say he speaks of it over tea.”

“He asked me to find out who killed them. Maher and Joe.”

“Of course he did.” There was relief in it, and the relief was what worried me. “He loved Joe.”

I looked at him loving Quill. You can’t argue with that across an oilcloth. The pillbox in his waistcoat made its dry fall of seeds, and he laid a hand flat over it, the way one covers a cough in church.

“Mr. Wozniak. On Thursday you told me you would say how you got to nine when you knew you could.”

“Yes.”

“Do you know it now?”

He looked at the crucifix over the door. “A man is dead who wished to tell you something and was not given the time,” he said. “I should prefer not to be the second. If I may, I will tell it in order, because it is the only way I am able. If I stop, please do not help me.”

I turned the pink notice over and wrote nothing on it.

He told it the way he might have said a rosary, with his eyes on his hands. In December of 1946 his sister’s husband, Stefan Kowal, sexton of St. Casimir’s, had come up the bakery stairs at midnight with a man, a woman and two girls who had walked off a Greek freighter that afternoon without a paper among them and with nowhere in Port Calder to sleep that a priest’s housekeeper wouldn’t count. The photograph on the shelf looked down on us while he said it, the heavy man in the sexton’s coat with a face like a locked door. “He had a temper like a kettle,” Teddy said, following my eyes. “It boiled, and then he wept, and then he carried your coal. In June of last year it stopped his heart in the vestibule of the church, at sixty-one. He is the one who ought to be telling you.”

Teddy had been fifteen years at the hotel by then, seven of them on nights. He knew a linen cupboard at the east end of the eighth floor with a padlock on it and no guest ever inside. He put the family in it for nine nights, with Pearl Hightower carrying soup up under the pillowcases in a laundry basket. On the ninth night, with one of the girls coughing, he did what he had not done in the fourteen years since he first found it out. He pushed on the back wall of the shelves, and it gave.

“A stair,” I said.

“A stair, and at the top of it a floor.” He lifted a hand and put it down. “That winter there were four. By spring there were nine more, and Stefan was carrying iron cots up the service stairs one at a time with a laundry tag tied to each, and Joe Lambert was taking the car up on his rounds with a basket of folded sheets that was heavier going than coming. Pearl fed them. Joe kept the car. I kept the desk, and the stairs, and said nothing to anyone for six years.” The tin rattled. “Three hundred and eleven people, Miss Szymanski. All with names.”

“You counted.”

“I did not need to count. It is written down.” He shut his mouth on the end of it, a second late, and I let the words go by like a streetcar I meant to catch at the next stop.

“Maher,” I said.

“Mr. Maher was Stefan’s friend at the Customs. A tally clerk who could not add, he used to say, whenever he wished to add one more name for us.” Teddy turned his glass a quarter turn on the oilcloth. I had watched another man do that with a teacup that morning, and I put the thought down where I could find it. “He was kind to us for two years. Afterward he was something else. I will not say what, of a dead man, in my own kitchen, with his body not yet in the ground.”

“And the key.”

“There are three. Joe’s, which you carry. Mine.” Two fingers touched his watch pocket. “And the one Mr. Quill keeps in his safe, which to my knowledge has never been out of it. At the lobby panel, beside the call plate, there is a keyhole you would take for the electrician’s. I turn it and the car comes down from wherever it is, like a dog called in. Inside the cab you lift the painted plug with a thumbnail. Mr. Quill’s man painted it over that morning, but paint is only paint. You put in the key, press the eight, and hold it to a slow count of three. The car goes on past eight for six seconds more. And then it stays.” He looked up. “It is deaf to the lobby, you understand. It stays on nine until somebody turns a key at the panel to fetch it home, and all that while the needle sits in the dark. That is what I saw.”

“Joe told you it was sulking.”

“Joe said the car was sulking and the guests should use the service lift. In twenty years Joe did not lie to me, and that night he looked at his shoes and lied, and I let him. Somebody had gone up with a key. I thought it was he. I thought he had his reasons.”

I let that sit between us a while. Everyone who knew the way up to that floor was in this room, or in the ground, or in a building I could see from the window.

“Then tell me why you lied to me,” I said. “On Thursday, at this table, you had never seen him before Friday.”

“Because of a thing my sister keeps.”

“A book.”

His eyes came up. They were pale brown, wet at the rims, and for the first time since I’d known him there was no apology anywhere in them.

“Black,” I said. “A brass clasp. She held it against her chest at the Gospel as if somebody might take it off her at the elevation.”

“You see hands.”

“Hands and shoes. The face comes last.”

“Then you will understand me when I say you must not ask what is in it.” He drew a breath through his nose. “If you read it, Miss Szymanski, you will burn it. Not today. But you will.”

“I don’t burn things, Mr. Wozniak.” It was out before I’d looked at it, and I thought of a typewriter case on a filing cabinet, behind a door with a new Yale lock.

“No,” he said, studying me with something that was not quite hope. “No, I did not think you did.”

I tried the next door. “A singer called Marchand stood across Front Street from your hotel for ten minutes just after midnight on election night. White gloves. Then she crossed over.”

His hand left the blotter. “Who saw her?”

“A counterman at Tommy’s. I saw her myself on Saturday, in a dressing room, with a snapshot of a low ceiling and some coat hooks stuck in the mirror.”

He closed his eyes. “Ten past twelve. She asked for Mr. Delaney by name. I told her he had retired, which a guest does at midnight, and she said then she would leave him a note, and I looked down at the register so as not to see which way she went. The Councilman’s people were coming out of the Pacific Room by then, forty at once, wanting their coats and their bills. When I looked up she had gone. I did not see the lift. I did not see her come down.” He opened them. “I told the Sergeant no one had asked for Mr. Delaney. It was the second lie I have told a policeman in my life, and I told it as though I had been practising.”

“She was one of yours.”

He said nothing. In a dispatcher’s ear that is an answer. A line that stays open with nobody on it is still a line.

“Say again where everyone was,” I said. “Midnight to four. In order.”

He gave it to me the way he gave a guest his keys, one at a time, laid on the counter. Joe in the boiler room, he supposed. Pearl at home by then. The party emptying until past one, the Pacific Room staff carrying out chairs. “And Mr. Quill retired at ten minutes to twelve. I saw him cross the lobby from the party. I did not see him again until I rang his room at ten past four.”

“You rang him. He was in his room.”

“If you are thinking what you are thinking, you may spare yourself.” It was the first sharp thing I had heard him say, and it turned his ears pink. “At five minutes past two the operator rang the desk. Santa Barbara for 806. I put the plug in myself and wrote it in the toll book, the time and the room and Miss Calder’s name. He telephones the elder niece when he cannot sleep. She is seventy-eight and deaf, and he is obliged to shout. I saw the lamp for 806 burning on the board at a quarter to three, when I looked up at the dial, and dark at half past three when I looked again. I thought: poor man. He has no one else to talk to at that hour.” He nodded at the door. “The book is on the desk. You may see my handwriting.”

I wrote 2:05, Santa Barbara, 806 on the back of the notice, and under it, because I’d have put down his weight if he had offered it, lamp 2:45, dark 3:30. He watched me do it with the look of a man who has gone to the dentist and been told it was nothing.

By the Waltham it was twenty to eleven when I stood up. The hotel had given him the evening for Joe, he said at the door. A relief clerk named Okonski had the desk until midnight, and Teddy had spent an hour of the afternoon at Mt. Zion with the deacons, a white man in a maroon jacket among forty deacons, who had given him coffee and not asked why he had come. I hadn’t asked either. He told me anyway, as a man pays a debt in small coins.

I went out onto the landing and started down. He came after me as far as the top of the flight and put his hand on the banister, a rail polished by the palms of everyone who had ever hurried on those stairs.

“You took Joe’s key,” he said. It wasn’t a question.

I stopped on the fifth stair. “Pearl told you.”

“Pearl told me the shoelace was not on him when they carried him up. And you put your hand to that pocket whenever someone says nine. You are not a woman who touches her pockets.” His own hand went to the watch pocket and came away. “He wore it twenty years. He lent it to no one, not to me. It is yours to carry now and I do not ask for it. If you must go up, then go. I would rather you did not see it empty.”

“Empty.”

“They are all gone since October. The last family left on the seventeenth. There is only the furniture, and what they wrote on the walls.”

I went down three more. The board that sang sang under my shoe, and he winced for it, as though a plank were a person he had to answer for.

“Miss Szymanski.”

I looked up. He stood at the head of the flight in the light of the bare bulb, small and stooped, the white eyebrows pinned over his eyes like a pair of moth wings.

“Don’t go up,” he said.

I waited. Below us a tray went down on the bakery floor, and the whole stair hummed with it.

“If you go,” said Teddy Wozniak, quite quietly, “count the steps.”

chapters.title: A Floor Nobody Built
chapters.html:
The key went into the hole the way a tongue goes to the gap where a tooth was, without being told where to look. Nobody had painted that hole. Whoever dabbed the cream over the plug on the fifth of November had painted what could be seen, and a brass keyway under a half dollar of dry paint is not a thing that can be seen until a woman splits her thumbnail down the middle prying the coin up, which I had done a minute before, in the cab, with the door closed and the light on and Teddy Wozniak’s card on the desk outside saying he was away.

It was one in the morning by my father’s Waltham, three minutes to by the lobby clock, which runs slow and has never been ashamed of it. I had walked from Hake Street in rain that came down so straight you could have hung washing on it. The Harbor lobby was empty in the way a church is empty on a Tuesday: the fern in its brass pot, the marble gone dull under one lamp, the desk with its blotter squared and its pencil laid parallel to the edge. The jacket was gone from the chair. The card said NIGHT CLERK AWAY FROM DESK, PLEASE RING, and beside it stood a brass bell. I didn’t ring it. A bell has a way of fetching people, and I hadn’t come to be fetched.

Above the lift door the lobby repeater showed L. Inside, the Certificate of Inspection hung where it had hung when Joe Lambert read it out to me, in oak and brass and a glass that gave me back my own hat. Landings served: 9. Floors open to public: 8. I looked at the eight buttons, L and two to eight, and at the numbers on the arc over the door, and at the plug that was no longer a plug but a hole with a key in it. Then I pressed the 8 with my left hand, and with my right I turned Joe’s key a quarter turn to the right, and I counted.

One. Two. Three, slowly, the way you count when the number is a promise.

The car rose, with the small shudder at the second floor and the hum in the cables that comes up through the soles of the feet. I counted that too, because I count everything: thirty-eight seconds to the eighth, where it ought to have stopped. The needle crossed the numeral 8. The car did not stop. The brass ran on another inch and a half to the tick with no number on it, and the needle followed it, and sat. Six seconds. The shudder came again, softer, and the door slid open on the dark.

I’d bought a nickel torch at Gundersen’s for a dollar nineteen and meant to charge it to Mr. Wozniak. I didn’t switch it on at once. I stood on the sill with the cab light laying a yellow slab across the floor in front of me, and smelled it: cold lamp oil, chalk, laundry soap, mouse, and under those the ghost of boiled cabbage and wet wool, which is the smell of a great many people having once been afraid in the same place and trying to make it smell like supper.

I stepped out. The floor was felt, a thick grey runner laid over the boards the way a piano teacher muffles a practice room. I lifted my hand and my palm lay flat on the ceiling without my arm straightening, plaster, dry, cold as a plate. That told me where I was better than any needle could. Then I put the torch on and counted paces under my breath with my left hand trailing the wall.

Fourteen. At the thirteenth the ceiling dropped, where a steel girder crossed under the plaster and brought it down to six feet and an inch or two; I ducked it without being told, as people must have done before me, and the corridor widened by a yard to make room for a door on each side. On the right-hand wall ran a rail at the height of my knee, with small brass hooks screwed into it every foot. One of them held a mitten. It was red wool, a child’s, with the thumb darned in green.

I had seen that rail. I had seen it behind a woman in white gloves, in a snapshot stuck in a dressing-room mirror, under a ceiling that touched her head.

The plaster on the left was chalked.

I held the torch on it a long time. The names began at the height of a child’s hand and went up as far as a tall man could reach, and they were in every hand there is: block capitals, a schoolteacher’s copperplate, a scrawl by someone who learned his letters late. They were first names only. Wacław. Halina. Józef. Beside them, dates, in the order the Old World writes them, day and month and year, and here and there a small drawing. A cross. A star. A fish with a smile. Rūta 3.XI.47. Andris. Oksana, 12/1/50. Under a ship drawn in six strokes, with smoke going off the funnel in a curl, three names in a child’s block letters: JANEK. BASIA. ZUZIA. Higher up, in a copperplate that leaned like a woman into wind: Irena 21/10/49.

I thought of a low voice saying Write it however you like. I thought of it and put it down.

Along one stretch of wall at the height of my shoulder, every name carried the same date. Halina. Teodor. Marta. Józef. I counted nineteen before the plaster went bare where someone had rubbed with a sleeve, and every one of the nineteen read 15/3/48. Monday the fifteenth of March. I know what day of the week it was, because the night before I had sat at a wire-room desk in a headset with a carbon sheet under my hands, and a man with a worried voice had asked me whether cars would clear the Pier 6 gate, and I had told him the wire had no information.

I had put my thumb on a pencilled 31 in the Harbor Commission, and a tailor had measured thirty-one people for coats by lantern, and here were nineteen of them, in chalk, with their names.

I don’t know how long I stood there. The rain drummed on the terracotta outside, which from the inside is a flat rattle like peas dropped on a skin; every louvre in the Frieze had been painted black on the inside, and not a thread of street-lamp came through. The torch beam shook a little. I held the wrist with the other hand.

Declan Maher, then. A tally clerk with small clean hands who had been a friend to this wall for two years and afterward something else. He had bled Ferrante a hundred dollars a month, and Ferrante at least had a hall and forty men and a toothpick. What did he get from a woman with a stage name and no country? From a man who had written Józef on a plaster wall and gone to drive a taxi in Chicago? He had known three hundred and eleven names, and every one was a handle. And every one of them had a reason to want him quiet.

I had been hired by a man who sat across an oilcloth and mourned a dead stranger and never once said what the stranger was. I was to avenge a leech on the back of this wall. My client had lied to me from the first minute, with his pencil and his pillbox, and I could not have said he was wrong to. The question I’d carried up in the car was who killed a man nobody knew. The question on the plaster in front of me was a different one. Who is keeping this, and who gets hurt if it comes out.

I went on, because the alternative was to stay.

Five doors led off the corridor, three on the left and two on the right, and in the five rooms stood forty-two iron cots. I counted them room by room, nine and eight and eight and nine and eight, with the grey blankets folded to squares at the foot and pillows in bare ticking. A number had been painted at the head of each frame in white, and I recognised Pearl Hightower’s hand in them before I could have said why: a numeral that had never been in a hurry. There was a kitchenette with a gas ring and a long table covered in oilcloth, a row of enamel mugs on hooks with a name inked on each handle, a copper boiler in a room with a drain in the floor. A calendar of saints’ days hung by the stove. It was open at November, and someone had gone on turning the pages as the days went, to the thirteenth, Saint Stanislaus Kostka, and then stopped. On the wall beside it, at the height of my knee, was a pencil drawing of a train. It had a funnel and four wheels and a face on the engine. Whoever drew it had given it a passenger in every window.

At the far end the corridor opened into a long room, thirty-odd feet of it, with the card tables stacked against the walls in leaning towers under their green baize and a chandelier hung from the ceiling in a bedsheet gone grey, like a cow in a coat. In the east wall stood a safe the colour of old bottle glass, taller than I am, with a dial the size of a saucer and a line of gold lettering worn to a gleam too faint to read. The dust lay on everything. In the middle of the room somebody had pulled a single cot out from the wall and left it, and the mattress still held the long shallow dent of a man, as mattresses do. Not like a certain bedspread on eight.

On the third table from the door, which had been left unstacked, there were two clean circles in the dust. Each was the size of a tumbler. They stood a hand’s width apart, and a week of settling had begun to take them back. I put my torch down level with them and looked along the baize. Nothing else had been set on it. Teddy’s two glasses, then. Somebody had lifted them and carried them off, and nobody had thought to dust.

Behind me, along the corridor, the cables spoke.

It was a hollow knock in the shaft, a hum, and then the thin, descending whine of the car going home. I ran. Fourteen paces back, and I counted them, because that’s what I do when I’m frightened. The car doors had shut. The shaft door was a blank brass-bound panel. On the wall beside it, where on any other floor there would have been a call button, there was bare plaster; nobody calls a car to a floor that isn’t there.

I put my ear to the door. Far down the shaft, the weights were still moving.

I thought of the lobby panel, and a key I didn’t have. Then I thought of a room I had sat in at nine o’clock that morning, drinking tea I’d not much wanted, and over its door a brass arc with a needle on it, and under the arc a small brass toggle behind a hinged glass cap. Someone had been sitting under that arc in the small hours, with a hand next to a glass cap, watching a needle come to rest on a blank.

I didn’t say whose room it was. There was no one to say it to, and the corridor had heard worse.

Two men had carried a dead man from this floor to 807, one night last week, and they had not taken him through the lobby. I went back along the dust with the torch held low, as a dispatcher reads a street from a map, and I found where the dust was trodden into a broad path of feet, running from the cot to the east wall beside the safe. The oak panelling there had been laid in long boards, and one of the boards was an inch narrower than its neighbours, and there was a thumb-catch in it painted to match the grain. It swung inward on a hinge as silent as a church door.

The stair went down at once and steeply, bare wood on a steel stringer, no wider than a man’s shoulders. I counted aloud. At the sixth step my foot came down on a tread that was not nailed, and it rocked, and I went forward with the torch beam leaping across the wall and caught the rail in time. After that I put my feet down like a woman crossing a creek. Fourteen. A door with a barrel bolt on my side of it, oiled, bright. I drew the bolt, and the door opened inward on a wall of sheets.

The linen cupboard smelled of bleach and lavender and hot iron, and it was lit by a single bulb on a cord. In front of the shelves, in a grey uniform with her back as straight as a shelf, stood Pearl Hightower. Her gold spectacles hung on their chain against her chest. In her left hand she held a ring of forty keys closed in her fist, and not one of them made a sound.

“I do not guess, Miss Szymanski,” she said. “I counted the car going up.”

“It’s gone two in the morning, Miss Hightower.” I switched the torch off. My hands wanted something to do, and I let them have a pocket. “I’d thought you’d be home.”

“Mr. Wozniak telephoned my sister’s house at eleven and asked would I sit up in the building tonight. He did not say for whom. He did not have to.” She looked at my shoes, then at my hands, then at the dust on the knees of my stockings, and drew her own conclusions at the speed of a woman counting pillowcases. “I counted it going up, and I counted it coming down without you. At nine minutes to two, by the clock in this room. There is one way out of that floor for a person without a key, and I came and stood at the end of it.”

“Who sent the car down?”

“I do not guess.”

“You know.”

“I know what time it was.” The gold rims caught the bulb. “You have seen it, then.”

“I’ve seen the hooks,” I said. “And the wall.”

She did not move her face, not by the thickness of a hair. But the fist with the keys went white at the knuckle, and stayed white. “They were children,” said Pearl Hightower. “Some of them. I will tell you nothing of where they are now. Some are in Chicago and some in Spokane and some in the ground at Calvary, and I fed every one of them with my own hands for six years, and I should be obliged if you would not make me feed anything else on that floor. Come.”

She took me by the elbow. Her grip was like a clothes-peg. She put out the bulb, and locked the cupboard behind us with a key she found without looking, and walked me down a flight of linoleum stairs that smelled of floor wax and onions, and along a passage behind the kitchen where a night cook’s radio was playing a dance band very low to nobody. I had the sense of being returned.

“Miss Hightower. Teddy. Where is he?”

“In the boiler room, in Joseph Lambert’s chair, with his thermos. He will not come up until you have gone.” She stopped at the service door on Ferry Slip Row. Outside the rain went on, in the light of a single lamp. “Go home, Miss Szymanski. Go home and be sorry.”

“I am sorry.”

“Then you are halfway.”

She opened the door with her right hand. The ring of keys she took in her left and held against her hip, closed in her fist, so tightly that the knuckles stood out like a row of pale buttons and not a single key touched another. I stepped out into the rain. She did not say goodnight. The door shut on the lamp, and behind it, as it had never sounded for six years, nothing chimed at all.

chapters.title: What the Certificate Says
chapters.html:
A toy locomotive came out of a mountain of inspection files, drew four freight cars and a caboose along the edge of the desk blotter, and stopped with a small electric click at the foot of the telephone.

“The Overland Limited,” said Hubert Pomeroy, without looking up from a transformer the size of a bread box. “Due in Walla Walla at ten past nine. You’ll forgive me, Miss Szymanski. If I take my hand off the throttle she goes over the edge into the Division’s cabinet, and the cabinet holds the boilers for 1939.”

The State Division of Elevators occupied the third floor of the State Building behind a door lettered in gilt, and Mr. Pomeroy occupied most of the Division. He was a stout man of fifty-eight with a pink scalp, a watch chain that ended in a small brass elevator car, and the hands of someone who handles delicate machinery and cannot be trusted with a teacup. His office had no floor to speak of. A sheet of plywood the size of a door lay across two filing cabinets and a pair of sawhorses and carried a layout: a balsa station marked WALLA WALLA, a water tower, three tiny trees, a man the size of a clothes-peg waving a red lantern at nothing, and a tunnel built out of stacked State inspection folders, Form E-12, through which the Overland went in and out of the passenger elevators of Port Calder like a thought.

I’d come up in the State Building’s own car. Its certificate said Landings served: 6 and the panel had six buttons. I counted them twice. It was a habit that had been getting worse for about nine days.

“I’m here about certificate 4471,” I said.

“I have no certificate 4471.” He said it to the transformer, and a good deal too fast. “That is to say I have every certificate in the district, in a manner of speaking, so it’s difficult to be certain which — mind the signal, you’re standing on Pendleton. Sit. No, not there, that’s the siding. There.”

“The Harbor Hotel. Front Street and Ferry Slip Row. An Otis of 1926, converted in ’41. You signed it last March.”

The locomotive did a complete lap of the blotter. Then Hubert Pomeroy sat down on a stool with a train under his elbow and put both pink hands flat on the plywood, and the little man with the lantern shook.

“Joseph Lambert,” he said. “I read it in the Beacon. Page nine, under a notice about a spaniel. ‘Porter Dies in Fall.’ I had shaken that man’s hand every March since 1938, Miss Szymanski. He gave me a butterscotch. He hummed a hymn the whole way up, and I can’t hear that hymn now without wanting to examine a governor rope.” He swallowed. “Mrs. Pomeroy says I have not eaten since Wednesday. She says it as if I were doing it to annoy her.”

He got up, found a green cloth register on the shelf behind the Overland’s water tower, and opened it to the H’s with a hand that took two goes. Passenger Elevators, District 4. The Harbor Hotel stood at the top of a page in a careful engineer’s script. Under it ran the years, one line apiece, from 1938 to this March, and on every line the same two figures in the column headed Landings.

“Nine,” I said.

“Nine landings, eight floors open to the public. The Division counts landings. The Building Department counts floors.” He lifted his hands in a gesture of the purest helplessness. “We do not read each other’s mail. It’s a principle of good government. If the two ever met in a drawer, Miss Szymanski, there would be an inquiry, and an inquiry is a thing that happens to men with train sets.”

“Did you go to nine?”

“I rode to it. Every March.” He answered the question the way a man steps onto ice, with a foot at a time. “Joe turned a key and held the button for a count. We went on past the eighth for what I should call six seconds. The door opened on a very dark corridor and a very clean floor. I tested the door interlock, the buffer, the governor, and the gate, and I signed. I did not step out. I’m not a man who steps out. I am hired to look at ropes, and what is at the other end of a rope is the owner’s affair.”

“You never asked what was there.”

“Once. In 1939. Joe said it was machinery. A gentleman on the Estate’s staff said it was tanks. A week later, a ham arrived.” He closed his eyes. “Every December since. An eleven-pound Virginia ham with a card, with the compliments of the Trustee, and Mrs. Pomeroy glazes it with cloves. I do not say it is a bribe. A bribe is something you can be accused of. A ham is a courtesy.”

“That’s a long run of courtesy.”

“She makes a very good glaze.” He wiped his lip with his thumb. “Miss Szymanski, a man dies falling off a ladder he has climbed for twenty-two years. I wake at three and see the rails. I do not sleep. I know very well what I’ve been counting.” The Overland, which had been idling, he nudged into motion again with one finger, and watched it go as another man might watch a lit window across a street. “When I am frightened I run the Overland. She gets to Walla Walla every time.”

“I need you to say it to a judge.”

“If my name is not in the papers.”

“A court keeps a record, Mr. Pomeroy.”

“Then in a very small court.” He found a pencil and discovered he didn’t need it. “Give me ten minutes.”

It took him eleven, at a typewriter older than mine with two fingers and a rising colour, and at the end of it I held a single sheet on Division letterhead, certified a true extract from the register, signed H. Pomeroy, Inspector, and stamped with a seal. He breathed on the stamp afterward, as though it might hatch.

I telephoned Central Station from a booth in the State Building lobby. Dolan was out; Karras took the message in the voice of a young man who has been told to write down everything, and said he would give it to the Sergeant personally. The message was the arithmetic. At twenty past twelve a black-and-white Ford drew up at the kerb on Front Street in the rain, opposite the Harbor, and Dolan climbed out of the passenger side with his collar up and a matchstick in the corner of his mouth.

“The arithmetic,” he said.

“Read this.”

He read it under the lamp-post, holding it over his hat to keep the wet off, and then he read it again, slowly, the way a man reads a menu in a foreign language. A flat brown evidence envelope stood a corner out of his breast pocket; I knew the shape as I know a Christmas card. When he put the page in beside it he touched the two of them, twice, like a man checking for his wallet.

“A paperwork matter,” he said.

“Count it, Frank.”

“Count what?”

“The hotel. From the kerb. Count the rows of windows, and when you’ve done, count it again and include the cake.”

“The what?”

“The cornice. Fourteen feet of terracotta waves and fish. Count the fish.”

He took the matchstick out of his mouth. He turned his head from left to right in the rain, from the lobby row up, one, two, the way a man goes up a flight of stairs in the dark, with his lips moving. I stood beside him. I’d stood at that exact spot nine days before and arrived at nine on my second try. He got to eight. He stopped at the line of louvres under the terracotta and looked at it for the length of a long breath. Then his eyes went up and across the whole fourteen feet of the Frieze, all the dolphins and rippling waves, and I heard him say nine as softly as a man saying a name in church. He took off his hat.

The rain fell on his thin sandy hair. Karras, in the car, lowered his window an inch.

“Twenty-two years,” said Dolan. “I’ve been drunk under that building, and sober under it, and in a wedding party under it, and I would have sworn to eight in front of a judge.”

“You’d have been right about the windows.”

“I’ve been walking under a fish for twenty years.” He put the hat back on. “All right. Let’s go and ask the man.”

We went in. Dorrie Nash was behind the brass rail with a black ribbon pinned to her collar and her gum stopped in her cheek, and she said good afternoon to us both in the voice of someone who had been told to. Before we had crossed the marble, the door of the office behind the desk opened, as though the room had been waiting for him to come out of it, and Ambrose Quill stepped through with the cane over his left forearm and his silver hair parted as exactly as ever.

He was in the charcoal suit and the high collar. He came toward us, and halfway across the lobby he put the cane down on the marble and tapped it, once, softly, with a rubber tip that made no sound at all but a kind of apology. He had not tapped it for me.

“Sergeant Dolan. Miss Szymanski. How kind.” He cleared his throat twice. “You will take tea.”

“No, thank you, sir. I want to see the ninth floor.”

“The ninth floor,” said Quill, and his face rearranged itself with the mildest sadness. “Ah. Miss Szymanski has been telling you of the Mezzanine. I feared I had been indiscreet, Sergeant, in a moment of grief, with a young woman who has been a good deal tried this week. It is a tank loft. The State is so good as to call it a landing, since the car goes up to it for service, and the Certificate says so in a manner that I have always thought rather fanciful. The licence says eight floors open to the public, and that is the fact, because the public has never in its history been admitted. I gave a pet name to a machinery space to a lady who was distressed, and I regret that she took me for a man with a secret.”

“I’d like to see it,” said Dolan.

“Naturally. Come, and see the whole of what the car does.”

We rode up, the three of us, Quill pressing the 8 with the silver collar of his cane. The cab smelled of floor polish and warm brass. I stood nearest the panel, and as the car began to climb, I put out my thumb and found the plug.

It was polished. It had been cream; now it was brass, bright, clean as a new button, and it sat dry in its hole. I lifted the edge with my nail, and it came up the way a cork comes out of a bottle that has been uncorked before. Under it, flush with the panel, shone a second disc of brass, solid, filed smooth, with a few fine scratches round the rim where the file had slipped. There was no keyway. There was nothing for a key to go into at all.

“Mr. Quill?” said Dolan.

“The Otis people sealed it on Thursday morning, Sergeant.” Quill spoke gently, to the Certificate on the wall. “After poor Joe, I could not sleep for thinking of a stranger with a key in a moving car. I rang the depot at eight, and a man came at nine. And since Joe’s own key has not been found,” he turned his pale eyes on me for exactly as long as courtesy allows and perhaps a second beyond it, “I do hope it is in kind hands.”

Thursday morning. The car had gone up at one o’clock, with me in it, and by nine someone had filled the hole with brass and filed it.

I said nothing. The needle swung to the eight, a hair short of the mark, and the car stopped. There was no stir beyond it. Dolan stood in the corridor of the eighth floor in his wet hat, looking at a wall of oxblood carpet, a row of doors, a window onto the light well, and a cream door at the end lettered LINEN. He knocked at the nearest wall with his knuckle, once, and listened to it, and I watched him realise that listening to a wall tells you about the wall.

When we came down, Gilbert Swain was standing on the lobby marble with his hat in his hand.

I have never learned where he comes from. The cuffs were anchors, the hair oil was fresh, and the bay rum arrived about two seconds before he did. “Sergeant!” He had the smile of a man delighted to find that nobody has been hurt. “Would the Department inspect a bank without papers? Would it examine the Governor’s mansion on the word of a lady with a ledger? Any examination of these premises will be on a warrant, signed by a judge, and the Estate will cooperate in every particular. Naturally.”

“Gilbert,” said Quill, “the Sergeant is our guest.”

“The Sergeant is a public officer, Mr. Quill, and the Estate has insurers.” Swain’s eyes found mine and slid off like a coin off a wet table. “Would we want it said the Estate had permitted an unauthorised search? Would anyone?”

Quill spread his long yellow-white hands, a man overruled by his lawyer, which is the natural order, and he looked at Dolan with the look of a vicar who has been caught in a draught. “You see how it is, Sergeant. I am only an auditor.”

Dolan said, “Thank you for the tea I didn’t have, Mr. Quill,” and walked out into the rain, and I went after him.

He stopped under the awning at the kerb with his back to the hotel doors. Karras had put the window up again.

“I need a judge, Ruth,” he said, low. “I’d need a judge if I had a floor. And all I’ve got is a ledger page that says a hotel has an extra landing, which is a paperwork matter, and a trespass you can’t admit to.”

I kept my face where it was. It wasn’t enough, not for a man who had read it across a switchboard for eight years. “I haven’t said I was anywhere.”

“You didn’t have to. You’ve been looking at that brass like it owed you money.” The matchstick went across. “The Deputy Chief retires tomorrow. Rafferty wants quiet till he’s got his clock. Give me forty-eight hours. I’ll try to get him to sign a request. I’ll try. I’m not promising a thing, and you’re not to touch that lift.”

“What lift?”

“That one.” He nodded across the street. “Tomorrow night they’re feeding him at the Harbor. The Pacific Room, eight o’clock, chicken. I’ve got a spare seat, and I’d rather it was yours than the Deputy Chief’s brother-in-law’s. Wear a dress.”

“Frank.”

“I know.” He turned up his collar. “I know.”

He gave me nothing else. He got into the Ford, and Karras pulled out into Front Street, and I stood under the awning with my hands in my pockets and Joe Lambert’s key lying in the left one, a bit of brass that fitted nothing.

At six I walked to Tommy’s. The pie clock on the wall ran twenty minutes fast, as it had run all week, and the counterman had a ladle in each hand and no expression at all. I took the stool at the window, ordered a coffee, and watched the hotel across Front Street through my own reflection.

The windows went up, row on row, lit and dark and lit, and above the eighth row the Frieze stood in the lamplight with its waves and its fish. For a while there was nothing. Then, at the far end of the cornice, behind a louvre, a small yellow light came on and moved left to right along the black band, and stopped, and moved again.

It was a lantern. Someone had gone up by a stair I now knew the number of and was walking the Calder Club with a light, looking for a piece of paper that did not walk off.

Across the street, at the kerb, a black-and-white Ford sat with its engine off. Karras was in it. He had the notebook on his knee, closed, with the rubber band round it, the way a man sits when he has seen a thing and does not yet know how to spell it.

In the cab of the lift on the other side of that wall, I thought, a coin of new brass was shining where there had been a hole. The coffee went cold in front of me. I counted the fish on the Frieze, and then, to be sure, I counted the light.

chapters.title: Under the Hatband
chapters.html:
The Police Benevolent Association Band, eleven men in braided tunics, three of them Lutherans, played “The Wearing of the Green” for the retirement of a man who had been born in Dayton, Ohio, and it was the first dry night in two weeks. A moon like a clean dinner plate stood over Calder Sound. The Pacific Room’s tall windows were open at the top for the cigar smoke, and the cold came in at them and met the chicken.

I sat at table six in the one dress I own that isn’t black, which is navy wool and had last been to my father’s funeral, and the hat I’d worn for Plum. Dolan sat on my left in a dinner jacket that had been rented, with the tags still on the lining, and a gold ring on a chain tucked out of sight under his shirt. On his right sat a lieutenant from Traffic and his wife. Between the pickled beets and the roast capon I learned a good deal about the department’s pension plan, none of it cheerful. Karras sat at the next table, eating very neatly and watching the door like a boy who has been told not to.

The room held three hundred. I counted the heads of the men I knew and then, to be honest, the exits. At the head table beneath a banner reading GOD BLESS OUR DEPUTY CHIEF sat Desmond Rafferty himself, sixty years old and built like a mail chute, with white hair cut square across the nape and a face the colour of rare beef. On one side of him was the District Attorney, Hollis Barnwell, a thin careful man who cut his capon into equal pieces and ate them in order. On the other was Everett Plum, pink as a ham under the lights, the stickpin winking, passing his handkerchief across his lip every forty seconds, so that I began to time it. Gilbert Swain sat three seats along with his back turned to the room. Far down the table, in a white dinner jacket and a white carnation, his cane laid across his knees, Ambrose Quill was explaining something to Mrs. Barnwell with a gentle forefinger, and she was nodding as though to the Gospel.

At the table behind the band, with an orange on his plate that no one had given him and a hat on the chair beside him, Aldo Ferrante was peeling it.

Rafferty rose for the toast. He spoke for twenty minutes. He told us what forty years of service had taught him, which was chiefly that a good policeman gets to the corner before the crowd, and when he came to the line about the women who had served in the radio room in the early days, and how a brave voice on the wire had kept more men alive than a company of bayonets, he found my eye across the room and lifted his glass.

“Ruth Anne Szymanski,” he said. “Where is she? The best voice on the wire. I told Frank, you’ll bring her back one day.”

There was a patter of applause. I had my hands in my lap and my father’s watch against my wrist, and I put the two together until the clapping stopped. The man at the head table was smiling at me, and I knew the order he had given on a March night in 1948, because it had come down a line to me by way of a sergeant, and I had typed it, as I know my own address. Cars out of the area, 2300 to 0030. I smiled back at him, the way you do to a dog you intend to go on living beside.

“Smile,” said Dolan beside me, without moving his lips. “Then eat something.”

“I’m smiling.”

“That’s what you do when you’re not.”

The band struck up something I would rather not have been told was the Port Calder Police Anthem, and the room rose, and Ambrose Quill, who had come down the aisle against the crowd with the cane over his arm, like a man carrying a lantern through a fair, put his long hand lightly on my sleeve.

“Miss Szymanski. You must let me show you the one handsome thing in this room.”

It was a photograph on the piano. The Pacific Room’s baby grand stood by the stage with its lid down, and on it, in a silver frame the size of a tea tray, a family had been arranged on a lawn under a monkey-puzzle tree: a stout old man with a watch chain, a lady in a hat, two women in white with parasols and the same long chin. Quill held the cane before him with both hands.

“Mr. Hallam Calder, in 1913, with his wife and his nieces. I stood behind the photographer and held the plate.” He cleared his throat twice. “The ladies in white are Miss Honor and Miss Verity. They are in Santa Barbara now, the last of the line, God keep them. They have not seen Port Calder in twenty years. Miss Honor is somewhat deaf, I’m told. She writes me at Christmas in a very large hand.”

“They own all this?”

“They own, my dear, a name.” He smiled at the glass. “The rest is a trust.”

His shoes were black and flat and clean to the welt, and the rubber tip of the cane had come to rest on the carpet between them, a perfect round, the colour of a new eraser. I looked at it long enough for him to notice me looking, and he turned the cane a quarter turn on its tip and went on smiling.

Plum caught me at the cloakroom corridor. He came out of nowhere, sweating, the handkerchief in one fist and a water glass in the other that rattled against his teeth.

“Miss Szymanski! Friends!” There was no one else there. “A moment. I want it understood. Whatever happened at my little celebration on the fourth, it was, it was a conflagration of circumstance, you follow me, an inadvertical thing, and I had no part. A pier is a lease. I have never lifted a pencil in the matter of a berth. Two men, Miss Szymanski, two! The papers say a third man will be asked questions. I am a man of the people, and I ask you, would the people stand for it?”

“Mr. Plum, nobody’s said you did anything.”

“No. No!” He dabbed. “That’s what frightens me. My wife says I haven’t the brains to do harm, and I take it as a comfort, and tonight I find I can’t hold a glass.” He lifted it; the water slopped over his cuff. “You see?”

I did see. A man who could not hold a tumbler steady could not have held a decanter, nor a secret, and when he went back into the Pacific Room I put him down in my head as the worst conspirator in the history of the Seventh Ward, which was a distinction.

Dolan found me at ten, when the District Attorney was making his own toast. “Coat,” he said, and walked me round the back of the band into the men’s cloakroom as though we’d come to collect his. The attendant, a boy in a bellman’s jacket, looked at the ceiling and left the cubicle. It smelled of wet wool, bay rum, and the hair of three hundred men’s hats.

“I wasn’t going to show you tonight,” said Dolan. “I’m showing you tonight because I think by morning it’ll be a different thing.”

The evidence envelope came out of the breast pocket where I had seen it that afternoon. He held it flat, with his thumb across the mouth. Inside was a grey felt hat, and inside the hat, when he turned back the sweatband, a strip of ruled paper no wider than a wallet-card, folded in four.

“Maher’s,” he said. “Pugh bagged it on the Thursday and nobody opened the bag. Friday, after Lambert, I did.” He unfolded the slip with two fingers. “It was under the sweatband, where a man keeps a bill he means to remember.”

NINE. HALF PAST MIDNIGHT. BRING IT.

Block capitals, thick-nibbed, in a brown that went on to the edge of red where the pen had pressed. The paper had been torn from a pad. I held it under the cloakroom lamp.

“Ink like old blood,” I said. It was a phrase that had been lodged in my head for a week and I didn’t ask where from. “Bring what?”

“What does a Customs man bring? A paper.”

Paper does not walk off, Joe. I stood in a cloakroom with my mouth shut. The dry voice in the Frieze had said it, behind a louvre, in the rain.

“Who wrote it?”

“Block letters. Cheap pad. Could be a school child.” He put the slip back in the hat and the hat back in the envelope. “That’s not all. You told me about the jar.”

“Ostrander’s.”

“I asked the lab Wednesday, after the pit. They had it Thursday and finished this morning. Chloral hydrate. Knockout drops, Ruth. Enough to put a man to sleep for a day, or to stop a bad heart that had four whiskies to carry.” He did not look at me. “He was drugged, Ruth. Somebody put him to sleep, and he never woke up.”

“It’s a homicide.”

“It’s a homicide if Barnwell says it is. I put it in front of Rafferty at four o’clock. Rafferty said it’ll keep till Monday.” He laughed, once, without any air in it. “Retire first. Murder after.”

“Frank.”

“Hold on.” He put a hand flat against a coat-rail. “I’ve got to ask you something and I’d rather ask it with my back turned. Have you still got it?”

I knew what he meant. We had never once said the word in eight years.

“Yes.”

“Burn it.”

It sat in the cloakroom between us like a third man. Beyond the wall the band began a waltz.

“No.”

“He’s out the door at midnight with a clock and a pension, and in two days he’s a man in a rocking-chair. You could have used it any time in four years, Ruth.”

“That’s why I didn’t.”

“You could ruin the pair of us.”

“I know what I could do. I’ve known it every day. I haven’t done it.” My voice was quiet and not steady. “It’s a piece of paper, Frank.”

“It’s four years of both our lives.”

There was nothing more to say, and we said it for a while. He turned his back to me and leaned his forehead on his forearm against the coat-rail, among the hats, with the tags of the rented jacket showing at his collar, and I stood and looked at the broad freckled hand that held the envelope. I wanted to put my own over it. I did not, and neither of us was ever going to say that I had wanted to.

“Come on,” he said at last. “They’ll have missed the beets.”

At a quarter to one Swain’s Packard pulled away from the hotel kerb, and I let it go as far as the corner.

The Packard turned north up Front Street. I knew it would; there was nowhere to go from the Harbor at that hour but the pier, and I’d rather lose a man in four blocks than follow him for a mile. I walked. Six minutes, by the Waltham, past the shuttered mouth of Anchor Alley and the dark Customs Annex, with the cold coming off the Sound and my breath showing, and not a whisper of fog. The Heifer was silent. It sounds on thick nights only, and this one had stars on it like salt.

I turned into Capstan Row at the Shape Hall, dark on its corner, and went down the Row for two blocks to where it ends at the pier gate. Beyond the last warehouse, in the lee of a wall, stood a stack of wooden cable reels each taller than a man. I got behind them. The pier ran out into the water in front of me, planked and empty, with a single bulb in a cage burning above the gate, and under it the Packard stood with its lights off and its engine ticking as it cooled.

Swain was by the door of the car with his collar up. His anchors caught the bulb whenever he moved a hand, and he moved it a good deal. Opposite him, with his hat brim snapped down and his hands in the pockets of a long dark coat, Aldo Ferrante stood still.

“You ask a great deal,” Ferrante said. “Courtesy of the hour, Mr. Swain. I’m out of my bed.”

“The Estate has asked me to deliver this.” The envelope in Swain’s hand was cream, and I would have bet my rent on the watermark. “It is a mark of its goodwill.”

“How much?”

“Five hundred.”

Ferrante did not take it. “Two men dead,” he said, “and you bring me an envelope.”

“The Estate does not wish further incidents.”

“The Estate.” He said it softly, as a man says the name of a bad dog he’s been told is friendly. “Who is the Estate? Show me a face.”

“A trust has no face, Mr. Ferrante.” The envelope wobbled. Swain’s voice had been rising since he began, and I heard the exact place where it ceased to be a lawyer’s. “It’s a, it’s an arrangement. I only sign. Do you imagine I choose?”

“Then it’s got no neck.”

The word sat in the cold air by the pier. I felt it from behind my reels, and I’m fairly certain Swain felt it in his collar. He put the envelope in Ferrante’s coat pocket himself, since Ferrante’s hands stayed where they were, and backed to the car with the quick stiff steps of a man who has found the stairs dark. The Packard started on the second try. It turned the corner into Front Street and its taillamps went down toward the hotel like two coals.

Ferrante waited until the sound had gone. Then he turned, not quickly, and looked at the stack of reels, and did not look at the wall of the Shape Hall or the black water or the pier.

“Fish market,” he said to the dark. “Four o’clock Sunday. Come alone, or don’t come.”

I didn’t answer. I knew better than to speak to a man who had said don’t come. He stood a moment more, and I heard a small sound I had last heard in an office with St. Joseph on the wall: the click of a pocketknife opening. It closed. It opened. It closed again, evenly, like a man counting something to himself.

I counted eleven. Then his boots went away on the planks, and the knife went on, a long way into the dark.

chapters.title: Fish Market, Before Light
chapters.html:
Crushed ice slid off a shovel onto a halibut, and the gulls went up from the pilings in a single white argument and came down again. Under a row of kerosene lamps swinging from a beam, the municipal fish market was already at work at four in the morning: bay boats unloading, men in oilskins throwing crab baskets, and at the end of the third steel table, in a rubber apron over his good dark coat, with his hat brim snapped down, Aldo Ferrante was cleaning a cod.

He did it with a short curved knife and no wasted motion. He laid the fish on its back, ran the blade from vent to gill in one pull, and took out the insides in a single handful, which he gave to a gull as a man hands a coin to a child. The top joint of his left ring finger was missing, and the stump worked among the other fingers like a person who knows the way.

“You came alone,” he said, without looking up.

“I came with a torch and my mother’s blessing.”

“Then you came with company.” He rinsed the fish in a bucket of seawater. “My mother eats cod on Sundays. In Calabria she’d have waited for the salt kind, hung up like washing. Here she gets it fresh, and complains. I clean it myself. A man who lets somebody else clean his fish is a man who is going to be told lies at dinner.” He glanced at me then, from under the brim, and went back to the knife. “Stand where I can see you. People get nervous of a woman at their back.”

I stood by the ice. My shoes were wet through already, and the cold came up from the concrete and settled somewhere near the knees. I had slept two hours.

“I didn’t kill Maher,” Ferrante said. “I didn’t kill the porter. I tell you before you ask, so you can stop asking it with your face.”

“I’m not asking.”

“You’re Anton’s girl. You’ve never in your life asked anything with your mouth first.” He wiped the knife on the apron. “Last night you heard me tell a lawyer to show me a face. You heard him say a trust has none. I’d like you to know I’m a man who was told, in 1948, he was doing business with a family. The Calders, old money, church money. The House.”

“The House.”

“That’s what Stefan’s people called it. Stefan Kowal. The sexton.” He started on a second cod, a smaller one. “You know who he was?”

“Teddy Wozniak’s brother-in-law.”

“A man with a heart like a church and a temper like a stove. He came to the Shape Hall in the winter of ’46 with a Pole off a Greek boat and asked could the Local put a man to work. I gave the man a chit. Then he came with another. For nearly two years it was a favour, you understand, a kindness between Catholics. Then in March of ’48 a Liberty ship docked at Slip 3 with thirty-one people on it the Customs was not going to count.”

“The Esther Vane.”

“You know the name.” He did not seem surprised. “A tally clerk had to alter a manifest. A pier had to look the other way. A hall had to find thirty-one men’s worth of papers, and a place to put them.” The knife went into the fish. “That’s when it became a thing with a price, Ruth. I won’t say I’m proud. Four hundred dollars a head. A hundred and fifty to me for the hall. A hundred to Plum’s company for the pier. A hundred and fifty to the House.”

“For what?”

“For the roof. Whatever roof it was. I didn’t ask whose.” He lifted his chin toward the gulls. “In my line you don’t ask the name of the hand that takes your money. You ask the sum, and you ask if it will be there next week. I told myself it was Plum’s wife’s cousins, in Calder Heights, in their furs.” He shook his head over the fish. “Four hundred dollars. A man in a camp in Germany would have paid four thousand. I never thought of it as selling. I called it the fare.”

“And Maher?”

“Maher was a tally clerk who had the arithmetic and the nerves. The week they let him go in 1950 he sat in my office and told me that if I didn’t pay him a hundred dollars a month, he would write out the whole list for the Immigration, in his own hand, to the minute.” The blade turned. “He wasn’t wrong. Three hundred and eleven people, Ruth. Do you know what the Immigration does with three hundred and eleven? You think a deportation is a train ride. It’s a door. Some of them have no country left to be sent to. I’ve seen a man held on a freighter for a year because nobody would sign for him.”

He did not say it with any heat. A man in a rubber apron at four in the morning, telling a woman what he’d done.

“Last week he came for two thousand,” I said.

“He said he had the ship’s own paper. The master’s copy, with a signature on it that would hang the House. I told him a man can’t hang a house.” He laid the knife down. “I’ll tell you a thing. That day I thought about it. I thought about a pier, and a bad step in the fog. I’m telling you I thought it because you will hear that I did, and I’d rather you heard it from me. But somebody got there first, and I was at the Hall with forty men and a radio, and you’ve asked them.”

“I have.”

“Then you know.” He took a cloth from his belt and cleaned his hands, one finger at a time, including the short one. “Now I tell you the other thing. I think I’m next. Every man on the list of mouths. Maher, then the porter, who had no part in anything but a key. Who has the paper? The paper is a rope, and the rope has two ends. Somebody is going round the ring with a pair of scissors.”

“There’s a list?”

“There’s a book. Stefan kept the names. God keeps accounts, he used to say, and he wrote them in a prayer book in pencil, so that God could read them. I never saw it. I know what it is by the way a man looks when I ask about it.” He took out an orange from the coat pocket under the apron, and the pocketknife from the other, and looked at the two of them, and put the orange away again. “That envelope last night is what the Estate pays when it wants Maher’s paper found and my mouth shut. It’s been paying since the fourth. My boys turned your office on the seventh. They turned over the Kowal woman’s flat on the Tuesday and again on the Thursday. Nobody found anything. I’ve called them off. Don’t thank me. I want it understood, that’s all.”

“Why tell me?”

He leaned both hands on the steel and looked at the gutted fish, and the gulls, and the long grey line coming up at the end of the pier where the sky would be.

“Because your father is on my conscience, and he’s the only one on it who’s earned his place there.” The soft voice lost a little of its courtesy. “And because there’s a night in March four years ago that you and I both remember, Ruth, and I’d rather talk about it myself. Your wire went quiet for ninety minutes because I paid Rafferty. Fifteen hundred dollars. I didn’t ask who he paid after.”

I said nothing. The lamps swung. A boy came by with a barrow of ice and looked at neither of us.

“Say something,” said Ferrante.

“I’m counting.”

“What?”

“It’s been four years, eight months and two days,” I said. “I’m trying to get to the end of it.”

He let me. He took the cod by the gills, wrapped it in the Courier, and put it into a paper sack with a handful of ice; he did it with great gentleness, as a man would wrap something that had been alive that morning. “Go to your mother’s,” he said. “Go to church. The Polish women will know where the book is. Mrs. Kowal has the look of a woman who has swallowed somebody’s secret and is waiting for the priest.”

My mother had left a note on the table in her large flat hand. Mrs. Wach says the Kowal door has been kicked. I go with bread. You come when you wake. EAT FIRST. H. There was a boiled egg under a cup. I ate it standing, and went.

The Kowal flat was on Eleventh Avenue behind the church, up an outside stair, three rooms over a cobbler’s. The door had been kicked in once, long enough ago to have been mended with a plank. I knocked, and my mother’s voice said, “It’s open. It is always open. Look where that has got us.”

The front room had been put through a mangle. Every chair had been slit down the back and the horsehair dragged out in grey tufts. The carpet was rolled against the wall, the boards underneath lifted in two places. The Sacred Heart lay face-down on the floor. On a chest of drawers someone had stood Stefan Kowal’s photograph back upright with its glass cracked across, and in front of it a candle burned in a jam jar.

Bronia Kowal sat at the kitchen table in the wreck of it, in black, with her rimless spectacles and her rosary wound twice round her wrist and her handbag in her lap, held in both hands. She was making tea on a gas ring without looking at it. She looked at me.

“Miss Szymanski,” she said.

“Mrs. Kowal.”

“They are not Poles,” said Bronia. “A Pole would have taken the sugar.” She did not smile. “They came on the Tuesday. Then they came on the Thursday. They did not break the plates. This I notice.”

My mother stood at the sink with her sleeves rolled and a loaf of Sobczak’s rye under her arm like a rifle. She had been scrubbing something, I saw, since eight, and had found nothing she could scrub. “The pot has a chip,” she said to me. “She uses the chipped one. I told her.”

“It has always been chipped. Stefan’s sister gave it.”

“Stefan’s sister did not know good china.”

“Helena Szymanska has not, in twenty years, said a word about my pot that was not an insult.”

“This is because the pot is insulting.”

It would have been a joke in any other room. Bronia poured, and the three cups went down in front of us on a dish towel, and the steam went up over the cracked glass, and for a minute the two of them looked at each other across the table with the plain hostility of two women who have been at the same coffee urn since the Depression. Then my mother put the bread on the table and sat down and took Bronia’s hand, and Bronia let her.

“Teddy,” said Bronia, “is a good boy. He is fifty-four. He is not a clever boy. A clever boy would have gone to America and stayed there.” She drew the handbag toward her. “Stefan said, if there is trouble, give it to a woman who has never let anything go. I thought of Pani Wach’s sister. I thought of the Lasota girl. Then I thought of you, Helena. There is not a grudge in this parish you have not kept.”

“I let things go,” said my mother. “I let Anton go.”

“And then you went to the cemetery every Sunday until Easter.” Bronia took the steel clasp of the handbag between finger and thumb. It opened like a small mouth. “This is not a thing for a person who forgives. This is for a person who keeps.”

She laid it in my mother’s hands.

It was a small book, black leather, no bigger than a man’s palm and an inch thick, with a brass clasp that had been rubbed to the colour of weak tea and a spine that had cracked and been mended with thread. A modlitewnik, a prayer book, printed in Kraków in the year before my mother left it. My mother held it in both hands as one holds a baby that is not one’s own. Her glasses hung against her chest on their string. She did not open it. She lifted her head and looked at me, and I found that I was looking at the book.

“It will be well,” said Bronia. “It will be as God arranges.” Her voice stayed even. It was the evenness of a woman who has been carrying a bomb to Mass for sixteen months and has finally put it in a basket. “You will read it, Helena. You have the old hand. Not the girl. She would read it with her head.”

“I read with my head,” I said.

“I know,” said Bronia Kowal. “That is what I fear.”

I took the book. My mother’s hands let it go, with a small effort, and I saw that she was crying quietly into the neck of her scarf and that neither of the other women had said a word about it.

On the corner of Eleventh and Hake a man in a long dark coat stood reading yesterday’s Courier upside down.

I may have been wrong about that. The light was poor, and I’d had two hours of sleep. But a man’s hat is a statement, and I couldn’t have told you whose it was, and when the Number 14 came rolling up the street I put out my arm and boarded it with a dozen farmers’ wives and a boy with a trombone case.

Seven cents. I took the long seat at the back by the window and sat with the book on my lap in both hands, the way Bronia held her bag. We rolled up Front Street. The Sound went by on my left and the hotel went by on my right, eight rows of windows and a Frieze, and the conductor rang his bell at every stop. The man in the long coat did not get on. Nobody who did looked at me twice.

Ferrante had told me what it was. Teddy had told me what it was, in a kitchen, in a sentence that he had shut his mouth on. I had seen it held against a chest at the Gospel. I rode up Front Street to the end of the line with it unopened in my lap, three hundred and eleven names in a stranger’s pencil, and I thought: a book you haven’t opened is still a prayer book.

At the terminus I got off and waited for the car back. Then I got on again, and sat, and put the book in my coat pocket for the ride down. The streetcar lurched at the switch, and the clasp clicked against Joe Lambert’s key.

chapters.title: Pod Twoją Obronę
chapters.html:
My mother’s reading glasses hung on their string against her chest, and she had pulled the kitchen lamp down on its cord until it hung a foot above the oilcloth like a surgeon’s, so that the table lay in a bright round pool and everything else in the room had gone to brown. On the table, in the middle of the light, with its brass clasp the colour of weak tea, lay the book.

“Sit,” said Helena. “Not there. There. You will hold the lamp straight and you will not touch.”

“I’m not a child.”

“You are a woman who reads with her head. Sit.”

I sat. It was eight o’clock on Sunday night, and the rain had come back about four in the afternoon and settled in against the window over the sink as though it had a lease. My mother wiped her hands on her apron, one and then the other, and put on the glasses, and set a thumbnail against the clasp. It opened with a small, dry, definite click. I had heard that sound once already that day, in a coat pocket, against a key.

The front leaves were print: the prayer from which it took its name. Pod Twoją obronę uciekamy się. “Under your protection we flee,” said my mother, “Holy Mother of God. Do not despise our petitions in our necessities.” Her finger went along the line. “Every Pole knows it. A man says it on a ship.”

She turned past the Litany and the Stations to where the print ended, and the paper went blank and ruled, and the writing began.

It was in pencil, small and upright, in the hand of a man who had gone to school until he was twelve and had made up for it since. The columns were ruled by a thumbnail and the edge of a hymn card. Names; a place; a ship; a date. “Dates by the saints,” said my mother. “Of course. A Pole knows the Feast of Saint Lucy before he knows Tuesday.” She read, and put it into English a line behind, at the speed of a woman buttering bread.

Nowak. Józef, Maria, Zosia, Ania. A Greek ship, the Aegina. On Saint Lucy, ‘forty-six. Nine days upstairs. Offering, nothing. Under it, in a smaller pencil, as if added after: Pan Bóg zapłać. “God will repay.”

“He wrote that for himself,” I said.

“He wrote it for a Pole in the next room who had no money.” She turned the leaf.

I counted. It’s what I do when other people read aloud. There were twenty-eight lines to a page, and each line held a name, a ship, a saint’s day, a number under dni na górze, days upstairs. “Where from?” I asked, over a line that said z Przemyśla, and I tried it. “Premissle.”

“Przemyśl.” My mother did not look up. “Pshe-mishl. Like a man sneezing politely in church. Say.”

“Pshemishl.”

“The Americans have ruined you.” She turned another leaf. Dąbrowska. A widow and a boy of six. Saint Joseph’s day. Her voice dropped a note and went on at a steady pace, because she was reading, and it is hard to cry through a list. Some lines had a word in the margin I couldn’t catch. Chora. Sick. Chrzest. A baptism. And once, in letters that had been pressed hard enough to dent the page: urodzona na górze. Born upstairs.

“Now,” she said, and her voice changed. “Here is spring.”

The columns had altered. In the ruling of the page for March of 1948 Stefan had drawn two new lines in a harder pencil, and headed them, in capitals so small they might have been written with a pin: OFIARA. DO DOMU. My mother put her finger beneath each. “The offering. And to the House.”

“Say that again.”

“Do Domu. To the House.” She lifted a shoulder. “It is not a word that means anything. It is a house. The man has written, to the House, a hundred and fifty. And beside it, in the other column, four hundred.” She ran her finger down. “Four hundred. Four hundred, one hundred and fifty. Four hundred, one hundred and fifty. Rutka, from this page they pay.” She turned over, and I saw that the page opposite was written in a single strong line across two columns, the pencil gone black from being gone over twice. She read it silently. Then she took off her glasses, and pressed the bridge of her nose between a finger and a thumb, and put them on again, and began it from the start, like a woman who has dropped a stitch.

“Okręt Esther Vane. Na świętej Matyldy. Trzydzieści jeden dusz.”

“Thirty-one,” I said.

“Thirty-one souls.” She said dusz with her whole mouth. “The ship Esther Vane, on the feast of Saint Matilda, the fourteenth of March. A soul, Rutka. They count cattle by the head. He is a sexton, and he writes souls.” She turned the next leaf and the next, and I saw the names run down the page in his pencil, thirty-one lines, and a fee against every one. “Four hundred each. A hundred and fifty to the House.”

I did the sum on the notice. Thirty-one at four hundred was twelve thousand four hundred dollars. Thirty-one at a hundred and fifty was four thousand six hundred and fifty, which is what a night clerk at thirty-eight dollars a week earns in two years and four months. It went to a house, in a night. I put the pencil down. At the foot of that page, under the thirty-first line, there were three words in the same upright hand, and they were not a name. My mother crossed herself before she read them.

“Panie, przebacz mi,” she said. “Lord, forgive me.”

We were quiet for a time. The rain tapped at the pipe. I remembered what a man had said over a steel table that morning, wiping his hands on a cloth: I never thought of it as selling. I was looking at the arithmetic of a sexton who had.

She read on through ‘forty-nine more quickly, a name to a breath. In February her thumb stopped on a line I could see, upside down, across the table: u Sz., 7 dni, 4 dusze. She did not read it aloud, and she did not look at me. I looked at the line and then at the lamp, as one looks at a stranger’s face on a streetcar, and said nothing, and in a moment the page turned. It was the second time that week I had watched my mother not answer, and I had been taught better than to put the question.

The last leaves were another hand. I knew it at once. It was small and square, with a line under every figure and the sevens crossed, and I had seen it on a desk blotter at the Harbor Hotel and on a card tacked to a door in Hake Street. Łukaszewicz, five persons. Third October. Left the seventeenth. There was nothing under it but a line ruled to the foot of the page and the smooth white of the leaf.

“Teddy,” said my mother.

“He wrote them out.”

“He wrote them out to the end.” She closed the clasp and put her hand flat on the book, as you do on a loaf you’re not sure is done. “Three hundred and eleven.”

I looked at the leaves, the eleven pages of twenty-eight lines and a short twelfth, and I didn’t count them. I knew what the sum would be.

At ten there was a knock. It was soft, three and then one, the knuckle of a very light hand, and I’d taken two steps toward the door when my mother, without lifting her eyes from the book, said:

“That is Stefan’s knock.”

I stopped. “Whose?”

“Three and one. The parish knew it. Open the door, Rutka. Do not use the chain.”

The woman on the landing had rain running off her hat and one white glove. The other hand, bare, held a cardboard suitcase tied with string, and the nails on it were bitten to the quick. She looked past me down the hall into a bright kitchen where an old woman sat under a lamp with a book, and the grey-green eyes went wide, and I saw a thin crescent scar on her chin go white.

“Mon cher,” said Yvette Marchand, in a voice with no stage in it at all. “A sergeant came to the club at eight. A big one, with a matchstick. He asked where I was on Tuesday night. The Deacon said, on stage. The sergeant said the club’s book had me leaving before the half hour, and the Deacon said he does not keep a book on a woman’s cigarette.” She drew a breath. “Then he looked at me, and said Mm-hm, and gave me a street.”

“Come in,” I said.

She came as far as the kitchen door and stopped. The book lay on the table in the pool of light, with its clasp shut, and I watched her see it. She didn’t scream and she didn’t speak. She sat down hard on the nearest chair with the suitcase in her lap, and the one glove went to her mouth.

My mother took off her glasses. She said something in Polish, very low, a long sentence with a shape like a question and the sound of a hand on a head, and from behind the white glove, in a voice that came from a good deal farther back than Lublin, Yvette answered. Not in French, and not in the careful English of a club on Brine Street. The consonants of her mother tongue came out hard and wet, and she was a girl of twenty-eight on a landing with a hook-rail, and she was crying. My mother stood up. She said another sentence. Then the two of them were holding on to each other over the book, a short wide woman in an apron and a tall one in a wet coat, and neither one made any sound but the sound of the breath going in, and I stood in my own kitchen on the wrong side of a glass door, with the only Polish I had, which was how are you.

I put the kettle on. It seemed to be what the room required.

It took a long while. When they let go of each other, my mother wiped her face on her apron without embarrassment and opened the clasp, and she turned to the year 1949 as one turns to a street one lived on. “Here,” she said. “Find yourself, child. You will know your own page.”

It took Yvette less than a minute. She laid her bare finger on a line and it shook; my mother read it out, slowly, so that I could have it in English.

“Wolska, Irena. Parowiec Pacific Tern. Saint Ursula, 1949. That is the twenty-first of October. Nineteen days upstairs. Offering four hundred. To the House, a hundred and fifty.”

“I paid with my mother’s rings,” said Yvette. Her voice was level now, and I found it harder to listen to than the other. “She had three. I gave him the three, in Antwerp, a man with a hat. I had a laundress’s papers from Lyon. I was a Madame Marchand, who washed sheets.” She looked at the pencil. “I am in a book. I am written down in the name I was given, and in pencil, and someone has put a line under it.”

“In your own name,” said my mother.

“In the one I will not say.” She shut her eyes. “Forty dollars a month, Miss Szymanski. That is what he asked. From the first of July, ‘fifty-one, in an envelope left at Mrs. Abbott’s for Mr. Declan Maher. Sixteen times. Six hundred and forty dollars.” The scar stood out. “I sing French songs in a basement for scale. I paid it. I told myself it was rent.”

“And the fourth of November?”

“I had three hundred dollars in my stocking. Not for him. For my page. I thought, he has a list, he is a man who keeps lists, and I will buy it out of the world, and he will tear it, and I will be a woman with no past at all.” “I left the stage at the eleven o’clock and I stood across the street from the hotel for ten minutes, I think. I could see the lobby. Mr. Wozniak was at the desk. I asked for Mr. Delaney. He told me Mr. Delaney had retired, and he looked down at his register, so as not to see me.”

“Where did you go?”

“Up. By the stair. I did not want the lift, with its brass, and the little needle. I went to the eighth floor and I found 807, and I knocked, as one knocks on a door one hopes will not be answered.” The voice thinned. “And no one did. And while I stood there in the corridor with my hand on the knob, I saw a man go away from me down to the end, toward the window. From behind. In a dressing gown.”

I felt my own hands go flat on the oilcloth. “What colour?”

“Dark. The light in that corridor is brown. It shone a little at the shoulders. Quilted, I think. He was tall, mon cher.” She looked at me. “Taller than Mr. Wozniak by a head and a half. White hair, or the light. He carried a tray, with glasses on it, two, and something tall that caught the light. I heard them, a little chime, like water.”

“How old?”

“Old. A neck like a bird’s. But he was walking faster than an old man ought.” Her gloved hand turned over in her lap. “He went to the last door on the right and he did not try the handle. He had the key out already. He put it in, and went in, and shut it, and the light under it did not come on.”

“Did you know him?”

“I never saw his face.”

I thought it over, the way I’d have thought over a call that came in on a bad line. Teddy, who was a head shorter than that man by any measure. Joe, shorter yet, and dead. Pearl, who was tall, and a woman, and would not have chimed a glass in her own kitchen. I said it under my breath, as I do, with the fingers of my left hand tapping the oilcloth: Teddy. Pearl. Joe. Quill. Four people with a key to the door at the end of the corridor, and three of them could be crossed off by a tape measure.

I did not say the fourth. I thought of a man in a window drinking tea, sixty-three years old and clean to the welt, who had folded his hands on the head of a cane and asked me to find whoever killed his porter. I thought of a telephone call to Santa Barbara at five past two, written in a night clerk’s hand in a book, with a lamp burning on a board. A dressing gown at ten past twelve is only a dressing gown, and the man in it might have carried a nightcap up a stair and gone down again to his telephone. I had a back and a tray and a shine at the shoulder, and the word of a woman who had never in her life been believed by a policeman.

“Who have you told?” I said.

“Nobody. They do not ask a woman like me what she saw. They ask what she is.” She looked at the white cotton glove in her lap. “I tell you because Madame cried.”

“I’m not a policeman.”

“No,” said Yvette. “You are something that keeps a thing.”

My mother put Yvette to bed in mine, with a hot-water bottle and a nightgown of her own that came to Yvette’s shins. Then she took the bread knife from the drawer, wiped the blade on her apron, and carried it into her own room and put it under her pillow.

“Mama.”

“Tonight I am a woman with a knife. In the morning I am a woman with bread. Sleep, Rutka.”

I didn’t sleep. At a quarter to two the house was quiet, the rain had thinned to a drip from the gutter, and I sat in the kitchen with the lamp pushed up out of the way and the book in front of me, and read it as best I could with the words I had. A hundred little pencil lines. I found the leaf of the Esther Vane and the thirty-one lines and the four words of the Lord’s forgiveness, and I turned the leaf back to the one before it, the first one with the new columns, and held it to the light.
