There was a note in the margin, so faint that the lamp had missed it. Pencil, very small, at an angle, written by a man who didn’t mean to be read. Three words and a letter, and I could read them without my mother, because every Polish child learns one of them before she can tie a shoe and the other is the same in any language.

Dom = Hotel. T. mówi.

The House is the Hotel. Teddy says.

I sat with the sentence for a good while. A hundred and fifty dollars a head had gone to the House, and the House was the building on Front Street with a Frieze and a night clerk and a fern. Plum’s wife’s cousins, a man with a fish knife had told me. A trust has no face, a lawyer had said, with a catch in his voice. I held the book against my chest, as a woman had held it at the Gospel, and decided that in the morning I would telephone Lucille Fong at the Harbor Commission and ask whose name stood on the paper for the pier.

A board creaked behind me. My mother stood in the door of her room in her nightgown, with her hair down her back in a grey plait as thick as a mooring line, and the glasses on their string, though she had no business with them at that hour. She had not been asleep. She looked at the book under my hands and then at me.

“A name is a small thing to carry,” said Helena Szymanska. “Carry it.”

chapters.title: Returning the Envelope
chapters.html:
Through the frosted glass of Gilbert Swain’s door a typewriter was whispering. The girl at the keys was one of those who say each word under her breath as she strikes it, and I had spent eight years learning to lift a voice off a bad line, so I stood on the fourth-floor landing of the Calder Building with an envelope in my glove and took down the first line of the letter before I knocked. Dear Mr. Quill. Then a comma, a bell, and the long rattle of the carriage going home.

Mr. Quill audited for the Estate. Auditors get letters. I put it in the same pocket as the other things I didn’t understand yet, and knocked.

The girl was a Miss Tuohy, who had a cold and was nursing it with a lozenge and a grievance. She looked at my hat, then at the envelope, then at the clock, which said ten past nine, and told me Mr. Swain was in conference. I could hear Mr. Swain being in conference with a desk drawer. He came out before she had finished saying so.

“Miss Szymanski!” He held both hands out, palms up, the way a man does who wants you to see there is nothing in them. “Is it Monday already? And you’ve brought me my report.”

“I’ve brought you your money.”

His office was done in the colours of an expensive cigar: dark leather, a green-shaded lamp, law reports nobody had ever pulled down, and on the desk a bronze anchor the size of a fist, holding down nothing. The window looked across Cutter Street at the Selkirk, where it was raining on my name. I put the envelope on his blotter and he did not touch it. It was the same cream envelope, softer for a fortnight in my drawer beside a pink eviction notice. Seven of the Estate’s fifties were still in it. The rest I had made up out of my mother’s tin behind the flour, in ones and fives, and she had handed that tin across on Sunday night without a word, which told me what she thought of the Estate.

“Returning it.” He considered the envelope as if the post office had played a joke on him. “Is that a conclusion, Miss Szymanski, or a mood?”

“It’s a refund. You paid me to find that Mr. Wozniak was mistaken. He wasn’t. I’d sooner owe you nothing, Mr. Swain. It saves on Christmas cards.”

He sat. He turned one gold anchor cufflink a full turn on its pin, and then the other, which I had not seen him do in the Elks’ banquet room or in my own chair, and I added it to the girl’s whispering.

“Then let me be your friend instead of your client,” he said. “It’s cheaper. A complaint has come across this desk. From persons who prefer to be nameless, to the State Board of Licences, concerning your conduct at the Local 41 hiring hall on the morning of the tenth. A woman in a man’s overcoat, among three hundred longshoremen at a quarter to six, asking questions of a union officer. They have asked me to put my name to it.” He spread his hands again. “I haven’t. Would I tell you if I meant to?”

“I think you’d tell me so I’d have a week to be sorry in. Who asked you?”

“The persons I act for.”

“The Estate.”

“The Councilman’s lessors,” said Mr. Swain, and glanced at the door to the outer office, where, quite distinctly, the typewriter had stopped.

I took the envelope back off his blotter, to give him something to look at that wasn’t me, and held it up to the rain-light as I had held it in my own office on the sixth. Three letters stood in the paper, faint as a thumbprint on glass. “C.E.T.,” I said. “What’s it stand for?”

“Is a watermark a confession?”

“Is it an answer?”

“Calder Estate Trust.” He said it lightly. “Owners of the hotel and of the ground under Pier Six, of which the Councilman’s company is the tenant. You knew that, Miss Szymanski. Would you have come up four flights otherwise?”

“Pier Six, lessee Calder Pier and Terminal Company, E. Plum, president,” I said. “Lessor, Calder Estate Trust, by G. Swain, attorney-in-fact. Trustee, see Instrument of 1938.”

I had had it at half past eight from Lucille, down the telephone, in her switchboard voice. See Instrument, she’d said. I’ve seen instruments, Ruth. This one’s got a hat on.

“The Instrument,” said Swain, “is sealed at the Recorder’s, and the trustee is, if you’ll forgive a lawyer, a sealed instrument himself. He acts through me. By his own direction I am his face.” He lifted his chin. “Shall I tell you whether I’m fond of the arrangement?”

“Are you?”

“I’m paid,” said Mr. Swain, and for the first time that morning he did not make it a question.

I asked him where he had been between one and four on the morning of the fifth, since I was there and the question was free. He drew himself up. Would a man who sat down to chops with the District Attorney’s own secretary, a Miss Aldous, at the Elks Lodge at half past one in the morning, have leisure to go about killing people? The waiter’s name was Emmett, and he had disliked them both, and he had kept the check. It came out in a single breath, like a thing rehearsed in front of a mirror.

“Did Mr. Maher leave any papers?” he said, when I had my hand on the door.

I turned. “Did he?”

“A tally clerk collects paper. The Councilman is anxious that his company’s name not turn up in someone’s drawer.” The cufflink went round again. “I only ask.”

“Say again,” I said. “You only ask.”

He didn’t. Behind me Miss Tuohy had started up once more, and she was whispering the salutation as I went down the stairs, the way a clerk does to keep her place. Dear Mr. Quill. Dear Mr. Quill. Dear Mr. Quill.

Yvette had given me the address in my mother’s kitchen, along with her sixteen envelopes. Mrs. Abbott’s stood on Capstan Row, a three-storey frame box four doors up from the Shape Hall, so that Declan Maher had lodged for six years in sight of the man he was bleeding and could watch him hire. A card in the window said ROOMS, and under it, smaller, NO COOKING, NO LADIES, NO SINGING.

Mrs. Gertrude Abbott was sixty and built like a bolster, in a flowered pinafore over a man’s cardigan, with her hair in a net and a cold pipe in her pocket. She asked who wanted the room.

“I don’t want a room. My name is Ruth Szymanski. I think Mr. Maher mentioned it.”

She looked me over from the hat down, taking her time, and stopped at my left wrist, where my father’s Waltham sat with its face turned in against the bone. “Nurse’s way,” she said. “He said a long woman with a grey streak, and her watch on like a ward sister. Come in out of that.”

The parlour had antimacassars, a sampler that read GOD BLESS OUR HOME AND THE PLUMBING, and a stand in the hall with seven umbrellas in it, none of them anyone’s. She gave me tea I hadn’t asked for in a cup with a chip at the rim. She had been waiting a long time for somebody to ask her something, I think, and had got out of the habit of being asked.

“Six years he was here. Quiet. Paid on Fridays. Best handwriting I ever saw.” She poured. “Then at the end of October he cheered up. In a man like that it’s a bad sign. Paid a week in advance on the Friday, which he didn’t owe, and showed me a railway ticket. One way, north, Thursday the sixth, ten past six in the evening. ‘Gertie,’ he said, and nobody calls me Gertie, ‘I’m off to my sister in Portland.’ He hasn’t got a sister. They bring them to the door at Christmas.”

“Mrs. Abbott,” I said, “the Beacon’s been printing a name for two weeks. Delaney. A man who died at the Harbor Hotel on the fifth.”

“I don’t know any Delaney.”

“His name was Maher.”

She did not say anything. She set the teapot down on its crocheted mat, exactly in the middle, and sat on the arm of the nearest chair, which was not where she’d meant to sit.

“He kissed me,” she said at last. “On the Friday. On the cheek, in the hall, with his hat on. Six years and never so much as a Merry Christmas. I thought, there goes a man in love.” She looked at her hands. “It was only that he was frightened.”

I let her have the quiet. Out in the hall one of the umbrellas fell out of the stand, and neither of us went to it.

“He left something for you,” she said, and put her hand under the knitting in the basket. “The Monday night, the third, when he came for his shaving things. ‘If I’m not back by Wednesday noon, Gertie, a woman will come and ask. Long, grey streak, watch on the inside. You give it to her and nobody else.’ Wednesday noon came. I waited till Friday. Then I went on waiting because I’d got used to it.”

The envelope was brown, the size of a man’s hand, sealed with gum and a dab of candle wax with a thumbprint pressed in it. I broke the wax. There were two things inside.

The first was a pawn ticket from a loan office on Capstan Row, dated the thirtieth of October: one gold-filled wristwatch, engraved, nine dollars. The engraving was copied out on the ticket: D.F.M. Customs Service 1941. The second was a photograph.

Two men stood on a church step in their Sunday coats, squinting at an Easter sun. The one on the left was heavy and square in a sexton’s long black coat, with a pair of hands like spades hanging out of the sleeves and his hat jammed down as though it had offended him. The one on the right was thin and pale and younger than I’d ever seen him, holding a grey felt hat in front of him in both hands like a plate. He was laughing. In the cut edge of the frame, between them and a little behind, there was a hem of black skirt and the corner of a black handbag held in two hands, and nothing else of the woman at all.

On the back, in the best handwriting I ever saw: Easter 1947. S.K. and me. The only one who never asked me for anything.

“Is that all?” said Mrs. Abbott.

“It’s a good deal,” I said, and found I’d put my glove flat over the face of the man laughing, so that I could look at the handbag. I would have known it blind.

In November the parish gives its Wednesday evenings to the dead. There is a Mass at seven for the Holy Souls, said in a nave with twenty-odd people in it, mostly widows, each of them holding somebody, and my mother had not missed one since 1941. I went with her that week because I had sat three days in a kitchen with a book, and the book had begun to look back.

Before we left she put it in the oven, flat on the rack under the roasting pan, and shut the door with her hip. “In church a pocket can be picked,” said Helena Szymanska, who had never in her life been robbed in a church.

We walked home under one umbrella, arguing about whether a sexton can be a saint, and climbed the fourteen stairs of 1127, where the bulb on the landing had gone out. A shape rose from the top step with a broom across its knees, like a lamplighter who has been told the lamps are gone.

“Mrs. Szymanska. Miss. Do not be frightened.” It was Mr. Vaitkus, the cobbler from below, in carpet slippers. “I have telephoned the police from my shop. I did not go in. I am a cobbler, not a policeman.”

The door stood open a hand’s width on the dark. I put an arm across my mother, which she disliked, and went in first, and the floor under my shoes was soft.

Flour. The bin had been emptied down the hall, all twenty-five pounds, and walked through, so that it lay in drifts against the skirting like snow in a bakery. Every drawer was out. The pillows had been opened with a knife, and a goose’s worth of feathers was still coming down through the lamplight to settle on the flour. Anton’s wedding photograph lay face down with the glass starred, and the Sacred Heart beside it, face up, regarding the ceiling as though it had expected nothing better.

My mother stood in the doorway in her hat with her missal in her hand, shaking from the scarf to the shoes, as I had seen her do only once, the day they brought my father home in a blanket. She said something in Polish, a long sentence that began quietly and did not end where it stopped. Then, in English: “In my kitchen. With boots.”

She walked through the flour to the stove, looking at none of the drawers. She opened the oven, lifted the roasting pan, and took the black book out as one takes out a loaf, and held it against her chest in both arms.

“The oven,” she said, “is where we put the things we are too proud to say are broken. A cracked platter. A husband’s boots. Nobody looks in a Polish oven. They think, what is in there? Only bread.”

It was not the first thing she had hidden in that kitchen, I thought, and put the thought where I’d put the page she wouldn’t read.

“At eight o’clock,” said Mr. Vaitkus, in the voice of a witness who has rehearsed on a stair for two hours, “I hear boots over my head. Many nails. I know the ladies are in church. I take the broom and I bang the ceiling, so, and I sing, because a man who sings is a man with company. The Šešupė song, very loud. They stop. They go down the back stair, running. I think they do not like Lithuanian.”

“I don’t blame them,” said my mother. It was the first time she had smiled, and it was not much of a smile, but it moved the scarf.

At midnight, when the stove was lit and my mother had stopped shaking long enough to make tea, since she could not be expected to be both shaken and inhospitable, the policeman came. He climbed the fourteen stairs with his hat in his hand and had flour on his shoes before he reached the door.

Dolan stood on the threshold for as long as it took the matchstick to cross his mouth.

“I saw the address on the night sheet,” he said.

“You read the night sheet.”

“Not as a rule.” He came in. My mother said “Sergeant, you will have tea,” in a tone that was not a question, and he drank it standing in the wreck, like a man at a graveside. Then he crouched and read the floor.

“Hall boots,” he said. “Dock nails. You could stand outside the Shape Hall at six tomorrow and pick out twenty pair.”

“Ferrante told me he’d called his boys off.”

“Ferrante tells a lot of people a lot of things. He peels an orange while he does it.”

“It had crossed my mind.”

He turned the matchstick over. “The forty-eight hours I asked you for are gone, and three days more. I bought nothing. Rafferty won’t sign. Rafferty has a cottage in Santa Cruz and a fishing rod, and he’s not putting his name to a paper that touches the Calder Estate on the word of a dead clerk and a dead porter. The man who’s got his chair, Haskell, was a quartermaster for twenty years. He thinks a warrant is a kind of coupon.”

“And you?”

“I count to nine now, Ruth. I stood in Front Street and counted nine, and I haven’t been able to count to eight since.” He took the matchstick out and looked at it. “That’s the best I can do tonight. There’s a singer I’d like to talk to. Marchand. The Deacon says she hasn’t been near the club since Monday, and a woman who sings for scale doesn’t walk off a job she needs.”

“She left here Monday morning with a suitcase and my mother’s second-best coat,” I said. “She didn’t say where.”

She was at that moment asleep on Fifth Avenue in the Flats, under a quilt belonging to Deacon Tolliver’s sister, who had asked her nothing but whether she took sugar. Dolan looked at me for the time it takes to read a plate number. He looked at my mother, who stood in front of the oven with the poker in her hand, a woman of seventy defending a stove. Then he put the matchstick back.

“All right,” he said. “All right, Ruth.” And he let me have it, God help us both, and went down the fourteen stairs with the flour printing his heels.

After he had gone I did what I would have done in the wire room with a bad line: I stopped listening to the noise and listened to the pattern. The flour had kept everything. Two pairs of boots, each sole a diamond of hobnails, one pair with the iron missing from the left heel. They had gone through the bedrooms, the cupboards, the bin, the bread box. Then the prints crossed the kitchen in a straight line, side by side, the line of two men who have just remembered something about a Polish house. They stopped a hand’s breadth from the oven door. Beyond that, nothing. Then both pairs had turned together and run, scoring the linoleum under the white all the way to the back stair.

They had come within a hand of it. Mr. Vaitkus’s broom had saved the book, and an old woman’s pride about broken things, in about equal parts.

From the floor below, two knocks came up through the boards, the way you knock to ask whether all’s well. I stamped back. Twice.

chapters.title: A Brown Bottle
chapters.html:
Boots on marble, a good many of them, before the lobby lights were on.

I was standing at the desk with Teddy in the one lamp he allowed himself until seven. By the lobby clock, which runs three minutes slow, it was twenty-five past six, and I had been there eleven minutes, in which Teddy had thanked me three times and squared the blotter on a desk that was square already. I had come to tell him about the flat. The flour, the feathers, Mr. Vaitkus’s broom; the oven, and what had been in it. And Bronia, whose own door had been kicked in twice in a week, and who would be glad to hear that a book in a roasting pan had outlasted two pairs of boots.

“Thank God,” he had said. Then, in the voice of a man asking for a transfer on a streetcar: “If I may. A small favour. When this is over, you will walk Bronia to Mass on Sunday. Since Stefan she does not like to go alone. She puts her hand in the bag and there is nothing in it to hold.”

“You’ll walk her yourself.”

“That is what I meant to say.” The gold tooth caught the lamp.

Then the street door, and the boots. Dolan came in first with a matchstick in his mouth and his hat pulled down, then Karras with his notebook already open, then two uniformed men who stopped inside the door and looked at the fern. Nobody switched on the chandelier. The lobby stayed brown, and the marble took every step and gave it back a little late.

“Morning, Teddy,” said Dolan. Not Mr. Wozniak. I watched Teddy hear that. “Ruth. I won’t ask.”

“Don’t.”

“We had a call. Ten past six, to Central. A man who wouldn’t leave a name. The desk sergeant said he read it off like he was ordering from a card.” Dolan’s eyes went to the back of the desk. “Look in the night clerk’s locker at the Harbor. That’s all. It was enough.”

“Of course,” said Teddy. He stood very straight in his maroon jacket. “It is in the passage behind the key rack. If I may, I have the key.” He drew his watch chain out of his waistcoat, and on the chain, beside the little padlock key, hung another, long, brass, with a square head. Karras looked at it.

“And that one, sir?”

“A cupboard.”

“I’ll take it for now, if you don’t mind.” Karras said it as gently as I have ever heard a policeman say anything, and Teddy unhooked it himself and put it in his palm.

The passage behind the rack was a bricked slot with a row of grey tin lockers, each with a paper tag. T. WOZNIAK was fourth along. The padlock hung open on its hasp. And there, as Karras reached for it, was Pearl Hightower, who had come in by the staff door at half past six with her key ring held silent against her apron, and who said, to nobody in particular, “That lock is Mr. Wozniak’s own. He bought it at Bergen’s hardware in 1939. In thirteen years he has not once left it open.”

“It was open, ma’am,” said Karras.

“Then it was opened with a key. The management has a master for the staff lockers. I have never touched it.” She looked at Dolan with the gold spectacles on their chain. “I do not guess, Sergeant. I tell you what I know.”

“Everyone in a hotel has a key to everything,” said Dolan, not unkindly.

“Not everyone,” said Pearl, “has been told.”

The locker held a spare maroon jacket on a hanger, a tin of brass polish, an umbrella with a bent rib, a thermos. Behind the thermos, where a man puts a thing he doesn’t mean to drink, stood a brown glass bottle with a cork. On the hook below the jacket’s collar hung a brass tag on a ring. Karras lifted the tag with a pencil. 807.

“Teddy,” said Dolan.

“It is not mine.” He said it carefully, like a man setting down a full glass. “I have never seen that bottle. I did not put the key there. I know how it sounds. Forgive me.”

Karras drew the cork with a handkerchief, and the smell came out and reached me at two yards: sweet, then sour behind the sweetness, like pear drops left in a hot pocket. Teddy sat down all at once on the bench by the key rack, as if somebody had taken a stool out from under him.

“That’s what the lab found in Maher,” Dolan said, to nobody. Then he said the rest of it, the words they teach a man, in the voice of one reading out a bill he didn’t run up. Tadeusz Wozniak. In connection with the death of Declan Maher. Central Station. Teddy listened with his head a little to one side, politely, as to a guest explaining the hours of breakfast.

“May I take my—” His hand had gone to the waistcoat pocket, the small round tin, the little rattle.

“I’ll have to take that, sir,” said Karras. “Property.” He held up a brown paper bag and opened it, and Teddy took out the pillbox and gave it to him. It went into the bag with the wallet, the watch and the long brass key. “They give it all back at the desk. It’ll be listed.”

“I would like it listed,” said Teddy. “If you will be so kind.”

I heard the car before I saw it. The brass arc over the cab door had been dark since I came in; now the needle swung off the eight and came down the dial in a long smooth slide, thirty-eight seconds, and the doors opened on Ambrose Quill in his dark red quilted dressing gown, with his cane over his forearm like an umbrella and his silver hair parted exactly in the middle.

“Sergeant,” he said. He cleared his throat, twice. “Forgive the costume. I was told there were policemen in my lobby, and one doesn’t dress for policemen.”

He did not look at the bag, or at the bottle. He crossed the marble in his red leather slippers, knelt on one knee beside the bench, and put one long yellow-white hand on Teddy’s knee. “My dear Teddy. My dear fellow. I will see that you have counsel. You shall not want for it.”

“You are very good, sir,” said Teddy. His eyes were wet. He was grateful. I watched it happen in his face, and it was the worst thing in the room.

I looked at the hand on the knee, as I do, and at the slippers, with soles as clean as the day they were bought. And I looked at the shoulders of the gown, because they were in the way of everything else, and under the brown lobby light they shone. It’s a good quilted silk. It shines wherever it’s worn. I had drunk this man’s tea and been asked by him, in the voice of a man asking after a lost glove, to find whoever had killed his porter, and a great many men own a dark red gown. I put the thought down. I noticed that it stayed within reach.

Central Station at eight in the morning smells of burned coffee and other people’s coats. I sat on the bench outside the Detective Bureau until Dolan let me in, and when he did, it was to a desk with the brown bottle on it in a paper bag, and Karras in the next room with his door open.

“Don’t touch,” said Dolan.

“I’m not touching.”

He took the bottle out on the blotter. It stood about three inches tall. Eleven fat capsules the colour of weak tea lay in the bottom, and I counted them through the glass. The label was the size of a playing card and had been torn across the lower half, so that what remained read, in a druggist’s careful type: ...kin’s Pharmacy, Front St. Rx 4187... Oct 28. One capsule at bed... The patient’s name had gone with the tear. The last figure of the number was a small curled stroke that might have been a 2, a 3, or a 9.

“Forty-one eighty-seven,” I said, under my breath, as I’d have said an address off the wire. “Forty-one eighty-seven.”

“Don’t.”

“Don’t what?”

“Do what you do.” He leaned back. The chain with Moira’s ring on it swung out from his collar and back. “It’s a number on a piece of paper that I’m going to have to put in a bag. If a woman I used to work with says it under her breath in my office, I’m going to have to remember I heard her.”

“It’s only a number.”

“That’s what I’m afraid of.” He pushed the bottle back into its bag and the telephone on the desk rang before I could answer. He listened, and I watched his face do what it did when the voice on the other end rose a note at the end of every sentence.

“Mr. Swain,” said Dolan. “No. He hasn’t asked for one. — He hasn’t asked for anything. — I’ll tell him. — I’ll tell him that too.” He covered the mouthpiece with a freckled hand. “The Estate is anxious that its employee should have counsel. Mr. Swain will act himself. At no charge to the clerk.”

“He’s never exchanged ten words with Teddy in his life.”

“That’s what I told him.” He lifted the receiver again. “He said, would a man who wished the fellow harm offer?”

I did not say that it was the kind of question a man asks who has been given the answer in advance. I said it to myself, with my fingers on my knee, and I noticed there was only one pharmacy on Front Street whose name ended in kin’s, and that I bought my aspirin there. I did not tell Dolan. Karras was in the next room with his door open and his notebook in his hand, and a number is only a number until someone says it to a policeman.

“Can I see him?”

“Not today,” said Dolan.

The State Board of Licences sits on the fourth floor of the State Building, above the Division of Elevators. As I climbed past the third-floor landing I heard, faint behind a frosted door, the whistle of a very small locomotive going into a tunnel. I went on up.

The hearing room had a long varnished table, a flag, and three men behind the table who looked at their watches the way other men look at a hymnal. Nobody had told me to bring counsel. Nobody had told me anything but the hour: a process server had found me at noon at the Selkirk with a paper and a smell of damp wool. At the end of the table sat a thin woman in a grey suit with a folder, and when the chairman nodded to her she opened it and read the order in a voice as flat as a plate.

“Pursuant to the Act, the licence of Ruth Anne Szymanski, private investigator, of room three-oh-nine, Selkirk Building, is suspended forthwith pending a hearing of the complaint of Gilbert Swain, attorney at law, alleging conduct inconsistent with the licence, to wit...” She read the Shape Hall, the overcoat, the longshoremen, the union officer. She read it without a flicker. If she had been reading the names of the dead I could not have told the difference. “The hearing will be held on Monday, the first of December, at ten o’clock. The licensee may be represented. The licensee will surrender her card.”

“I may be represented by a great many people,” I said. “Is there a fee for being suspended?”

The chairman looked at his watch. The thin woman held out her hand.

The card came out of my pocket as soft as flannel. It had my name on it and a number, and on the sponsor’s line, in a hand like a man pulling a splinter, F. X. Dolan. She put it in her folder and shut the folder, and that was all there was to it. I had been in a building with a Frieze on it and a floor nobody built and a dead man in a cab, and nothing had made me feel as light as that: a card the size of a playing card, gone, and all of me still standing.

At twenty to five Dolan let me look at Teddy for one minute by the clock, and told me I hadn’t been there.

They kept him in the holding room off the Bureau, a square of green wall with a bench and a barred door. He was sitting on the bench with his hands on his knees and his back straight, a small man in a waistcoat with no tie and no laces in his shoes, and he looked like someone waiting to be called in to be fitted for a suit. His eyes were calm. His moth-wing eyebrows had been combed.

“Miss Szymanski.” He did not get up. “Do not worry about me. Worry about Bronia.”

I stood with my hands round two of the bars. “Who told you to say that?”

He shook his head. It was the gentlest refusal I ever had. His right hand went to the breast pocket of his waistcoat, found nothing there, and lay down again on his knee.

“Time,” said Dolan, behind me.

I went out onto the Central Station steps in the last of the light. It had not rained all day, a grey, dry, bitter day with a lid on it, and the lamps along Cutter Street were coming on one by one. A black Packard stood at the kerb by the side gate with its rear curtains drawn. As I looked it pulled out, softly, without hurry, and went down the hill. I saw only the dark of the back seat and, for the length of a lamp post, a pale oval at the window that might have been a face or might have been a folded newspaper. It was Swain’s Packard, I would have sworn to the grille. I could not have said who rode in the back.

I went round to the side gate and stood at the iron railing. Beyond it lay the yard that joined the Bureau to the cell block, forty yards of wet brick under one arc lamp. Two men came out of a door at the far end, and between them walked a small stooped man without a tie, and I watched him go across the yard in the white light, his unlaced shoes slipping at the heels, and halfway across he stopped, and patted his breast pocket, and patted it again, where the pillbox used to be.

chapters.title: Pills in a Paper Bag
chapters.html:
The holding corridor at Central Station smelled of disinfectant and wet wool, and most of the wool was mine.

Father Dziedzic had told the turnkey I was a parish visitor, and Helena had supplied the hat: black felt with a short veil, kept in tissue for funerals and the visiting of the sick, which made me look like a woman in an advertisement for regret. The turnkey was a man named Brophy with a bologna sandwich in one hand and a ring of keys in the other, and he had the air of someone who has watched a great many people arrive and had never once seen them leave in the order they came.

“Five minutes, Father. Does the lady carry a knife?”

“She carries a rosary,” said Father Dziedzic, which was true. My mother had put one in my hand at the door.

It was Friday, a little after six, and raining again. The priest was a round weary man of sixty-six who had known everything in his parish for thirty years and told it only to God, and he walked down that corridor with his black bag in front of him like a man pushing a pram. Teddy’s cell was the third on the left. They had taken his tie, his belt and his laces, so that he sat on the iron bunk like a man in a barber’s chair, in shoes that wouldn’t quite stay on. His waistcoat was buttoned wrong by one button. When he saw the stole come out of the priest’s bag, he said something in Polish, very quietly, and the priest answered, and then looked at me.

“I will ask you to wait where you cannot hear,” he said.

I went to the end of the corridor and counted the bricks in the wall at the level of my eyes. There were forty-one in the course. Behind me the murmur went on in Polish at the pace of a man reading a long list slowly, and once it stopped altogether, and I did not turn round. A pipe knocked somewhere under the floor. Brophy ate his sandwich in tidy bites and watched the ceiling.

When Father Dziedzic came out his face had gone the grey of old dough, and for a moment he took hold of my wrist the way one takes hold of a stair rail. “He has told me what he has told me,” he said. “Of that I can give you nothing. I will tell you only what I saw, which is a man at peace who is not at peace.” He let go. “Go in. I will wait here, and I will say the rosary, and the turnkey will pretend it is a hymn.”

“Miss Szymanski.” Teddy stood, because he could not do otherwise, and his shoes slipped at the heels. “You have come in a hat.”

“I’ve come to talk you out of something.”

“Then you have come too late, and I am sorry for it, because you are the only person I ever paid to be right.” He indicated the bunk. I didn’t sit. “Mr. Quill came yesterday.”

I said nothing. I would have given the Waltham for him not to say the rest.

“At five minutes past four. He brought a rug, which they would not let him leave. He sat where you are standing, with his cane across his knees, and he was very sorry. He said, ‘My dear Teddy.’ He said the police had a bottle and a key and a locker and a clerk who found the body, and that no jury in the world would look further. He said the Estate would be generous about counsel. And then he said that Bronia’s papers were not in order.”

“Her papers are in order. She’s been a citizen since—”

“Since 1931, on the affidavit of a man whom Stefan paid forty dollars to be a witness. A clerk’s cousin.” Teddy squared the edge of the blanket with two fingers. “Mr. Quill knows his name. He knows the date. I did not ask how. He seems to know everything that has ever been written on paper. It will go to the Service, he said, with a letter from the Estate’s lawyers, and Bronia will be sixty-two years old on a ship to a place that has no record of her. He said it so kindly. He said it as one tells a man the time of the last train.”

“He’s bluffing. The minute a paper goes to the Service the Estate’s name is on it too. He can’t touch her without—”

“He is not lying, Miss Szymanski.” Teddy looked at me as one looks at a child who has said the sky is green. “He is the hotel. A hotel does not lie. It remains.”

I did not like the sentence then, and I was to like it a good deal less.

“Think what it is,” he said. “If I am the man, there is no other man. No one climbs to the Frieze to look for another. No one reads in cupboards. The names stay in the book, and the book stays in the oven.” A flash of gold tooth showed. “I heard about the oven. It is the only arithmetic I have ever been good at. One life, against three hundred and eleven and a sister.”

“Quill wins.”

“Mr. Quill wins nothing. The book wins, if you still have the book.” He leaned toward me. “Burn it. Please. If it is burned, nobody is on a list. Nobody in the world is on any list.”

“No.”

“Rutka. If I may—”

“No.” It came out harder than I meant. “I don’t burn things, Teddy. I keep them. It’s the only trade I’ve got.”

He sat back. After a time he nodded, as a man nods at a bill he has been expecting. “Then keep it. A keeper is not a murderer. I have been a keeper six years, and for a few weeks I will be the other thing, in the newspapers. I think I shall manage it.”

His hand moved to the pocket of his waistcoat, found it empty, and came away. “They have my pills in a bag.”

“I’ll see to it.”

“It is nothing. Thirty years I have the heart.” He rubbed finger and thumb together in the air, the small rattling gesture I’d watched across a fortnight and six rooms. “It is only that at night, when I lie down, I like to hear them in the pocket.”

Brophy was jingling his keys at the far end. Teddy rose again. “You counted the steps?”

“Fourteen.”

“The sixth is loose.”

“I know. I stood on it.”

“Good,” said Teddy Wozniak. “Good.” And that was the last thing he said to me that was meant for me alone.

I stayed. Father Dziedzic went back to his parish and I sat on the long bench in the Bureau under the clock with the rain on the window and my hat on my knee. At five to nine they brought him down between Karras and a turnkey. Swain was there already, with a leather case and a wet umbrella and a smell of bay rum that reached the bench. Dolan stood against the wall with a stenographer’s pad open in front of a young man who looked frightened of it.

Through the glass of the interview room I watched it done, as one watches a play in a language one knows. Swain laid down three typed pages. Teddy read all three, with his lips moving slightly on the long words, and squared the pages on the table when he had finished. Swain unscrewed a fountain pen of his own and held it out. Teddy looked at it, and at Dolan, and said something, and Dolan gave him a police pencil with the eraser chewed. He signed at the foot of the third sheet in a small, upright hand, and I saw the pencil go down for each letter of the name.

Swain’s face was wet and glad. Karras was looking at the floor. Dolan was looking at the signature as if it were a thing he had once owned.

Afterward I caught him in the corridor. He had his hat in his hand and his coat half on. His face was the colour of the wall.

“Frank. His pills.”

“What pills?”

“The tin. In the bag with his wallet. Nitroglycerin. He has a heart, and he needs it at night.”

“They’re in the bag in the sergeant’s office,” said Dolan. “I’ll see to it.”

“Tonight.”

“Tonight, Ruthie.”

The desk sergeant leaned out of his cage. “Telephone, Frank. It’s the old man. Says it’ll keep till you’ve sat down, but he doesn’t think it’ll keep.”

“Rafferty?” Dolan looked at me, then at the stairs. “Wait,” he said. “Go home, Ruth. I said I’ll see to it.” He put his hat on crooked and went through the swing door at the end of the passage, and I heard it flap behind him twice and stop.

I sat on the bench another quarter of an hour. He did not come back. The desk sergeant, when I asked him, said the sergeant had left for the night, and was it a message? I said no. Property was in a locked office with a locked cupboard in it, behind a door I could not open, and I stood and looked at the door for some time. Frank Dolan had never in his life said I’ll see to it without meaning it. That was the whole trouble with him. He meant everything, and he finished about half.

I went home. I went up the fourteen stairs, and at the top I stopped and said, aloud, to the closed door, “He’ll see to it.” And then I went in and did not sleep.

At five in the morning there was a tread on the stairs. I had known it for eight years, the weight and the pause on every landing, and I knew it this time before it reached the second floor because there was no matchstick in it. I stood in the kitchen in my stockings with the lamp lit and heard it come up the last fourteen and stop at the door.

I opened it. He stood on the landing with his hat in both hands, turning it by the brim.

“Ten past three,” he said. “Brophy found him. On his side, with his knees drawn up, like a man trying to keep warm. Ostrander says the heart. Ostrander always says the heart.” He turned the hat a full circle. “The bag was on the sergeant’s shelf, Ruth. I looked at it at four. The tin was in it.”

“Frank.”

“I had a call. Rafferty. It went on, and I—”

I shut the door. I did not slam it. I closed it quietly, as one closes the door on a sleeping child, and stood with my palm flat on the wood and heard him stand on the other side of it. After a while he went. I counted him down. One. Two. Three. The weight and the pause on the landing. Seven, eight. He had a bad knee on the stairs that he’d never told anyone about. Eleven. Twelve. Thirteen. Fourteen, and the street door’s brass handle, and its long groan, and its shut.

By afternoon the Beacon would have it in eight words on page one, HOTEL CLERK DIES; CONFESSED SLAYING TWO, over a column about the price of turkeys. It was the tidiest thing anyone ever said about him.

I went on counting. Fifteen, I said. In the kitchen the book lay in the pool of lamplight on the oilcloth where my mother had left it, with its clasp shut. Sixteen. Behind me a board creaked, and Helena stood in the doorway of her room in her nightgown with her rosary in her fist, and her lips moving, not yet stopped. Seventeen. Eighteen. I was counting stairs that had never been built, and I knew it, and I could not stop, and I was in the twenties when she said it.

“Rutka,” said my mother, very quietly. “Stop.”

chapters.title: Requiem for a Night Clerk
chapters.html:
Six men carried a small coffin up the nave of St. Casimir’s, and the nave smelled of wet candles and wetter wool.

I knew five of them. Mr. Okonski, the relief clerk, who had Teddy’s desk now and looked as though it had been left to him in a will. Mr. Sobczak the baker, in a suit that smelled of yeast. Hennessy the doorman. Deacon Tolliver in black, with no toothpick for once. At the front left corner, with his eyes on the sanctuary lamp and his clean fingernails white on the brass handle, Nick Karras, who had not been asked and had come anyway. The sixth was a man from the Shape Hall in a clean collar, whom nobody had asked either, and who looked at no one.

It was Monday, the twenty-fourth, ten in the morning, and the rain had settled in for the week. My mother had put Bronia in the front pew and herself beside her, shoulder to shoulder like a wall against a wind. They had been rivals at the coffee urn for twenty years and neither of them said a word about it. I sat in the fourth with Lucille, who had taken the morning off for an aunt who had been dying since March. Behind us Pearl Hightower held her key ring in her fist, so that not one of the forty could chime, and beyond her Dorrie Nash from the day desk sniffed into a handkerchief with a black ribbon pinned to it.

A wreath stood on an easel by the altar rail, white chrysanthemums on a frame the size of a wheelbarrow, with a satin ribbon across it in gold letters: THE HARBOR HOTEL. It took all the light there was. Beside it the coffin looked like what it was, a small thing, made for a small stooped man by somebody who had measured him by eye.

Ambrose Quill had the aisle seat of the second pew on the right. Nobody had reserved it; the sidesman had given it to him with a bow. He sat tall and still, with his hat on his knee and the cane across his forearm, a silver head parted exactly in the middle, and when the bell rang he went down on his knees without the small grunt a man of sixty-three allows himself. Kneeling puts the soles toward the pew behind. His were as clean as the day he bought them.

Father Dziedzic preached for six minutes. He said Tadeusz Wozniak had kept a door in this city for thirty years, and that when a stranger knocked, it had opened. He did not say which door. He looked once at the second pew, with his round weary face, and then at the roof.

At the back, in the last pew on the left, a woman in a black felt hat sat alone with her handbag upright on her knees. Lucille leaned over and breathed it into my ear. “That’s Joe’s widow.” On each side of her lay a yard of bare oak. A church makes a shape of the people who aren’t sitting next to you, and she had been given a good deal of it.

We stood on the steps afterward while the six men slid him into the hearse. Quill came down beside Bronia with his hat in one hand, and at the foot of the steps, where the gutter ran an inch deep in leaf mould and rain, he lifted the cane. He did not plant it. He held it level, clear of the wet, the way you hold a thing you don’t want marked, and stepped across on his own good legs, and laid it over his forearm again. I saw the tip in the grey light, two feet from my face. A small round disc of grey rubber, flat and even and new. Not a scuff on it. Not a grain worn off one side.

“My dear Mrs. Kowal.” He cleared his throat, twice. “May I?” And he took her hand in both of his. “It is the least a house can do. He was the best servant the Harbor has had in thirty years, and servant is a poor word. You shall want for nothing. You have my word.”

“You are kind, Mr. Quill,” said Bronia, who had been taught all her life to thank people. “The flowers were very large.”

I wanted to put my hand over her mouth. I would only have been rude.

He turned. “Miss Szymanski. He was fond of you.”

“He paid me.”

“That is how the fond are sometimes obliged to show it.” He inclined his head, as a man does to a woman he respects, and went off down Hake Street under a black umbrella held by Hennessy, tapping the pavement once, for the benefit of the church.

Calvary lies where the hill gives up and the Flats begin, so that the dead there drink the same water as the living. They had cut the grave in yellow clay and laid a plank across it. The rain came down the priest’s stole in a single line. Six men lowered him, and Bronia let fall a handful of the clay, and it made the sound it makes for everyone.

Afterward she stood on the plank walk with her handbag held in both hands, though there was nothing in it now but a rosary, a handkerchief and the key to a door that had been kicked in. She did not look at me. She looked at the clay.

“Teddy was a good boy,” she said. “He was fifty-four, and a good boy.” It was the sentence she had given me over the urn, with the tense changed, and the change was the whole difference. Then, in the quiet, formal English she kept for the unbearable: “Keep it. Use it as you must. Not the names.” And she let Helena take her arm.

At the cemetery gate Pearl waited beside the woman in the felt hat. They had the look of two people who have stood a long time without speaking and found it restful. She was small and straight, and her left forefinger had the callus of a needle.

“Mrs. Lambert,” I said.

“Miss Szymanski. Miss Hightower told me who you were.” Her voice was low and unhurried. “Joe thought well of that little man. He said Mr. Wozniak was the only one at the Harbor who said good night to the elevator.”

I had Joe’s key against my hip. It had been cold in my pocket for a fortnight, and I could not take it out in front of her; I had not earned the right to hand her a piece of brass with no sentence to go with it. “I have something of Joe’s. I’ll bring it to you, and the rest with it.”

“Joe taught me to wait,” said Odessa Lambert. “I’m good at it.” A deaconess came with an umbrella and took her away, and the two hats went off together down the wet road.

Pearl let the umbrella turn the corner. Then, as if remarking on the weather: “Mr. Quill left the hotel at twenty minutes to four last Thursday, and came back at ten past five.”

“Where did he go?”

“I do not guess. I count. He does not leave the building on a Thursday; in thirteen years I have known him to leave it on a Thursday never. He told the desk he had been to his dentist.” The gold spectacles caught the light and let it go. “I know his dentist. His dentist is on Tuesdays.”

Dolan’s Plymouth stood at the kerb a hundred yards down with its engine running and the near window open an inch. I got in. The heater worked on his side only, and under the peppermint he had been eating there was rye, three drinks of it, I judged, by the care with which he took the corner.

“I didn’t go in,” he said. “I don’t go into them. The last one I stood at the back of, a woman looked at me.”

“Moira’s.”

“Moira’s.” He drove for a block. Then he took a folded square from inside his coat and laid it on the seat between us. A photostat, white on black: a ruled page headed CENTRAL STATION: VISITORS TO PRISONERS, Thursday, 20 November, eleven lines in eleven hands. I found the seventh. 4:05 p.m. A. Quill. T. Wozniak. Employer. Out 4:31.

“Twenty-six minutes,” I said.

“Karras pulled it. Took the book out of the sergeant’s cage himself, on his own time, because it didn’t look right to him. He’s twenty-nine and everything looks wrong to him.” Dolan chewed the air where the matchstick would have been. “He’s been right oftener than I have. He handed it to me Saturday and I put it in my pocket. I’ve been carrying it around since like a stone in a shoe.”

“Pearl Hightower says Quill went out at twenty to four and was back at ten past five. The desk was told the dentist.”

“Whose dentist’s on a Thursday?”

“His is on Tuesdays.”

Dolan laughed without any sound, and then stopped. The windscreen wipers went over twice. “There’s something else, and you’ll want to hit me, so I’ll drive slow.” He did. “Nineteen-fifty. The Anchor, on Brine Street. It was the month Moira died. A man at the next stool, small, pale, decent, just let go by the Customs, who told me everyone’s got a paper somewhere. And I said, the best paper in this town is in a typewriter case on Cutter Street.” His jaw worked. “I said you’d kept the carbon of the whole of Pier 6. I said it to make him laugh. His name was Maher, and I never put it together till he was on a slab.”

I looked at the road. A streetcar went by with its lights on in the day, the Number 14, with nine people in it who all had somewhere to be.

“I put a man in your path with a story I told to feel less alone,” said Dolan. “He wrote your name on a blotter. That’s mine, Ruth. Add it to the other.”

“What other?”

“The ninety minutes. I’ll testify. All of it, 1948, what Rafferty said and where I stood. I took three hundred dollars out of his hand in the lot behind Central, in an envelope, and I spent it on the surgeon. The city’s plan wouldn’t cut for what she had. She had two years more.” He glanced across at me. “You’re not going to say anything.”

“I’m going to say you’re an idiot.”

“It’s less than I’ve earned.”

“It’s what I’ve got.” I watched the wipers. “Rafferty rang you Friday night.”

“To tell me I’d done a clean piece of work. That Moira would’ve been proud.” The Plymouth slowed, as though it had heard. “I stood at the sergeant’s telephone for twenty minutes while the man who bought me for three hundred dollars told me what a fine policeman I was. And I forgot a tin of pills. That’s the length of it. I’ve been trying to make it longer.”

“I’m not going to say anything about the tin, Frank. Not today.”

“No.” He nodded, slowly, as at a sentence. “I’d like the carbon, Ruth. Not for me. It’s the only thing in this town that says what Rafferty said, and when.”

“Not yet.”

“When?”

“When I’ve got something to lay it beside.”

He turned into Hake Street and stopped at the kerb below the Szymanskis’ stairs. The wipers went over once more and he switched them off, and the rain closed the windscreen like a hand.

I stood on the pavement until the Plymouth’s tail light had gone round the corner of Eleventh. Then I said it aloud, to the gutter, in case the gutter had anything to add.

“A man who leans on a cane for twenty years wears the tip down on one side.”

The gutter ran on toward the Sound. And I saw it again as it had been on the church steps in the grey light: a small round disc of new rubber, lifted level over the water, and not a mark on it.

chapters.title: A Cane Without a Scuff
chapters.html:
Mr. Sorkin took one pencil from behind each ear, laid them side by side on the glass of the prescription counter, and said that he preferred to begin with his instruments.

It was nine on Tuesday morning, the twenty-fifth, and Sorkin’s Pharmacy on Front Street smelled of camphor and liquorice and wet umbrellas. Two great carboys of coloured water glowed in the window, one red and one green, as they had since before the war. He was fifty-five, narrow and exact, in a white coat buttoned to the collar, with a blue pencil behind the left ear and a red one behind the right, and he looked at the two of us over a pair of half-glasses the way a man looks at a prescription in a doctor’s bad hand.

“Miss Fong, I know. Your father buys my tincture of benzoin and does not say thank you, which in his case is a mark of respect.”

“He says it with his eyes,” said Lucille. She had her tortoiseshell glasses pushed up on her forehead, which she does when she means to be persuasive, and a pencil in her hair. “I told Mr. Pruitt my aunt was dying. I’ve used the aunt four times. He thinks my family is made of paper.”

“This is Ruth Szymanski,” I said. “I’m a private investigator, or I was till Thursday. Mr. Sorkin, I want to describe a label to you.”

I described it. Sorkin’s Pharmacy, Front St. Rx 4187, and a figure torn off. Oct 28. One capsule at bedtime. He heard me to the end without a word, and then he turned and ran a finger along the shelf behind him, where black cloth ledgers stood in a row with the years painted on their spines in white, 1931 to 1952, like a family of identical sons. He took down the last. He wet his thumb.

“Forty-one thousand eight hundred and seventy-one,” he said. “Mrs. Dibble. A tonic for her nerves. Forty-one eight seventy-three, Mr. Okonski, for his stomach, and I am sorry for his stomach.” His finger stopped. “And between them. Forty-one eight seventy-two.”

“Who?”

“A. Quill. Resident of the Harbor Hotel. Chloral hydrate, five-grain capsules, number sixty. Dr. Hartigan’s prescription, written the ninth of February, and refilled seven times, the last on the twenty-eighth of October.” He closed the ledger on his finger. “Eight bottles of sixty since the winter. A great many nights without sleep for one old gentleman. I thought, here is a man with a conscience. I was wrong, perhaps, about what kind.”

“What’s he like?”

“A very correct gentleman. Pays on the first of the month, in cash, to the cent. When I have the rubber heels in, for the old gentlemen who wear overshoes, he asks for a pair to put on his own. He cannot abide a scuff.” He took his glasses off. “Detective Karras came on Friday with half a label in an envelope. A young man, the Greek, with clean nails. I said I should wish a day to check the refills. He said Monday. On Saturday the Beacon told me the case was closed, and nobody came back.”

“Why didn’t you telephone?”

“A pharmacist telephones nobody, Miss Szymanski. The police come to him.” He replaced the blue pencil behind his left ear with the care of a man laying down a good knife. “I read that the clerk died in his cell. I thought: a man’s pills are the last thing anybody looks at in a hotel. And I sold the bottle.”

“Will you say that to a judge?”

“I will say it to a judge, to a priest and to my wife,” said Sorkin. “They will each ask a different question, and I shall have the same answer for all of them.”

The Pacific Telephone building stands on Third with a brass door that has not been properly shut since 1931. The exchange is on the third floor, one long room with a ceiling lost in cigarette smoke, and as we came out of the stairwell it hit me like the smell of my own coat from a trunk: forty headsets, forty hands, the soft crack of cords and the murmuring of forty women saying Number, please to the whole of Port Calder. I stood in the doorway until Lucille took my elbow. I had a groove in my hair, once, that matched every one of theirs.

Mrs. Dorothea Nugent was the night supervisor and had no business being there at noon. She was fifty-nine, small and square, with a grey roll of hair and a cardigan the colour of a pigeon, and she had come in because she had not slept in the daytime since 1941 and Lucille had asked. She took us to a glass cubicle at the end of the board and shut the door on the noise. From a steel drawer she took a bundle of buff tickets with a rubber band round them.

“November the fifth, Port Calder to Santa Barbara. Station to station. Originating, Harbor Hotel, room eight-oh-six.” She laid the ticket on the desk between us. “Started two-oh-five a.m. Ended three-twenty. Seventy-five minutes. Eighteen dollars seventy-five.”

Lucille whistled through her chipped tooth.

“A call that long, somebody talks,” said Mrs. Nugent. “I’ve supervised this board for nineteen years and I can tell you what a seventy-five-minute call sounds like. This one didn’t. At twenty to three my girl on position nine flagged it to me: a Santa Barbara line open and quiet. I plugged in on the monitor key. At the Santa Barbara end, an old lady, asleep or very nearly. At the Port Calder end,” and she turned her head a little, as if the sound were still coming down the wire, “a clock, and nobody breathing.”

“A clock,” I said.

“A good one, with a tick like a man tapping a pencil. I’d know it on a hundred lines. Nobody in that room. A receiver laid down on a table, and a person elsewhere.”

“Mrs. Nugent,” said Lucille, “I need a long-distance line to a lady in Santa Barbara, and I need to be the Telephone Company.”

“Number, please,” said Mrs. Nugent, and lifted a receiver.

I will not forget Lucille Fong with her glasses pushed up, bent over the desk in that glass box with the receiver in both hands, using her best voice, the one from the old days, the one that could soothe a drunk off a ledge by telephone. “Miss Honor Calder? Pacific Telephone, Customer Accounts, ma’am. I’ve a query on a long-distance charge to your number on the fifth of November. From the Harbor Hotel, Port Calder.” The line crackled. She listened. “No, ma’am, Harbor. HARBOR. — Yes, ma’am, a Mr. Quill. — I’m sorry, ma’am, would you say that again? — SEVENTY-FIVE MINUTES.” A pause. Her eyebrows went up into her fringe. “Ten? You’re quite sure it was ten?”

I could hear the voice from where I stood, small and cracked and far away, like a record played in another house.

“Ambrose rings when he can’t sleep, dear. He talks of the Christmas accounts, ten minutes, and then he says he’ll let me read the figures, and I say yes, Ambrose, and I put it on the pillow, dear, and that’s the last I know. I’m seventy-eight. He was always so good to us. He held the plate when they took the photograph.”

“The plate,” said Lucille faintly.

“At the piano. Such a steady hand.”

Lucille thanked her, hung up very gently and sat down on the corner of the desk. “She put the receiver on her pillow,” she said, “and a man left a clock to talk to her for seventy-five minutes. Ruth, I could cry. She likes him.”

“Everyone does,” I said. “It’s how he works.”

On the stairs afterward, where the smoke thinned, she stopped on the landing and said, “What have you got in that pocket? You’ve had your hand on it since Sorkin’s.”

I took out the book. The brass clasp was warm from my hip. She didn’t ask to open it. She put her palm flat on the cover, the way you lay a hand on a child’s head or a table that is being dragged away, and held it there.

“You saw the certificate on my father’s wall,” she said. “Ruth. Whatever you do, it isn’t going in a file.”

“It isn’t.”

“Say it again.”

“It isn’t going in a file, Lucille.”

She nodded. She took her hand away and pushed the glasses back down onto her nose, and became the Senior Clerk of Vessel Records once more. “Then I’ll take you to my father.”

The certificate was gone from the wall at Fong and Son. Where it had hung there was a pale oblong on the paper, edged in dust, the size of a man’s regret. Walter Fong saw me look at it. “I have taken it down for cleaning,” he said, and not one muscle in his face moved, and the dry joke arrived a beat after it, as his always did. “It has been taking a long time.”

He measured me with his eyes first, which I had been expecting. “You have lost four pounds since the seventh,” he said. “In the left shoulder, where it always goes.” Then he went into the back of the shop and came out with a ledger as long as my forearm, bound in black oilcloth, with March 1948 on a paper tag.

He opened it on the cutting table under the lamp. Down the left side ran thirty-one lines in a hand like copperplate. Pea coat, 38 reg. Pea coat, 40 long. Pea coat, 36 short. A watch cap size for each. At the head of the page: 14 March. Pier 6 shed. Cash. And along the foot, in the same small perfect writing: Paid from Pier 6 office. Order of the Estate.

“I wrote what the voice told me,” said Walter Fong. “I did not ask which estate. In my trade one learns not to look at the customer. One learns, however, to write down what he says.”

“Mr. Fong, may I photograph this?”

He considered it with his head a little on one side, the half-glasses at the end of his nose. “A ledger is a thing meant to be looked at,” he said. “It is only people that I would prefer not to have photographed.”

I had a Brownie Hawkeye with a flash gun, bought in a pawn shop for four-fifty the year I got my licence and used until then for nothing but divorces. I used the whole roll. Lucille held the lamp. Her father stood at the end of the table with his hands folded over his tape measure, looking at his own handwriting, and when the last bulb flashed and popped he said, to the lines, not to us, “They were all sizes. I remember the small ones best.”

I sat for a while afterward on the step in Anchor Alley, where the laundry steam came out of the vent in the wall and wandered up past the fire escapes. The rain had thinned to a mist. I took the pink eviction notice from my pocket, turned it over to the back, where I had written 2:05, Santa Barbara, 806, lamp 2:45, dark 3:30 a fortnight before, and I took out a stub of pencil, and I put the things in a column underneath.

Cane: no wear.

Gown, red, quilted, shiny at the shoulders. On a hook in 806. Yvette: tall, old, fast.

Ink: rust-brown. The pass he signed me. The slip in the hat.

“Mezzanine.”

The dial over his door. The toggle under the glass.

Clock, no breathing. 75 minutes. 10.

Rx 41872.

I looked at it for as long as it takes the Heifer to sound twice. Each thing, alone, was only a man’s habit: a cane he carried for show, a gown he had been given, a word he’d picked up in a card room twenty years ago. A man may own a thing and still be innocent of it. But a column is not a pile, and it ran down the back of that notice in a straight line to the one place there was room for a name. I wrote it. A trust has no face, a lawyer had told Ferrante at the end of a pier. It had a silver head, parted exactly in the middle. I wrote underneath: Dear Mr. Quill.

And then, because the Waltham’s face was turned to my wrist and I had to turn my wrist to read it, I read what I had known for an hour and did not want to know. It was twenty to five. I was out of a job, a licence, a client and a friend, and I had a pharmacist’s book, a clock on a pillow and a ledger of sizes, none of which would hang a man who sends flowers.

At a quarter to six I went back to Sorkin’s and asked to use the telephone booth. He had already written it out, in his small clear hand, on a sheet of the shop’s paper, with the date and the number and the quantity: I, Abel Sorkin, being a registered pharmacist. He signed it with his fountain pen and then, because the blue pencil was nearer, ruled a line under the name with it. He gave me the pencil to take down what I was told.

Dolan answered on the second ring. “Dolan.”

“I have a pharmacist and a phone line,” I said. “Sorkin’s book puts the bottle in A. Quill’s name, Rx 41872, chloral hydrate, the seventh refill on the twenty-eighth of October. The toll ticket says seventy-five minutes on the line from 806, and the lady in Santa Barbara says he talked for ten. There was a clock at his end of the line and nobody breathing. I need the paper.”

A long, careful silence with a matchstick in it. “Which paper?”

“The one Maher died for. The master’s copy of the Esther Vane, with a signature on it that hangs the House. Without it all I’ve got is an insomniac’s prescription and an old lady on a pillow.”

“That’s a good deal, Ruth.”

“It’s a good deal for a lawyer to make into a mood. It isn’t enough to hang a man who sends wreaths.”

“No,” said Frank Dolan. I could hear him breathe. I could hear, behind him, the Detective Bureau going about its evening, a typewriter, a door, somebody laughing at nothing. “No, it isn’t. Then get me the paper.”

I hung up. I stood in the booth for a time with the receiver in my hand and the dial tone going, and then I put the receiver back in its hook. When I came out Mr. Sorkin was waiting at the counter with his hand out. I gave him back the blue pencil. He turned it once in his fingers, as if to make sure it was the same, and put it behind his left ear, where it fitted into a groove worn for it.

chapters.title: What Joe Said About the Frame
chapters.html:
The oven door stood open for warmth, as it does in our kitchen when the coal runs short, and my mother sat asleep in front of it with her glasses on their string and her hands folded on a bread board in her lap, as if she had been interrupted in the middle of a conversation with it.

It was midnight on Tuesday. I had walked the floor between the table and the window for an hour and a half, counting boards, and had got as far as a hundred and seventy of them, which is a good many more than a kitchen has. The pink notice lay on the oilcloth with its column of words. I had read the column so often it had become wallpaper.

“Rutka.” She had not opened her eyes. “You walk like a horse.”

“I’m sorry, Mama.”

“A horse that walks all night is a horse that doesn’t know where the stable is.” She opened one eye and the glasses slid down. “So. You know who.”

“I know who. I can’t show it. I have a pharmacist and a telephone operator and a sizing book, and not one of them has ever seen him do anything. The paper’s what hangs him, and the paper’s gone. He turned the whole of the ninth floor over, Mama, and the Frieze, and Maher’s room, and he didn’t find it. Neither did anyone else.”

My mother took the bread board off her lap and set it on the table, square. “A man who cannot be shown,” she said, “has put the proof somewhere. When a thing is hidden, ask who walks past it every day and sees nothing.”

I was standing with my hand on the back of a chair. In my head I was standing in the cab of the Harbor’s elevator on the fifth of November, between the oak and the brass, with the floor going up under my shoes, reading the only thing there was to read.

The car had had a lean. I remembered it now. The first morning I had put it down to my own tiredness, but it ran a quarter inch to port, the oak panels a hair out of true, the button plate sagging on its screws, the brass rail dipping at one end like a mouth. Lambert had said it was getting old. That cab’s got moods, Miss. And between those crooked panels, at about the height of a tall man’s eyes, a frame hung as true as a plumb line. I had read the certificate as the car climbed, Landings served: 9, Floors open to public: 8, and thought nothing of the frame. It was the one square thing in that cab. It was the only thing in there that did not lean.

Fellow in 807 read it a good minute, Miss, on the Monday. Called it the only honest thing in the building.

A good minute. A man alone with a porter whose back is turned to the brass and whose mind is on a hymn. A man who has the length of a ride and a pocketful of thumbtacks. Who looks at a man reading a certificate in an elevator? Nobody. Everybody has stood in that cab, and read that frame, and gone out at their floor, for twenty-six years. It hangs in front of the whole of Port Calder and not one of them has ever lifted it.

“Mama,” I said. “I’m going out.”

“Take the scarf,” said Helena Szymanska, and shut her eyes. “And the other one. For the neck.”

I rang the Harbor’s service entrance from the booth on Eleventh at half past midnight. A kitchen porter fetched Miss Hightower, and I heard a dishwasher going somewhere behind them, and a tap. “It’s Ruth Szymanski,” I said. “I’m looking for the honest thing in the building.”

A silence, with water in it. Then Pearl: “I do not guess. Two o’clock. The kitchen yard.” She hung up.

I walked down to Front Street in the rain with my collar turned and my father’s Waltham ticking against the bone. There is a quarter of an hour on the way, between the ferry slip and Anchor Alley, when the whole of Port Calder is asleep and one is the only person left awake in it, and I counted the lamp posts, and there were sixty-one. The kitchen yard on Ferry Slip Row was as I had left it a fortnight before, but the bin where I had landed in the peelings was empty and clean, and I felt unreasonably let down.

Pearl stood in the kitchen door in a white apron over her black dress, the ring of forty keys held in her fist so that nothing chimed, and between her finger and thumb a different key, long and black, old as the building. “The boiler door,” she said. “I have not turned it in ten years. Joe used it to go out and smoke where Mr. Quill could not smell it. Come.”

We went down. The boiler room was as it had been on the eleventh. A thermos stood on the bench where Joe had left it, and his chair stood at the end of it, and nobody had moved either. Beyond that a stair came out through a door behind the laundry chute, and at its foot Pearl bent, and caught the neck of a canvas sack taller than a child, full of soiled linen, and began to drag it toward the service lift.

“For cover,” she said. “A housekeeper with a sack at three in the morning is a housekeeper doing her work. The van for the laundry comes at five.” She did not look round. “Mr. Okonski is on the sixth floor with a flashlight and a face. A maid of mine has been very convincing about the radiator.”

“Does he know about—”

“Mr. Okonski knows about radiators.”

The lobby was dark except for the one lamp on the desk, and the fern, and the three-minutes-slow clock, and the brass arc over the cab door, where the needle lay quiet on the L. The desk stood empty with Teddy’s blotter squared on it for no one. It is a terrible thing to see a man’s habit going on without him. I did not look at it twice.

Pearl dragged the sack into the car after me and let the gates close. “Five,” she said, and I pressed it. The car began to lift, with its long soft sigh, and for the first time in my life I stood in a cab with the lights on and my hands free and the only thing in front of me was a piece of framed paper.

State Division of Elevators. Certificate of Inspection No. 4471. The type was a little blurred behind the glass. It hung dead straight. I put my fingers under the lower edge of the frame and lifted, and it came away from the wall on its two brass screws with no more effort than a coat from a peg. The screws had turned too easily. Somebody had drawn them lately and had not set them hard.

Behind the frame, held against the oak by two thumbtacks, was a Manila envelope.

I do not know how long I stood with it in my hand. I know the car had stopped, and that Pearl had turned off the motor with the little brass lever, and that the lamp in the ceiling gave a faint tick, as if it were counting. The flap was not sealed. Inside lay two sheets. The first was the Esther Vane’s manifest, the master’s copy, in the thin grey type of the Antwerp agent: forty crew, by name and rating, and the figure forty ruled off at the foot and initialled. The second was a typed half-sheet on a different paper, white, heavy, with a watermark I could read against the cab lamp: three letters, C.E.T.

Received for the Calder Estate Trust: 31 cases, personal effects. Pier 6, Slip 3. 14th March 1948.

And below it, in a brown the colour of an old scab, a signature in a hand as upright as a row of fence posts: A. Quill, Trustee.

I knew the colour before I read the name. It was the pass he had signed for me at his desk on the fifth, and the slip in the lining of a dead man’s hat. It had been the green-black of a bottle on a desk in 1948, and the years had dried it to this. Behind the manifest, folded once, was a half-sheet torn from a tally pad, and a line of clerk’s writing, the best I ever saw, slanting a little to the right as if the man wrote with the wind behind him.

Miss Szymanski. If you’re reading this I was a fool. The count is thirty-one. The signature is his own. Don’t let them make the others pay.

“Give it to me,” said Pearl.

I had not heard her move. She stood at my elbow with her head lifted, like a woman listening for a kettle. “Listen.”

I heard nothing, and said so.

“A bell. Very high. It tinks up the shaft like a spoon on a glass.” She waited. “Mr. Quill has had a bell put in 806, I think, since the Thursday you went up. It rings when this car leaves the lobby after midnight. We left the lobby four minutes ago.”

I should have thought of it. I had been so occupied with the frame that I had put the dial and the bell and the man behind them out of my mind like a bad tooth. “He’ll be on the stairs.”

“He will be at the lobby by the time you reach it. He is a man who likes to be waiting.” She held out her hand. “Give me the envelope. Whatever you hold, he will see it, Miss Szymanski. He reads a face like a column of figures. Mine he reads and sees nothing, because I have been invisible to him for twenty-six years, and that is the best thing about a housekeeper.”

I gave it to her. She dropped it into the sack among the soiled sheets and thrust it down with her forearm to the shoulder, and tied the neck again with the same knot. “Where does the linen van go?”

“One-one-two-seven Hake Street. Second floor, over the cobbler.”

“The Harbor sends its good tablecloths to be hand-done by the women of the Flats before the holiday. There is a ticket for each.” She wrote on a laundry slip with a pencil from her apron, Mrs. H. Szymanska, 12 damask, hand-press, and tucked it into the neck of the sack. “Your mother will be surprised at six in the morning. She will be a Christian about it. Now you will put that frame back where it hangs, and you will ride down alone with nothing in your hands, and you will not look back at me.”

I lifted the frame onto its two screws with fingers that had stopped being steady. I did not get it straight. Pearl pressed the brass lever, and the car came to life under us and began to sink; she stopped it at the fifth with her hand. The gates rattled. She dragged her sack out onto the carpet and into the dark of a corridor with a sound like a very large and very patient animal, and she did not look at me, and the gates shut on her back.

I rode down alone. Thirty-eight seconds is a long time with a bell ringing somewhere above your head.

The doors opened on the lobby. He was waiting.

He stood on the marble beyond the threshold in his dark red quilted dressing gown, with his cane over his forearm and his silver hair parted in the middle, as composed as if he had been there all night. Behind him, at the desk, Mr. Okonski held a flashlight in both hands like a man who has been interrupted at something he did not understand. The lamp lit Quill from below and made his pale eyes pale.

“My dear Miss Szymanski.” He cleared his throat, twice. “It is very late for a visit.”

“I was looking for the honest thing in the building.”

“And did you find it?”

“Not tonight.”

He smiled. It was the smile he had given Teddy on his knee on the lobby floor, kind and sorrowful and entirely without error. He did not say anything. He did not ask what I had in my pockets, and I will say for him that he never once made the vulgar mistake of searching a woman. His eyes left my face. They went past my shoulder into the cab, to the oak wall and its brass, and came to rest on the frame, hanging crooked.

It was the only crooked thing in a cab where everything leaned. He did not need to cross the floor. He read it from the door, as he reads everything, as a ledger with one figure out of line.

chapters.title: Thanksgiving Eve
chapters.html:
Dolan ate my mother’s eggs the way he did everything that morning, as if someone might come for the plate.

Three of them, fried in butter until the whites went to lace, and a heel of rye that he tore instead of cutting. Between the first forkful and the last he said nothing at all. It was twenty to seven on Wednesday the twenty-sixth, and rain ran down the kitchen window in the grey that passes for dawn on Hake Street in November. At his elbow, on a clean dish towel, since Helena allows no paper on an oilcloth where there are eggs, lay a manifest in the thin grey type of an Antwerp shipping agent, a half-sheet watermarked with three letters, and a note from a dead man. He had read them standing, twice. Then he had held the half-sheet up to the window, moving his lips over the name at the foot, and sat down and asked if there was anything to eat. It is what a policeman does when he has been handed something he is going to have to carry.

The linen van had come at ten to six, a Dodge with HARBOR HOTEL on the door in gilt, and a driver who passed my mother a slip and a canvas sack as long as a child and left without waiting to be thanked. She signed for twelve damask. She counted twelve damask. She also found, in the middle of them, a Manila envelope rolled in a pillowcase, which she laid on the table without a word before she went back to counting. By the time Dolan’s Plymouth stopped below, three of the cloths were in the washtub and she was saying things about the Harbor’s gravy in two languages.

He wiped his mouth on the back of his hand and, at a glance from my mother, on the napkin by his plate. “A housekeeper put evidence in the wash,” he said to the empty plate. “Barnwell is going to enjoy that. Mrs. Szymanska, I ask your pardon in advance for what I’m about to say.”

“Say it,” said my mother, without turning from the tub. “In this house a man may swear in any language he has. God has a good ear and a long list.”

Dolan swore. He did it quietly, in Irish, which he does not otherwise speak, and it went on about as long as a decade of the rosary. My mother nodded at the end of it, as she does at a sound piece of pastry.

Then he took the evidence envelope from his inside pocket, where it had lived against his ribs for a fortnight, and slid out the slip from Maher’s hatband. NINE. HALF PAST MIDNIGHT. BRING IT. He laid it on the towel beside the receipt. One was a clerk’s block capitals and the other a gentleman’s copperplate, tall and upright as fence posts, but the ink was the same rust brown in both, the colour of a thing that had once been green.

“Ink like old blood,” said Dolan.

“You can say that to the Judge.”

“I’ll say it to Barnwell, and he’ll say it to the Judge in better words.” He turned the half-sheet over to the blank back. “Why would a man sign it? Thirty-one people, his own name, his own ink. Four years in a drawer.”

“Because he’s an auditor.” I had been awake twenty-six hours and the answer came out whole, the way they do at that stage, like a tooth. “He can steal anything he likes, Frank. He can’t leave a receipt unsigned.”

On the oilcloth he laid a brown envelope. “Karras developed your roll last night in the station darkroom. Thirty-one lines in a hand like a row of pins, and across the foot, Paid from Pier 6 office, order of the Estate.”

The District Attorney keeps his office on the second floor of the County Building, at the top of Lamplighter Hill, down a corridor of green linoleum that smells of floor wax and other people’s trouble. Dolan’s Plymouth heats on the driver’s side only, so I arrived warm on one side and damp on the other.

In the outer office a woman of forty in a green cardigan was typing with the pleasant fixed face of someone who has been asked to look as though she isn’t listening. The plate on her desk said MISS ALDOUS. I had never seen the woman who ate chops with Gilbert Swain at half past one on the morning of the fifth, and I had imagined someone more expensive.

Hollis Barnwell was fifty-two, long and grey and very clean, with heavy lids and a way of turning a page by its corner as though the paper might be hot. His hat sat crown-down on the blotter, so that nothing could fall out of it. He had never lost a case.
