Port Calder said so with respect, and the Detective Bureau said it with a certain flatness, because everyone knew the reason: he had never taken one that could be lost.

He read for eleven minutes by the clock over the door. He took a glass from his drawer and looked at the signature as a jeweller looks at a flaw, and at Maher’s note, and at the watermark against the window, and then he set the glass down square to the blotter and folded his hands on it.

“If this were mine,” he said, “I should want to know three things. Forgive me, Miss Szymanski. I understand you are not at present licensed, so I will think of you as a private citizen, which is the more reliable witness. How the paper came to be where it was. How it came to be here. And what, beyond a signature, it proves.”

I told him: Maher, the Monday, the cab, the frame, Pearl, the sack.

“A private citizen removed a document from an elevator at three in the morning, with the help of an employee, and it spent three hours in a laundry sack.”

“In my mother’s kitchen.”

“Which is better custody than I have seen the police give.” He did not smile, but his eyes took a short rest. “I shall ask the court not to ask. As to what it proves.” He laid a finger on the half-sheet. “A Trustee signed for thirty-one cases of personal effects landed at Pier 6 on a night when Customs counted forty crew. That is a receipt. It is not a crime. The crime is what the cases were, and the only persons who can say what they were are persons I understand you will not name.” His finger moved to Maher’s note. “The others.”

“I can’t name them.”

“Then I shall not ask. A prosecutor who has not asked cannot be made to tell.” He folded his hands again. “I have a very short memory for what I am not told. It is my only vice.”

Dolan chewed the unlit matchstick. “And Quill?”

“Against Mr. Quill I have a signature, a pharmacist’s ledger, an old lady in Santa Barbara who is seventy-eight and kind, and a sedative that half the old gentlemen in the county take for their nights. Against that I have a confession from a man who is dead and so cannot recant.” His voice did not rise. It never did; it only grew more exact. “The Beacon has told this city for four days that Wozniak did it. The defendant is sixty-three, with a cane, and has forty old retainers who will weep on the stand and say that he gave them each a ham.”

“He knows the frame’s empty,” I said. “He looked at it at four this morning.”

“Then he has been asked a question, and I expect he will answer it politely.” Barnwell drew a pad toward him. “What I want is the Estate’s books. The receipt ledger that stands behind that half-sheet, in his hand, every item received since 1946. With the ledger this paper is a count. Without it, a scrap. A warrant for the Estate’s records at the Calder Building and at the hotel: room 806, and whatever there is above the eighth floor. Judge Pardoe sits until noon, and after noon he keeps the holiday with his sister at Stannard’s Ferry. I will have him hear it at his house at four, over coffee, and he will sign if the coffee is good.”

“Has the sister got a telephone?” said Dolan.

“I believe she regards it as a vulgarity.”

“It’s Thanksgiving,” Dolan told the ceiling. “Everything in this town is somebody’s sister’s.”

“Until the paper is signed,” said Barnwell, “nobody enters that hotel. Nobody asks a bellboy the time.” He looked at me. “You have a question.”

“If he burns it.”

“The ledger?” He considered it with real courtesy. “Miss Szymanski, he is an accountant. A man like that does not burn his books. He files them.”

It was the soundest reasoning I heard that day, and I have never entirely forgiven it.

We went out through the outer office. Miss Aldous had the telephone at her ear and her back to us, the cord wound twice round her forefinger. “—not till four,” she was saying, in the pleasant voice of a woman declining a second helping. “I told you, Gil, nothing is—” She heard the door and turned the rest of it into a cough.

On the stairs I said, “Gil.”

“Half the County Building telephones Swain,” said Dolan. “He represents the half that isn’t in jail.” He put on his brown hat with both hands, which is how he does it when he is angry. “I’ll tell Barnwell. He’ll move her to the files.”

“By Friday,” I said, and we went down the rest of the stairs without another word, counting different things.

I slept in my clothes on top of the bedspread until two, when my mother put a bowl of soup on the chair and a hand on my foot. By half past four I had the Waltham wound and my hat on. She had hung the last of the damask from lines across the kitchen ceiling, so that twelve white cloths dripped into twelve pots like the flags of small countries that had given up. The book was in the oven under the roasting pan, where it lived now.

“You are going to that hotel,” said my mother.

“To Tommy’s. It’s across the street from it.”

“Rutka. A street is a very small river.” She wound a grey wool scarf round my neck and tied it in the knot she keeps for children and parcels, and I let her. “Come back dry.”

Tommy had a card in the window, CLOSED THURS., and eleven pumpkin and six mince chalked on the slate. I took the stool by the window and wiped a porthole in the steam with my sleeve.

The fog came up off the Sound at a quarter past five, the way water comes into a cellar: first at the foot of the street, then in the middle, then everywhere. At twenty to six the Heifer started up at Calder Point, two long low notes, and I counted forty and heard it again. Across the road the Harbor stood with its eight rows of windows lit, and above them the Frieze was a dark band with nothing in it but fog moving along, slowly, the way a hand goes across a slate.

At twenty past six a black Packard slid out of the fog and stopped at the hotel’s door.

Gilbert Swain got out in a camel coat with a leather bag held in both arms against his stomach, wearing the face of a man who has been handed a baby to carry on a train. He looked up Front Street, and down, and across at the steam on Tommy’s window, and went in. Through the lobby glass I watched him set the bag on the desk before Dorrie Nash and her black ribbon, say something with his chin up, and dab his lip with a handkerchief. Forty seconds, by the Heifer. Then the Packard was gone, and the bag sat on the marble with nobody’s hand on it. A lawyer with a secretary, a cold and a car, carrying his own bag. In my experience a man who carries his own bag has told no one what is in it.

At a quarter to seven I saw the light.

It was no more than a thread, low and yellow, in the black band above the eighth floor, behind a louvre near the Ferry Slip end. It moved a few feet toward the west and stopped. Fog came across it and the thread went on burning through the fog, a little duller, like a coal under ash.

I set a nickel on the saucer by the wall telephone and Tommy turned his back, which is as much privacy as a lunch counter has. Dolan came on at the Bureau in the voice of a man who had been kept by a telephone for an hour and had not liked it.

“He’s on nine,” I said. “Swain brought a bag at twenty past six. At a quarter to seven there’s a light in the Frieze.”

“The warrant’s not signed.” He said it fast, like a bad score read out. “Pardoe left for his sister’s with the coffee unfinished, and Barnwell’s gone after him in his own car with the papers. We’ll be there at seven-thirty. Karras and me and two in uniform. You hear me, Ruth? Seven-thirty.”

“Say again.”

“Seven-thirty. Don’t you—”

I hung up on the rest of it. In the wire room you leave a time with someone before a man goes into a building, and if he hasn’t called by then, you send. It is the first rule they teach and the only one that ever saved anybody.

I put in a second nickel and gave the operator Anchor Alley. “Fong and Son,” said Walter Fong, the way a man reads a name off a stone. I told him to tell Lucille the kitchen yard of the Harbor Hotel, on Ferry Slip Row, at eight o’clock, and to bring a coat.

There was a pause just long enough for a man to look at the ceiling. “Whose coat?”

“Any coat.”

“There is no such thing as any coat,” said Walter Fong. “I will see to it.”

The kitchen door on Ferry Slip Row stood open on steam. Twenty-two turkeys lay in rows on the long steel table, trussed and pale, like longshoremen laid out for a union meeting, and a cook with a face like a boiled ham was stuffing them at a speed that meant he had somewhere to be. Nobody looked at me. A woman in a hat walking through a hotel kitchen on the eve of a holiday is a delivery.

Pearl Hightower stood by the service stair in a white apron over her black dress, the ring of forty keys in her fist, silent as a stone. She spoke first.

“You have come by the front. The front is the wrong door.”

“I came by the side. Where is he?”

“I do not guess.” The gold spectacles caught the steam and let it go. “Mr. Quill came out of his office in a dinner jacket, which he does not wear on a Wednesday, and took Mr. Swain’s bag himself. From the pantry he took the five-pint can we fill the sconces from in the Pacific Room when the current fails. At twenty to seven he went up in the service lift with the bag in one hand and the can in the other.” She breathed once, through her nose. “The bag was not shut. I saw the corners. Green cloth, six or seven, with leather spines.”

“The linen cupboard?”

“The padlock hangs open on its hasp. The back of the shelves is not fastened from this side. It never has been.”

I knew then, and was ashamed how long it had taken me. A man who wants a ledger burned has a grate in 806. He does not carry lamp oil up fourteen steps for a ledger. He carries it for a floor.

“Ring your bell,” I said.

“I will ring it when I smell it, not before. A bell rung for nothing is the end of a housekeeper. I have twenty-six guests, three of them old ladies who will not leave a room without their teeth.” She did not move. “The sergeant?”

“Half past seven.”

“The kitchen door will be kept open for the sergeant.”

I thought of the .32 in the bottom drawer of my desk on Cutter Street, eight minutes off and eight back and a lock to argue with, and of the fact that I had never in my life carried it. Then I put my hand into Pearl’s apron pocket and took out a flashlight. She let me. It was nickel-plated, with a dent in the barrel. “The batteries are new,” she said. “I put them in on the fourteenth.” It took me until the first landing to understand that she had been keeping it twelve days for somebody.

The staff stair is a hundred and thirty-eight steps from the kitchen landing to eight. I counted them to keep my feet in order, the way a man whistles on a dark road. The eighth-floor corridor lay empty and dim, a dance band thin behind somebody’s door and a smell of somebody’s pork chop. At the east end the linen cupboard stood open, the padlock on its hasp new enough still to shine. I put my palm against the middle of the back of the shelves, and it moved, inward, on a hinge somebody had oiled, like a heavy book opening.

Beyond it was dark, and a smell came down out of the dark, sweet and flat, like a garage on a hot day.

Fourteen steps, Teddy had said, and he had said to count. I put the light on the first.

One. Two. Three. Four. Five. On the sixth the tread gave under my shoe with a small dry crack, like a knuckle, as it had given for Teddy, and for Pearl, and for two men carrying a third; I had known it was there for thirteen days, and I stood on it anyway, because I was counting, and counting is something the feet do.

“Six,” I said, out loud, to nobody, and nobody answered, and I went on up.

chapters.title: The Safe in the Card Room
chapters.html:
Lamp oil in a closed place does not drift. It settles, like damp in a coat. By the ninth step I could taste it, flat and sweet, a coin held under the tongue, and the beam of Pearl’s flashlight went on ahead of me up the last five treads of bare pine and found at the head of them the edge of an oak panel standing open, and beyond it, low on the boards, a light the colour of weak tea.

I stopped with one foot on the top step.

“The sixth, I think,” said a voice in the room beyond. It was not raised. It did not need to be; the stair carried it down to me as a pipe carries water. “I have always meant to have it seen to.”

I switched off the flashlight. There was no use in it. He had kept a lantern lit for the best part of an hour, and he had known since the cab at four that morning, or since the day I came up his front steps with a pass signed in green-black ink, that I would be the one to climb. I put my hand flat on the oak and went through.

The Calder Club room is thirty-six feet by twenty, and I had seen it once, by the nickel glare of a torch, a dead room under grey sheets. Now it had been lit for company. A hurricane lantern stood on the boards beside the nearest of the card tables, turned low, and the circle it made took in a cane-bottomed chair, a pair of black oxfords, the lower half of an ebony cane, and the legs of a table with a square of green baize on it. The rest of the room stood back in the dark the way an audience stands back from a stage: the stacked tables along the wall, the chandelier in its sheet like a bell under a cover, the long black mouth of the corridor at the far end. Behind my shoulder, in the east wall, the safe stood open with its door flung wide and the gold lettering worn to a ghost, and nothing inside it but pigeonholes.

Ambrose Quill sat at the table in a black dinner jacket and a stiff white collar, with his cane across his knees and his silver hair parted exactly in the middle, as composed as if the evening had been arranged for him. In front of him on the baize lay a ledger bound in green cloth, open at a page of small upright figures, with a silver pencil laid across the gutter, parallel to a line he had just ruled. By his right foot stood a five-pint can with a spout. By his left, a leather bag lay empty on its side.

“My dear Miss Szymanski.” He cleared his throat, twice. “It was the Mezzanine, in my day.”

“Nine,” I said. “Pomeroy’s register has it as nine, and the Frieze has it as nine, and Sergeant Dolan took his hat off to it in Front Street.”

He tilted his head as at a clerk who has been loud. “Do sit down.”

“I’ll stand.”

“As you wish.” He did not rise. A gentleman rises for a lady. I put it in the column where I keep such things, and went round the table to the far side, so that the baize and the lantern lay between us.

I had thought for eleven days about this room, what I would say in it and what I would do with my hands. What I did was remember the wire room. You do not argue with a caller. You read it back to him, address by address, until he stops telling you that you have it wrong.

“I’ll read it back,” I said. “Two-oh-five on the morning of the fifth, the operator rings 806 for Santa Barbara. Seventy-five minutes, eighteen dollars and seventy-five cents. Miss Honor Calder says you talked for ten and she put the receiver on her pillow. Mrs. Nugent at the exchange plugged in at twenty to three. A clock at your end, and nobody breathing.”

He took up the silver pencil. “Conjecture,” he said, and made a small mark in the margin of the ledger, as though I were a figure he was checking.

A long way off the Heifer called, two notes, low. I counted forty and went on.

“Rx forty-one eight seventy-two. Chloral hydrate, five-grain, number sixty, seventh refill, the twenty-eighth of October. Your name in Mr. Sorkin’s book, and the bottle in Teddy Wozniak’s locker came off that refill.”

“Hearsay.” The pencil ticked.

“Your ink. It dries rust-brown. The pass you signed me, the slip in Maher’s hatband, the receipt for the Esther Vane.”

“It is a very old formula.” I will swear there was a warmth in it. “Dorset.”

“A tall man in a dark red quilted gown, shiny at the shoulders, on the eighth floor at ten past midnight. A tray, two glasses, the key already in his hand. Walking faster than an old man ought.”

“Possible.”

“Two glasses on nine and none in 807. Maher’s shoes off on nine and on in 807. You and Joe put them on him, and you forgot the sock.”

“Possible,” said Mr. Quill again, and marked the margin.

It was somewhere about the third of these that I understood he was not defending himself. He was auditing me. Each entry I read out he took as a senior takes a junior’s column, with courtesy and without hope, sustaining it or striking it, and what I could not forgive was that I would have given most of them the same marks. Everything I had was conjecture, or hearsay, or possible. A good deal of the world is.

“The cane,” I said. I looked at it across his knees. “Twenty years of a bad hip, they tell me. A man who leans on a stick wears the tip down on one side. Yours is as round as a new pencil eraser. You have never put your weight on it.”

He looked down at it. “I take care of my things.”

“Joe Lambert.” My mouth had gone dry. “A man who spends his evening greasing the guide rails, with an oiler full to the spout and not a smear on his palms. You hit him with it, and you put him in the pit.”

Mr. Quill laid the pencil in the gutter of the ledger and looked at the lantern. For the whole of the Heifer’s forty seconds he did not move, not a finger, and I could hear the flame ticking on its wick, and under the floor the old hotel going about its holiday. “I was very fond of Joseph,” he said.

It was the only answer of the evening that I felt in my hands.

“The Esther Vane,” I said, when I could. “Thirty-one cases, personal effects. Received by the Trustee.”

“I invoiced them.”

“They were people.”

“The insurers required a signature.”

I would have liked to hit him with something. I looked down and found that my hands were holding my father’s Waltham, turning it round and round on the bone with the face to the inside of my wrist. It said twenty-seven minutes past seven.

“And Teddy,” I said. “You sat on his bunk with a rug and told him about his sister’s papers. He signed with a chewed pencil and died with his knees drawn up.”

Mr. Quill took a moment over it, as over a figure he had not expected to find in that column. “The Estate,” he said, “has outlived four generations of Calders. It can outlive a night clerk.”

The Heifer called, and I let it go by uncounted, because I had run out of ways to ask the same man the same question, and I laid down the only card I had left.

“Sergeant Dolan is outside.”

“I doubt it.” He closed the ledger over the pencil, gently, as one shuts a prayer book, and laid his long yellow hands on the cover. “Judge Pardoe keeps the holiday with his sister at Stannard’s Ferry. She has no telephone; Mr. Swain was good enough to let me know. The sergeant is a punctual man and an honest one, and I think he is in a motor-car on a country road with a District Attorney, waiting to be handed a signature.”

“The manifest isn’t behind the frame any more,” I said. “It’s in Hollis Barnwell’s safe. You can burn this floor and every ledger in Port Calder, Mr. Quill, and a half-sheet with your name on it will go on being there.”

He did not answer. The Heifer called, and I counted forty, the whole of it, and he sat with his hands flat on the green cloth and his pale eyes on the lantern, and I watched him add it up. It took him no time at all. The figure had been in front of him for hours. Then he stood, with a small creak of the knees, and laid the cane over his forearm, and picked up the can.

“A fire in a roof space is a thing one insures against, my dear,” he said, and began to pour. He did it as a man waters a plant, unhurried, a little at a time: along the baize, down the leg of the table, across the boards toward the cot that stood pulled out from the wall with a dent in its mattress the shape of a sleeping man. “The brigade will be at the cornice in six minutes.”

The smell stopped being a smell. It became the room.

I kicked the lantern. It stood on the floor between his shoes and mine and I had been looking at it for half an hour. It went over on its side with the glass starred, and the flame sat on the wet boards for the length of a breath, and then it ran, quick and blue along the track he had laid, and the baize went up with a sound like a sheet shaken out of a window.

Mr. Quill stepped back out of it with the care of a man avoiding a puddle. There was not a mark on his dinner jacket. He did not hurry. He was through the panel with the cane over his arm before I had got round the table, and the oak swung to behind him, and I heard the iron fall into its brackets with the small bright sound of a latch on a good gate.

The ledger lay on the baize in the path of the fire. I thought of nothing at all and took it, five pounds of green cloth already hot at one corner, and shoved it inside my coat against my ribs. Then I put my shoulder to the panel. It gave the width of a finger and stopped against iron.

Down in the stair, as if down a well, the cane began to go.

I counted it. There is nothing else to do with a sound like that. A man who is hurried drags, and a man who limps puts the stick down early to take the weight. This was neither. The tip met every tread flat and level with a pause between that a clock would have been proud of, and I have never in my life heard anything go down a stair so well.

One, and I kicked the panel low, where an iron bar is weakest, and the iron was not weak.

Two, and the baize was a sheet of flame to the ceiling and my face tightened in it like a drumhead.

Three was the safe. I put my head into it: pigeonholes, eighteen inches of steel, a door that would swing home on me and be a coffin with a good lock. I took my head out.

Four was the corridor. The oil had run ahead of the fire down the grey felt runner and into the doorways of the dormitories, and when I put the flashlight along it the cots stood in their rows with their blankets shining, rank on rank, forty-two of them, and the flame coming after me down the felt as fast as a man walks.

Five was the wall telephone. I lifted the earpiece and there was not even a hiss. The cord had been cut at the skirting that afternoon, and the copper end shone like a new penny.

Six, and the loose tread spoke under him, a small dry crack like a knuckle, exactly as it had spoken under me. The cane did not falter.

Seven was the kitchenette. A laundry copper bolted to the floor, a bench, a gas ring, a row of enamel mugs with names inked on their sides, and above the bench a louvre painted black on the inside, a yard above my reach.

Eight, and the first of the cots caught. It took the flame with a cough, and then, a second later, with another.

Nine was the wall. The left side of the corridor, where the names were. The fire reached the plaster and the lime on it browned, and the chalk went from white to the colour of weak tea: Wacław, Halina, Józef, Rūta; Irena, with her date; JANEK, BASIA and ZUZIA under their drawing of a ship. I had held a torch to them once for as long as it takes to say a rosary and had not copied one down. They turned the colour of old paper. Then they turned the colour of nothing.

Ten, eleven and twelve were smoke. I went down on my knees where the air was, a hand’s breadth off the boards, and I thought of Teddy squaring a pencil on a blotter, and of my mother’s oven, and of nothing.

Thirteen, and I came back to the panel on my hands and knees, since it was the one place on that floor I knew.

Fourteen, and I laid my ear against the oak and heard the last of them, far below, on the tile of the linen cupboard, and then a door.

I know it took longer than fourteen steps. A man cannot walk down a stair in the time it takes to watch a wall of names go out. But that is how I have kept it, the whole of that minute, put in order by a stick: fourteen taps, level as a metronome, the loose tread taken without a hitch. A man who leans on a cane wears the tip down on one side. He had never leaned on his in his life. There was no limp in him anywhere.

chapters.title: The Cornice
chapters.html:
The paint on the louvre was blistering.

I watched it from the kitchenette floor, where the air was, a hand’s breadth above the linoleum: a black skin on a slat of fired clay, a yard over my head and out of my reach, rising in small bubbles like the skin on boiled milk and splitting one by one, and under every split a point of orange the size of a pin. It was the only window the ninth floor had. Somebody in 1929 had built a card room in the roof of a hotel and painted the vents black on the inside so that the lamps would not show in Front Street, and in twenty-three years nobody had thought of anything better.

Behind me the fire had the Club room, and the corridor, and the dormitories on either side of it. I did not turn to look. I knew the sound, a long ragged roar like a flag in a gale, with a counterpoint of small ticks and pops that were the iron cots letting go of their paint. The smoke had come down off the ceiling to the height of a standing woman’s chin, so I stayed low. It was not black, as I had expected. It was brown, the colour of strong tea, and it tasted of lamp oil and of my own hair.

I got up on the bench. The enamel mugs stood along the back of it with their names inked on their sides, and they had begun to sweat. I put my back to the wall and my flat shoe to the lowest slat, and kicked.

The clay went in, three slats and then four, a rain of black flakes, and the iron frame held. I kicked the frame. It squealed on its pins. I kicked it again, and the whole panel left the wall in one piece and dropped out into the fog, and for as long as it takes to say it I heard nothing at all; then, a long way down, a flat clang in the yard. Cold air came in at the hole like a hand, and the fire behind me stood up to meet it.

The hole was two feet by eighteen inches, with the frame still standing round it. I wound my mother’s grey scarf round my right hand and took the iron in my left, bare, because there was not enough scarf for both, and the iron burned. I will not describe it. I will say that I did not let go, which is a different thing from being brave.

I went through on my side, one shoulder and then the other, with the ledger in my coat catching on the frame, until I lay along a ledge on my belly with my legs still inside. Then I drew them out. A tongue of flame leaned from the hole after me and went up into the fog.

The ledge was two feet wide, wet terracotta, sloped a degree outward for the rain, with a fish on every foot of it. Below me there was nothing. I mean that as a measurement: eight floors of it, and the cobbles of Ferry Slip Row at the bottom, and a fog thick enough to lean on, so that if I fell I should at least be spared the sight. I stood up, which took three tries, and put my face to the Frieze and my arms along it. The fish were carp, or something near them, a foot long, with their lips pursed in relief, and each had a lip a hand could close on. Between them rose the terracotta waves, ridged like a washboard and no use to anyone.

I went east. I did not know how far I thought the corner was.

I counted the fish. It was not a habit that night. It was a handrail. Hand over hand, shuffle, one; the lip of the next, shuffle, two. By nine the louvre beside my face had begun to glow. At fourteen a slat spat a flake of burning paint past my ear. At twenty the whole band behind me lit, from the inside, the louvres going from black to dull red to orange one after another down the south face, so that I edged along the rim of a lampshade with the colour coming through the fog onto the back of my neck, and the Frieze I had stared at from the kerb for three weeks stood out before my eyes in perfect relief: the waves, the fish, my own fingers closing on a lip. In the wall the roar went up a tone.

At thirty-one the ledge turned a corner, and my left hand found two iron staples set in the clay, wet as dock rope. I am aware of what number that was. I did not remark on it to the fish.

The ladder was the eleven rungs I had climbed on the eighth of November in the rain, with a lantern talking behind a louvre. I could not close my hands on them. I hooked my forearms over each rung instead and let my feet find the next, like a woman going down a well with a sack of flour in each arm. Eleven. My shoes met the grating outside the eighth-floor end window. It had been an eventful month, I thought, and I was not sure which of us had come further, the grating or I.

The bell began while I stood there. Not the electric kind. A hand bell, brass, swung by a woman who had swung it once a year in a drill for twenty-six years and never once for real, and who swung it now as though she had been waiting for the chance.

I went down the fire escape with my forearms on the rail. At every landing the window beside me was lit, and in the window someone was being walked briskly to the stairs: a maid in grey, a guest in a dressing gown and a hat, an old lady carrying her teeth in her hand, each shepherded by one of Pearl’s girls in a white apron with a clipboard, from the top down, with a bell. Pearl told me afterward that she had begun with nine. “There was nobody on nine, Miss Hightower.” “I know that,” she said. “It is the habit of six years.” Ninety-one steps, I had counted going up, and I counted them going down, and the answer was ninety-one, which was the first thing that had gone right all evening.

The yard was full of people. Kitchen hands in white, maids in grey with their coats thrown over, thirty guests in dressing gowns and furs and hats, standing in the order Pearl had given them, in a fog the colour of a lampshade. Above them the light well was a shaft of orange cloud. In the kitchen door, with a clipboard in the crook of one arm and the ring of forty keys silent in her fist, stood Pearl herself, counting heads under her breath.

The service door beside the laundry chute opened on the yard as I reached the last landing, and a tall man in a dinner jacket came out of it with a cane over his forearm and walked into the crowd at the pace of a man leaving a restaurant where he has dined well. Nobody looked at him. Everyone was looking up. A tall old gentleman leaving a fire is the most natural thing in the world; there is always one. He turned toward the mouth of the alley and Ferry Slip Row, and I let go of the last rail, and dropped the last six feet, and landed in front of him.

He cleared his throat, once. For the first time in my acquaintance with him, he did not do it twice.

His eyes went to my face, which I had not seen and which must have been something, and then down to the front of my coat, where five pounds of green cloth made a square bulge under the belt. I watched him read it. I think it was the only time I ever saw him lose a figure.

The cane came up in his right hand, the silver collar level with his shoulder, as a man lifts his stick to hail a cab or tip a hat. It stayed there for a count of two. Then it came down.

“Mr. Quill.”

Dolan stood in the mouth of the alley with his hat on the back of his head and no matchstick. Karras was at his shoulder with the notebook put away at last, and two uniformed men behind them with the fog on their capes. He was looking not at us but up, over the roof of the kitchen wing, where the fog above the light well glowed like the inside of a lantern and the Frieze stood out in it, a band of orange light over eight rows of dark windows. Nine, if you counted it. Dolan counted it.

“I count nine.”

“The plans say eight, Sergeant,” said Mr. Quill.

“Plans lie.”

Karras stepped round me and took Mr. Quill’s wrists, one and then the other, the way one takes a pair of gloves from a shelf, and the cuffs closed. Mr. Quill allowed it. He held out his hands as a man holds them out to be measured, and the cane, which had been over his arm, slid off it and struck the cobbles with a small clean sound and rolled and lay at my feet in the light from the kitchen door. I looked at the tip. A perfect disc of grey rubber, flat and round and dry, as unmarked as the day he bought it.

“Ambrose Quill,” said Dolan. He said it as he had said Teddy’s name in the lobby, reading out a bill he had not run up. “I’m holding you for the deaths of Declan Maher and Josiah Lambert, and for the setting of a fire in the Harbor Hotel with a woman in it, and for whatever else Mr. Barnwell finds by morning. You can have a lawyer. I’d get one that isn’t Swain.”

Mr. Quill said nothing at all. Not a word that meant nothing, either.

Pearl crossed the yard with the clipboard against her chest and the keys silent in her fist, and stood in front of him. For twenty-six years she had been invisible to him, and she let him see her. “Mr. Quill,” she said. “Forty-six, with the kitchen. Every one counted out by me. I shall count them in.” She turned back to her door. He had no answer, and I do not think he expected one.

“Seven-thirty,” I said to Dolan. “You said seven-thirty.”

“It’s eight minutes to eight.” He looked at my hands. His face did what it had done on my landing at five in the morning, once, and stopped. “Pardoe signed on his sister’s porch step with a pencil at twenty to. I’ve got it in my pocket. It’s the best paper I ever carried, and it came half an hour late.”

“The law’s always late, Frank.”

“I know,” he said. “It’s what I’m for.”

I took the green ledger out of my coat and gave it to him. The corner was scorched. “The Estate’s receipts,” I said. “Footed. I believe it balances.”

Dolan took it in both freckled hands. Mr. Quill, between Karras and the constable, looked at his own ledger in the sergeant’s grip, and then not.

Lucille Fong came round the corner of Ferry Slip Row at a trot, in a man’s overcoat that touched her ankles, with a second coat folded over her arm. Her glasses were pushed up on her forehead and one end of a scarf was trailing. She stopped when she saw the yard, and the glow, and me.

“You said eight,” she said. “It’s four minutes to. I’m early.” She held up the coat. “Pa says you are to put your arms in it and not tell him about it. He cut it the day you came to lunch. He said it was a professional embarrassment to leave a left shoulder like that to Sears.”

It was grey herringbone, lined in black sateen, and it fit. It fit in the left shoulder, which cannot be said of any garment I have worn since I was nine. Lucille put it round me, because my arms would not go into sleeves, and buttoned it to the neck as if I were six, and then she saw my hands.

“Ruth.”

“They’ll heal.”

“Ruth.” She had her mouth shut hard, and the chipped tooth showed on the lip. “I’m going to sit down.” She sat on an upturned bucket in a yard full of strangers with her father’s overcoat bunched about her, and pulled her glasses down onto her nose, and watched the fire with the fixed attention of a woman reading very small print.

I went round to Front Street through the people in dressing gowns, to see the hotel from the kerb where I had stood on the fifth of November and counted its floors.

The brigade had come up Front Street with its bell going, Engine Company Four, two lines run to the hydrant at Ferry Slip Row and a third up the ladder truck to the cornice. They had been at it in six minutes from the first bell, by my father’s Waltham. I looked at the dial twice. He had been right about that, too.

The Heifer sounded. I counted forty out of habit, and was glad, in a plain way, of the habit.

A hose played along the Frieze in a long white arc. The louvres, which had been red, went black again where the water touched them, and then, one after another along the band, the slats gave up their frames and fell, steaming, into the street, like tiles off a kitchen wall. Each one took a name with it. I knew which, and I stood in Walter Fong’s coat with my hands wrapped in Lucille’s handkerchief and my face wet and watched them go.

I will say what I felt, because a book that leaves it out is lying. I was glad. A wall of chalk names is evidence. Evidence is photographed and numbered and carried into court on an easel, and every Rūta and Halina in the Port Calder directory would have been a name a clerk could look up and a man from the Service could find. The fire was thorough, and I was grateful. And while I was grateful I thought of a small hand holding a stub of chalk to plaster at the height of a child’s coat hook, and it did not help.

At about nine the ash began to come down. It came out of the glow where the Frieze had been, grey flakes as light as moth wings, turning over and over through the fog onto the roofs of the cars and the shoulders of the firemen and the hat brims of the crowd. A boy near me put out a hand and caught one. It was a small curl of burned paper with a ruled line across it, from a saints’ calendar or a card-room ledger or a child’s drawing of a train; nobody will ever know. He looked at it and blew it off his palm, and it went up and came down again on Front Street with the rest.

It fell all that night, soft and grey, like paper snow, and there was not a word on any of it.

chapters.title: What the Keeper Keeps
chapters.html:
My hands were wrapped to the wrists in gauze, so that I held the fork between two bandaged fingers the way a man holds a cigarette in a boxing glove, and it went toward the plate and missed.

“Open,” said my mother, and I opened, and a piece of turkey arrived.

She had refused on principle to cook a bird on Thursday, a holiday for Presbyterians, and had bought one on Friday morning at twenty-nine cents the pound, the price having fallen overnight with the patriotism. It was a good bird. I was thirty-six years old and had walked out along a cornice in a fog, and I sat at my mother’s table with a napkin tucked into my collar and was fed like a canary, and I have known worse mornings. The rain had come back in the night, like a relative. The Beacon lay on the third chair with its front page folded in, because Helena would not have QUILL HELD in the room while we ate.

“Eat,” she said, with the fork. “A woman who walks on cornices should have something under her.”

At ten I sat on the steps of Central Station beside Frank Dolan, under the stone lintel that keeps off half the rain, and he put a cruller between two of my bandaged fingers as he had put doughnuts on my desk in November, and neither of us mentioned it.

I had told him on Thursday night, in a ward at Municipal, with my hands in gauze the colour of tea. The Royal. Under the felt. I did not say take it. I said where it was, which for four years I had told no living person, and it came to the same thing. He went himself. The superintendent of the Selkirk stood by in his slippers and signed across the flap of the envelope, and Dolan said the felt had been warm, which I said was impossible, and he said he knew.

“Barnwell has it in the safe beside the manifest,” he said now. “He read it standing up. He said it was a very well typed log.”

“It’s a good machine.”

“He said it would do.” He counted on his freckled fingers, as he does, with the Beacon folded on his knee. “Quill. Arraigned at eight, held without bail for Maher, for Lambert, for the fire and for the fraud, which Barnwell has a long word for. Tea in his cell. He asked for a pen and they gave him a pencil. He looked at it a good while and wrote nothing.”

“Swain.”

“Came in at eight with a lawyer of his own and his cufflinks in his pocket. Talked three hours and never asked a question, which I’m told is a first. Two hall men, Mulcahy and Reese, hired through a hiring boss at Quill’s word to turn your mother’s flat inside out. Those are your boots.” He moved to the next finger. “Plum resigned by telegram to the City Clerk at six this morning, owing to a conflagration of circumstance. He used inadvertical twice. Ferrante walked up to Barnwell’s front door yesterday, between the turkey and the pie, with an orange and a lawyer, in that order, and the grand jury sat at ten. He’ll go down for the hall’s share and talk for the rest, and Barnwell says the orange was the most honest thing he has been handed this year. Pomeroy has sent the Estate’s receiver a cheque for sixty-three dollars and fourteen cents.”

“For what?”

“Fourteen hams. Eleven pounds apiece, at forty-one cents the pound. There’s a letter on Division stationery. The receiver has never in his life been sent a cheque for ham.”

He unfolded the Beacon across his knee and showed me the foot of the front page. WOZNIAK CLEARED, it said, in the same type they had used for CONFESSED SLAYING TWO, over four lines of regret that did not use the word sorry. “They set it the same size,” said Dolan. “I’ll give them that.”

“And yours?”

“Your licence. Swain withdrew the complaint at nine, and the Board’s letter is on its way to the Selkirk by the hand of the thin woman in the grey suit, who I’m told is mortified and doesn’t look it.” The matchstick went from one side of his mouth to the other. “Rafferty is being served this afternoon in Santa Cruz, with any luck holding a fishing rod. And Haskell called me in at eight. For the good of the service. I go at Christmas, with a letter. The pension goes with the badge. The Board’s rule is that a man who takes three hundred dollars out of a captain’s hand has no claim on the fund.”

“Is that a rule?”

“It is now. I’d have written it myself.”

The rain came off the lintel in a thin curtain a yard in front of our shoes. Beyond the side gate lay forty yards of wet brick under an arc lamp, and I did not look at it.

“Didn’t you want to be a lieutenant?” I said.

“I wanted to be somebody I could stand.” He considered the matchstick. “It’s a smaller ambition, and a good deal harder to make rank in.”

I ate the cruller. It took some time. He waited, and did not help.

Union Station at eleven on Saturday night is a hall of varnished benches under a ceiling that has been collecting soot since 1911, and the night train north stood at Track Four with its steam going up into the roof like a cloud that had lost its way. Yvette waited by the gate in a coat the colour of oatmeal, bought off a rack on Third with Deacon Tolliver’s sister standing guard. She had a cardboard suitcase, a ticket, and no gloves.

I had seen her bare hands in my mother’s kitchen, the bitten nails, but never in a public place, never held out before her like something she was carrying. She turned them over once, as though to check that they were hers.

“You won’t tell me,” I said. “The name.”

“I will tell no one. That is the point of it, Miss Szymanski.” The Polish l came through on the word, and she let it. She smiled, the first whole smile I had seen from her, and it made the scar on her chin go crooked. “Marchand, like people who sell things. I have sold what I had. Write it however you like. I have written it myself.”

My mother, who had stood all this time with a parcel in both arms like a woman at a christening, pushed it at her. “Bread. A person who goes north without bread arrives in a bad mood.” Yvette took the parcel and then took my mother, and the two of them stood in the middle of Union Station in their coats, the tall one bent, the short one on tiptoe, saying things to each other in Polish that I did not translate for myself. My mother’s glasses were pushed up on her forehead. She was crying without noise, in the Polish manner, as a tap runs.

Yvette gave me her gloves. They were the white cotton ones she had sung in, washed and starched and folded into a square. I tried to take them with my bandaged fingers and could not, and she laughed, a low surprised laugh, and put them in the pocket of Walter Fong’s coat and patted the pocket flat.

She did not wave from the window. She laid her bare hands on the glass and kept them there while the train took her out from under the roof. Lucille, who had come straight from the Commission with her pencil in her hair, stood beside me and watched the red lamp on the last car go out in the dark.

“A paper son’s daughter would keep it,” she said, to the track. “I’m only saying.”

“I know.”

“You don’t. I’ve never said it. I want to hear if it works out loud.” She lifted her chin. “Lau. That’s the name. It’s been Lau since a boat in 1909, and I have not said it in this city. Say it back to me. So it’s not lost.”

I knew what she was asking. We had sat eight years on one headset, and she knew that I knew. “Lau,” I said. “Say again. Lau.”

“Received,” said Lucille Fong, and took off her glasses and wiped them on her sleeve, and did not look at me for the whole length of the platform.

The first Sunday of Advent at St. Casimir’s is purple and rain and one candle. Frank Dolan stood at the top of the church steps through the whole of the High Mass, the sexton told my mother afterward, with his hat in both hands and a brown paper bag in the crook of his arm, and was wet to the knee. He does not go into churches. He stands where he can see the street.

Bronia came out on my mother’s arm with the handbag held in both hands, and Dolan went down a step to meet her. “Mrs. Kowal.”

She stopped. He held out the bag. It had a property tag on a string, T. WOZNIAK, in a clerk’s hand. She took it and opened it and looked in, and took out a tin pillbox, small and round and dented at the lid, and held it in her palm. Then she shook it once, gently, the way you shake a purse to learn whether a coin remains, and it rattled. She said nothing. She opened the steel clasp of the handbag and put the tin inside, in the place where the book had been.

“He said you were a polite policeman,” she said.

“I was a slow one,” said Dolan.

“Yes,” said Bronia Kowal. She did not say it unkindly. It was an entry, and she was a woman who had kept a ledger.

Then she turned to me and took my bandaged wrists, one in each small hand, as carefully as if I were a pair of eggs. “A book wants a keeper,” she said, “not a shelf.”

“I’ll put it where it can’t be found.”

“By them.” Her rimless spectacles caught the rain. “Not by you.”

Dolan put on his hat and went down the steps and into the street without another word, which for him was a speech.

Odessa Lambert stood at the iron gate in her black felt hat, with her hands folded over a handbag of her own, as straight as she had stood at Calvary. She had been waiting, I think, since the nine o’clock. Joe taught me to wait, she had said, and I had promised her a sentence to go with a piece of brass.

I gave her the key. It hung on the shoelace he had worn for twenty years, and it had lain in my pocket for seventeen days, against a clasp and a glove. Then I told her all of it, there at the gate, with the Sunday traffic going by: the cab, the plug, the ninth floor and who had lived on it, the night he carried a man down a stair, what he said to me on the telephone from the drugstore booth, and the oiler, and the pit, and what I took from his neck. I did not make it shorter. She listened without moving, the left forefinger with its needle callus lying along the clasp of her bag.

When I had finished she took the shoelace and let the key hang in the rain, turning.

“He hummed ‘Abide with Me’ for six years straight,” said Odessa Lambert, “and I never once asked him why.”

I had no answer to that, and she did not wait for one. She closed her hand on the key.

That evening my mother set the first wafer of Advent on the oilcloth and broke it with me, as she has every year since I was four, and wished me health, and that I eat, and did not look at my hands.

At nine I took the book up to the roof of 1127 Hake. It was fourteen stairs to the landing and eight iron rungs to the scuttle, and I counted them and did not mind. I carried the book against my chest in the crook of both arms, as my mother had carried it out of the oven.

It had stopped raining for an hour, as it does before it starts again. The roof was tar and gravel and wet, with a chimney stack I sat in the lee of, and the Flats lay below me in their small lights, and past them Front Street, and past that the Sound. There was no fog, so there was no Heifer. I found that I missed it. Ten blocks off the Harbor stood with its eight rows of windows, and the black band above them was dark all the way along, with sky in it where the louvres had been.

Calder Point had its light. Every twelve seconds it came round across the Flats, white and quick, and for the length of a breath the roof of 1127 Hake lit like a stage and the page in my lap whitened. I turned the book to it and read what it gave me, and waited for the next.

Pod Twoją Obronę. Under Your Protection. On the first of the blank leaves at the back, in pencil, in the upright hand of a sexton who believed that a man who writes a false name in a holy book lies to God: Nowak, four souls. Aegina. St Lucy’s day. Nine days upstairs. Offering, none. And under it, as small as a thing said under the breath: Pan Bóg zapłać. May the Lord repay it.

I counted the names. Twenty-eight to a page, eleven full pages and three lines on the twelfth, the sum that Teddy had given me in his flat over the bakery with his back turned, boiling milk. Three hundred and eleven. I ran my bandaged finger down every line and the number came out right.

I stopped. A number is what you give a policeman. It is what Quill gave the Estate, and what the pier shed gave Ferrante; it is the thing you say when you have stopped looking at the face. I shut the book on my finger, and the light came round and went, and in the dark I sat with the rain starting again on my hat.

Then I opened it at the front and began again. This time I did not count. I read them aloud, one at a time, to the roofs and the lamps and the Sound, the way you read an address back on the wire so that the man at the other end knows it has been received.

“Nowak,” I said. “Say again. Nowak.”

A week later the State Division of Elevators sent Hubert Pomeroy to the Harbor with a clipboard, a screwdriver and a new frame under his arm. He stood in the lobby on the first dry morning in a fortnight and watched a man from Otis cut a ninth button into the car panel, beneath the 8, where the plug had been: round, brass, the size of a half dollar, with a numeral on its face. A second man with a fine brush painted a 9 on the dial over the door, where for twenty-six years the needle had swung onto nothing. Pomeroy read the certificate aloud to nobody, in the voice of a man who has been frightened and found it clarifying. LANDINGS SERVED: 9. FLOORS OPEN TO THE PUBLIC: 8. The second line stayed, because the ninth was a floor of black boards and bare iron with the sky showing through the louvres. The first line was no longer a secret. He said it was the only certificate he had ever signed that he had read.

The Estate was in the hands of a receiver, a nervous man named Gruber, who had found within an hour of arriving that the only person in the building who knew where anything was kept was the head housekeeper. By the Tuesday Pearl Hightower was acting manager. She rode up in the car with Pomeroy to see. I did not go in. I stood on the pavement of Front Street in the thin sun, with my hands in the pockets of Walter Fong’s coat, one of them closed on a pair of white gloves, and looked up.

From the kerb where I had counted, the hotel stood with its eight rows of windows clean in the light, and above them the cornice, and in the band of the Frieze the louvres were gone and the open holes ran along the whole front like the eyes of a mask, with sky in them. Sparrows had already found the sills. The waves and the fish still ran beneath, carp with their lips pursed, a foot long, in perfect order. A man beside me looked where I was looking and said to his wife that he had never noticed the top of that building before, and that it was quite a handsome piece of work.

A quarter of an hour later Pearl came out through the revolving door. The ring of forty keys was on her wrist, and she did not hold it in her fist. They chimed at every step, all forty, as loud as a sleigh in the dry cold, down the length of the steps and along the kerb. She stopped beside me and looked up where I was looking.

“The floor will want new boards,” she said. “The copper is sound.”

“Is that all?”

“I do not guess, Miss Szymanski. I counted.” She did not say what. She went on along Front Street toward the kitchen door with the keys going, and a passer-by turned to stare, and she let him.

I stayed where I was a good while, in the thin sun. Eight rows of windows. The Frieze. The sky in the Frieze. There was nothing to add up. A man went by with a pram, and a streetcar, and out beyond the ferry slip a ferry sounded, low and long. I let it go by. I did not count.
